1492: Mary Johnston's 1922 novel about Columbus and the discovery of the New World, told with her usual historical richness. Adventure, court intrigue, and the great voyage fill a sweeping narrative. The author of To Have and to Hold at her most ambitious.
20304-a-trip-to-paris-in-july-and-august:
A Trip to Paris in July and August 1792 is a firsthand travel account. The writer had three reasons for going to France that summer. He wished to test whether living in France might suit him. He also expected a counter-revolution or violent measures very soon.

He wanted to be there, if he could, at that great moment. Third, he wished to examine the gardens near Paris in detail. Weeks later, the monarchy fell in blood, which he nearly foresaw. Readers get an Englishman's calm notes from the edge of revolution.
20319-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, the London Charivari, for December 31, 1892, closes volume one hundred and three. A comic author laments that his works are a drug in the market. A new set of men has come to the front since his day. In twelve months he has sold barely a dozen pages of work.

Worse, those pages ran in a magazine that soon stopped printing. Punch mixed such jokes with cartoons, verse, and sharp social comment weekly. Its year-end numbers summed up the season with wit and bite. Readers get Victorian humor at its most famous address, Fleet Street's Punch.
20338-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, the London Charivari, for December 24, 1892, is a Christmas number of the comic weekly. Guests at a dinner served in the Russian style sit sad and bored. They have sent a policeman after itinerant street musicians outside. Inside and outside, silence reigns triumphant over the whole dull house.

Was it not a time for moving on, the joke asks dryly. Six weeks without the option of a fine was the standard threat then. Punch loved to mock dull parties and pompous hosts each week. Readers get a festive slice of Victorian satire, crisp and brief.
20759-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, the famed London comic weekly, fills its December 10, 1892 issue with sharp talk. One piece mocks the grievance monger as the worst of all bores. A man ruined by spite, it says, will still be shunned if he bores all ears with his wrongs.

Jokes, verse, cartoons, and sly takes on the news fill each Punch number. The London Charivari, its subtitle, promised fun at the cost of the proud. This single issue freezes one week of Victorian wit in print. Readers can taste what made London laugh, and what it laughed at, in late 1892.
21028-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Gold and silver have nothing to do with each other, snaps a voice in Punch for December 17, 1892. Fixing a ratio between them cannot mend money woes, the squib insists. Bimetallism, then a hot cause, takes Punch's comic fire this week.

Volume 103's late December number keeps Punch's mix of jokes, verse, and cuts at the great. Money, politics, and social folly all feed its weekly wit. One dated issue like this is a time capsule with jokes still in it. Readers taste the exact humour London shared in the last weeks of 1892.
ambrose-of-milan-concerning-repentance-n:
Rigorists taught that serious sin after baptism could never be forgiven, and Ambrose of Milan answered with mercy. Concerning Repentance insists that no sin places a person beyond restoration. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Peter denied Christ three times and was restored to lead the Church; Ambrose builds his case on such stories. Tears, confession, and changed conduct mark the road back, he says. The book rebukes despair as firmly as it rebukes carelessness. Its teaching became a cornerstone of the Church's doctrine of forgiveness. Pastoral theology at its most merciful speaks from these pages, and the argument still matters.
ambrose-of-milan-concerning-virgins-npnf:
Marcellina, Ambrose's own sister, took the veil as a consecrated virgin, and her brother wrote Concerning Virgins for her and women like her. The three books praise the virgin life in rich biblical imagery. They appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

The practical effect astonished even Milan: young women flocked to the consecrated life after Ambrose preached this teaching. Fervent in tone, the treatise shaped the Western ideal of holy virginity for centuries. Ambrose presents dedication as freedom and joy rather than mere refusal. Modern readers may argue with parts, but the book's influence is beyond dispute. It also offers a rare window on women's religious choices in the ancient city.
ambrose-of-milan-concerning-widows-npnf2:
Widows received their own companion volume from Ambrose of Milan, Concerning Widows. Where the earlier book praised virgins, this one counsels women who had lost husbands on the dignity of their state. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Ambrose treats widowhood as freedom for devotion, prayer, and generous giving. Practical advice covers raising children, managing households, and resisting pressure to remarry too fast. The tone stays compassionate and respectful throughout. Ancient pastoral care for women rarely sounds this attentive to real circumstances. Readers meet a bishop who knew his flock by name and circumstance. The counsel reflects long experience at actual bedsides and doors.
ambrose-of-milan-exposition-of-the-chris:
A young emperor asked for instruction, and Ambrose of Milan wrote him a five-book defense of the faith. The Exposition of the Christian Faith, prepared for Gratian, appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Its target is Arianism, then strong at the imperial court.

Ambrose draws arguments from every corner of scripture to prove Christ's full divinity. A bishop instructing an emperor makes this imperial theology in the plainest sense. The writing stays clear and forceful even when the doctrine runs deep. Historically, the book helped turn the court toward the Nicene confession. Few treatises show so well how teaching and power met in the ancient Church.
ambrose-of-milan-on-the-duties-of-the-cl:
Cicero wrote a famous handbook on duty for Roman gentlemen; Ambrose of Milan adapted the idea for clergy. On the Duties of the Clergy tells priests and bishops how to speak, act, handle money, and serve their people. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Practical wisdom fills the pages, drawn from a bishop who faced down emperors and fed his city in crisis. Ambrose taught Augustine, and something of that mentoring voice survives here. The book became the first Christian manual of pastoral ethics. Modern pastors still recognize its situations: flattery, funds, factions, and fatigue. Few ancient handbooks feel this usable across so many centuries.
ambrose-of-milan-on-the-holy-spirit-npnf:
Milan's Arian party denied that the Holy Spirit is fully God, and Ambrose answered in three books. On the Holy Spirit argues the Spirit's divinity straight from scripture. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Ambrose shows the Spirit at work in creation, prophecy, and baptism with the powers of God himself. The treatise helped secure the West's Trinitarian faith at a contested moment. Augustine learned much of his theology from Ambrose's preaching, and works like this one show the master at his desk. Careful readers will note how often worship supplies his best arguments. The book remains a model of calm, biblical defense.
ambrose-of-milan-on-the-mysteries-npnf2-:
Newly baptized Christians at Milan received a short, luminous guide to what had just happened to them. Ambrose's On the Mysteries explains baptism, confirmation, and the Eucharist to the fresh initiates. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Water, oil, bread, and cup become signs loaded with meaning as Ambrose unveils them step by step. He treats the rites as gifts to be wondered at, not puzzles to be solved. The tone stays warm and awed throughout the brief treatise. Many judges rank it among the most beautiful introductions to Christian worship ever written. First-time readers of the fathers often start here and are glad they did.
ambrose-of-milan-select-letters-of-st-am:
Emperors, bishops, and friends all appear in the Select Letters of Saint Ambrose, a chosen set from his wide correspondence. The letters appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Church and empire collide in several of the most famous of them.

Ambrose rebukes the emperor Theodosius after the massacre at Thessalonica and demands repentance from the most powerful man alive. Other letters defend church property and advise his flock on daily troubles. Together they show the bishop as statesman, the man who taught the West that emperors answer to God. Church-state history rarely comes from the hand of its maker. These letters are that rare thing.
aphrahat-the-demonstrations-of-aphrahat-:
Twenty-three treatises called Demonstrations came from Aphrahat, a Christian sage writing in Syriac inside the Persian Empire. The Demonstrations of Aphrahat the Persian Sage appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. He wrote in the 300s, far from the Greek-speaking schools of the Roman world.

Faith, love, prayer, fasting, and the last days each receive their own demonstration, built straight from scripture. Greek philosophy barely touches his pages; the flavor stays biblical and Semitic. His church lived under a rival empire, which gives his counsel on persecution real weight. The set stands as the oldest substantial Syriac Christian literature we have. It proves the faith had deep roots east of Rome remarkably early.
arxiv-2512-00292:
Delafossites are layered materials whose properties shift sharply with composition and stacking. Jovin Ryan Joseph, Do Hoon Kiem, Sinchul Yeom, and Mina Yoon build interpretable graph neural networks for them in 2025. The networks classify both structure and magnetism in these compounds.

Delafossites combine two metals with a chalcogen in a versatile family of quantum materials and layered oxides. Their usefulness depends on atomic detail that is hard to survey by hand. Interpretable predictions matter because materials scientists need reasons, not just labels, before spending months synthesizing a predicted compound. Graph networks fit materials naturally, since atoms and bonds already form a graph. Classification of both structure and magnetism in one model saves separate pipelines.
arxiv-2512-00692:
Kerry Seekamp studies a recent combinatorial game-like process in a 2025 math paper. In 2023, Defant introduced toric promotion, a cyclic cousin of Schützenberger's classic promotion operator. Promotion acts on labelings of a graph, shuffling the labels through a series of swaps called involutions.

Repeating toric promotion eventually cycles back to the start, and the size of that cycle is its orbit. Seekamp studies these orbits when the graph is a bridge sum, built by joining graphs with a single connecting edge. Understanding orbit sizes helps map the long-run behavior of the process, a basic question in dynamical combinatorics.
arxiv-2512-00792:
Liyu Zerihun wrote a 2025 paper on how much capacity vision transformers really use. These models are heavily over-parameterized, meaning they carry far more weights than the task may need. Yet the patterns they learn often sit in a much smaller, low-rank space.

Zerihun's framework estimates a model's intrinsic dimensionality, its effective rank. First, a full-size teacher model is trained. Then its weights are factorized at several ranks, and smaller student models learn from the teacher by distillation. Watching how accuracy changes with rank shows where the real capacity lies. That knowledge can guide leaner designs.
arxiv-2512-01192:
Bikai Gao and Atsushi Hosaka build a model for baryons in a 2025 particle physics paper. Baryons are particles made of three quarks, including the proton and neutron. A parity doublet model pairs each baryon with a partner of opposite parity, linked by the symmetry between left- and right-handed quarks.

Their linear realization uses the SU(3) flavor symmetry that groups quarks into families. They include certain chiral representations, built from triplets and sextets of quarks, while excluding the octet-based one. A term called the bad diquark plays a named role. Such models test how baryon masses arise from chiral symmetry.
arxiv-2512-01292:
Ngoc Huynh Trinh and co-authors study how to outline organs and growths in medical scans. Doctors need clear maps of scans to plan care. Hand maps take time, and one scan can be read in more than one fair way. A single fixed map hides that doubt.

The team uses a diffusion model that works in a small, squeezed space. The model can draw more than one fair map for the same scan. That range shows where the edge is clear and where it is not. Showing doubt in this way can help doctors judge when to trust a map.
arxiv-2512-01492:
Larosa and co-authors report first views of a cascade in velocity space near the Sun. In thin space plasma, hits between parts are rare. That lets fine traits form in how speeds are spread. A cascade of those traits is thought to flow to small scales.

Data comes from the Parker Solar Probe, which flies close to the Sun. The team splits the speed spread into Hermite parts. They track how energy moves across those parts. First views near the Sun test long-held claims about how solar wind heats and churns as it flows out.
arxiv-2512-01692:
Carolina Coimbra Vieira, Ebru Sanliturk, and Emilio Zagheni study information seeking in forced migration. Refugees must pick where to go fast, under deep doubt. What they read shapes that pick. Wikipedia is a key public source in such crises.

The team links data from the Ukrainian refugee crisis to Wikipedia use. They track which pages surged and when. Patterns show what facts refugees sought at each stage. Those patterns can guide aid groups to publish clear, timely pages for the next crisis. Page view spikes can precede official counts, so Wikipedia signals may give aid planners a head start of days in a crisis.
arxiv-2512-01792:
Ahmed Aberqi, Abdesslam Ouaziz, and Maria Alessandra Ragusa study solutions of a fractional Kirchhoff system with a singular term. The system couples two unknowns through a nonlocal Kirchhoff function. A log-type growth term adds a twist. Singular terms strain existence proofs.

The pair prove global and local existence results. Conditions on data and exponents mark where solutions live. Such systems model long-range effects in materials and image work. Existence groundwork must come before any numeric or applied use of such a model. Log-type terms model saturation effects. The ranges tell engineers where the model stays physically sane.
arxiv-2512-01892:
Generative AI systems sometimes produce false or harmful text, and companies add guardrails to catch it. A 2025 mixed-methods study by Heloisa Candello and nine co-authors asks the neglected follow-up question: how do ordinary users actually perceive those safety measures and the answers behind them?

The concern is real, since fluent systems can hallucinate with confidence while guardrails quietly reshape what users see. By studying people's perceptions directly, the team gathers evidence on whether current mitigation strategies earn trust or merely hide risk. Their findings speak to anyone designing AI products that people must rely on in daily life.
arxiv-2512-01992:
Chess gives a clean arena for testing whether language models can reason over long stretches and follow rules while doing it. Sai Kolasani and seven co-authors introduce LLM Chess in 2025, a benchmark that has models play full games against a random opponent and scores far more than wins.

More than fifty open and closed models are ranked using behavioral measures: win and loss rates, move quality, move legality, hallucinated actions, and game duration. A model that invents illegal moves fails instruction-following even if its strategy sounds clever. The benchmark thus probes generalization of reasoning through extended interaction, not one-shot answers.
arxiv-2512-02292:
The solar wind is full of switchbacks, sudden folds in the magnetic field, first mapped in detail by the Parker Solar Probe. Zesen Huang and three co-authors present in 2025 a three-dimensional numerical model of a solitary Alfvén wave packet, an Alfvénon, that resembles those switchbacks.

The packet travels with open field-line topology and carries magnetic field reversals, much like the structures the probe found nearly everywhere in the inner heliosphere. Modeling one in three dimensions shows how such a solitary wave holds together. Switchbacks are a leading clue to how the solar wind is heated and accelerated, so a working model of them matters.
arxiv-2512-02492:
Jiahui Chen and four co-authors build a system that makes long music performance videos from audio. Earlier tools could make a singer avatar follow a song, with lips and face in sync over long clips. Adding planned camera motion, as in a real music video, has stayed mostly unexplored.

Their YingVideo-MV framework works in stages, like a cascade, to build the full video step by step. It aims to keep the performer consistent while the virtual camera moves. Such tools could lower the cost of music video production, letting small artists test visual ideas quickly. Fans could one day make clips in this style at home, with no crew and no set.
arxiv-2512-02692:
Jing Chen and three co-authors study whether a nucleon can decay into three leptons, breaking a sacred counting rule. Baryon number is conserved in everyday physics, but many theories beyond the Standard Model allow it to break. Such decays, if seen, would prove new physics at once.

The team computes noncontact contributions, where an exchanged particle mediates the decay. Their low energy effective theory uses dimension six operators to encode the unknown high energy physics. Precise rates help experimental searches know which channels deserve the most effort and the longest running time. A null find at these rates would still cut the space of new laws that labs must take as live leads.
arxiv-2512-02892:
Amr Mohamed and three co-authors make diffusion language models answer faster by stopping when the text has settled. Diffusion models generate by refining a whole passage over many steps. That iterative sampling is slow, which hampers practical use despite the approach's promise.

Their SchED algorithm watches full span logit margins and halts once a smooth, progress based confidence bar is met. It needs no training and works across models. Early exits that know when to stop could make diffusion text models quick enough for chat and drafting tools. Words that firm up fast can stop fast too, and that stop rule is the whole trick that makes the speed gain safe to use.
arxiv-2512-02992:
Lucas Napolitano and a large DESI team stack many quasar spectra to reveal faint absorption lines. Quasars shine through gas clouds on their way to Earth, and each cloud prints absorption lines on the light. A composite spectrum, averaging many systems, lifts weak features above the noise.

In the composite built from DESI's second data release, the team identifies more than seventy absorption lines. Oxygen and hydrogen emission features appear at higher signal to noise than in any previous study. Such stacks census the gas between galaxies and trace how elements spread through the cosmos. Each line in the stack is a sign of gas long past. So the stack reads like a roll call of clouds the light met on its way to us.
arxiv-2512-03192:
Magnetic fields between galaxies are nearly impossible to see directly. B. Stern and I. Tkachev present a new way to hunt for them in this 2025 work. High-energy photons from distant sources can start cascades as they cross space.

A field would bend those cascades, causing a time delay and a faint halo of gamma rays around the source. Astronomers look for those signs. The authors' method aims to sharpen that search. Finding such fields would reveal how magnetism arose and shaped the cosmos. Gamma-ray telescopes already gather the data such a search needs, if analysis is sharp enough.
arxiv-2512-03292:
How often a polynomial hits prime values is a classic question. Noah Kravitz, Katharine Woo, and Max Wenqiang Xu study that distribution in this 2025 work. The Bateman-Horn conjecture predicts the frequency for irreducible polynomials with integer coefficients.

The authors average over many choices of coefficients. With enough averaging, they not only prove Bateman-Horn type results on average. They also pin down precise information about how prime values distribute. Such results deepen number theory's grasp of primes in polynomial sequences. Averaging over coefficients mirrors how polynomials arise in practice, giving results broad reach for analytic number theory.
arxiv-2512-03392:
Binary systems complicate gravitational microlensing, but also enrich it. T. Dex Bhadra and co-authors extend the BAGLE package for such cases in this 2025 work. Microlensing can find and weigh isolated dark objects that emit no light.

In many events, the lens, the source, or both form a binary pair. The authors present lensing equations for binary source and lens models inside BAGLE. Better models mean better mass estimates from real events. That helps surveys that hunt black holes and free-floating planets. Binary lenses can mimic planets, so careful models guard against false discoveries.
arxiv-2512-03492:
Functional programming offers a different way to teach coding. Rajshekhar Sunderraman discusses its use in introductory computer science courses in this 2025 work. The paradigm traces back to the Lambda Calculus and has a long history.

Pure functional languages like Haskell are known for robust software. Immutable data structures are one reason errors stay low. Bringing functional ideas into first courses may shape cleaner thinking about programs. The work weighs how to fit these ideas into crowded beginner curricula. Functional ideas like immutability can prevent whole classes of beginner errors in code, a benefit the author weighs for first courses.
arxiv-2601-06692:
Murad Farzulla builds a math frame for snags in teamwork between agents in a 2026 paper. Agents must team up though their wants, stakes, and facts all differ. When team work fails, a drag shows up that can be gauged.

That drag takes forms such as deadlock, thrash, and too much talk. It can also flare into open clash between the agents at work. His frame grows from a single rule, which he calls the axiom of consent. Acts that touch an agent need that agent's leave, he holds. The leave owed grows with the size of the stakes in the act. One rule thus yields his whole study of drag in joint work. Those who build agent teams gain a way to price the cost of snags.
arxiv-2601-06892:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Jen-Hsu Chang and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers constructions of totally Non-Negative pfaffian. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. The totally non-negative pfaffian (TNNP) is define for a skew-symmetric matrix such that all the sub-pfaffians are non-negative. It appears in the pfaffian structure of τ -function for the non-singular web solitons of the BKP equation .

One constructs TNNP using the Perfect matching, chord diagram and the Dyck paths enumeration. Its tridiagonal form is also investigated. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07092:
Yuliang Cai and three co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how self-driving cars can answer questions about a scene. The task is called Visual Question Answering, or VQA. A car takes in camera views and a text query. It must grasp what is near it and reply in words. The team's pipeline squeezes each scene down to key zones to save time.

Speed is the hard part of VQA on the road. A car must reply at once, with no lag. A late reply can put lives at risk. Past tools tend to scan the whole scene at full size. That scan eats time the car does not have. By working on squeezed zones of the scene, the new pipeline aims to keep replies fast. It still aims to keep the car aware of what counts for safe travel.
arxiv-2601-07392:
Alexandre Tuel and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with OceanSAR-2. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. The authors present OceanSAR-2, the second generation of our foundation model for SAR-based ocean observation.

Building on our earlier release, which pioneered self-supervised learning on Sentinel-1 Wave Mode data. OceanSAR-2 relies on improved SSL training and dynamic data curation strategies, which enhances performance while reducing training cost. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07592:
C. J. Clark and colleagues time gamma-ray pulsars with a sampling method borrowed from statistics. Pulsars are spinning neutron stars whose beams sweep past Earth like lighthouse light. Precise timing of Fermi telescope data can reveal many effects. These include timing noise in young pulsars and orbital changes in redback binary systems. Timing can even probe the background of gravitational waves. Their 2026 preprint uses Gibbs sampling.

Gibbs sampling explores complex probability models by updating one piece at a time. Pulsar timing models have many linked parameters, which makes direct fitting hard. A sampling approach can map the full range of plausible values instead of one best fit. The method matters for pulsar timing arrays, which hunt very low-frequency gravitational waves. Astronomers need timing they can trust at extreme precision.
arxiv-2601-07892:
Hong Huang and colleagues quantize language model weights to just three values, efficiently. Large models strain the memory of edge devices. Ternary quantization reduces weights to minus one, zero, and plus one. Current implementations, though, misalign with ordinary hardware. Their 2026 preprint, Sherry, adds fine-grained sparsification to reach an effective 1.25 bits per weight.

Sparsification means many weights become zero and can be skipped. Fine-grained control keeps the important weights while dropping the rest in hardware-friendly patterns. The aim is models that fit phones and embedded devices without losing much quality. Hardware efficiency decides whether a quantization scheme gets used at all. The paper serves machine learning engineers deploying models at the edge. It treats the hardware layout as part of the algorithm.
arxiv-2601-07992:
Alexander Eliseev and Sergei Seleznev question backtests that grade language models on data they already trained on. Economists now apply language models to tasks like macroeconomic forecasting. They often backtest the models, even though training data include the same period being forecast. The authors call their check fake date tests. Their 2026 discussion paper asks whether in-sample accuracy of such forecasts can be trusted. The results are presented as preliminary, to invite feedback.

A model that memorized past news can look prophetic without forecasting skill. Fake dates expose that by moving the claimed present. Honest evaluation matters before models inform economic decisions. The paper serves economists adopting language models and evaluators who audit them. It supplies a simple test that separates memory from genuine prediction. The authors publish through a discussion series for working papers.
arxiv-2601-08092: Wesley Quaresma Cota and Luiz Henrique de Souza Matos wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on algebras with a superinvolution, over a field of characteristic zero. For an algebra A, the star-codimensions form a list of counts, one for each step n from one on. Each count gauges how many polynomial identities the algebra obeys at that step. The authors focus on growth of these counts as a square, and on minimal varieties of unitary algebras with superinvolution.
arxiv-2601-08192:
Md. Faiyaz Abdullah Sayeedi and six co-authors propose a self-improving agent framework for medical imaging. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that large vision-language models now drive much medical image analysis. Most systems still act as single-pass black boxes with weak control over reasoning and grounding.

The framework follows four steps named in its title: route, retrieve, reflect, and repair. Each step adds a check that a single pass lacks. The design targets visual detection joined with linguistic reasoning about the image. For clinical readers, the value lies in spatial grounding and safety checks. A system that can revisit its own answer is easier to audit before use.
arxiv-2601-08392: Maddalena Genzini and five co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a quantum random number generator built on a chip. The design is semi-device-independent, so it needs just a bit of trust in the gear. It rests on a breach of a contextuality inequality, in KCBS form. Two silicon photonic chips form the system. One chip holds a heralded single-photon source. The other holds a mesh that can be reset to guide light. The mesh sets up qutrit states and takes the reads the KCBS test needs.
arxiv-2601-09292:
Greta Dolcetti, Giulio Zizzo, and Sergio Maffeis test how safe tool call agents are in the wild. Such an agent can call soft tools, such as mail or files, from a chat ask. A foe can craft an ask that bends a call to harm. The team runs four open models that claim tool skill, and hits them with three attack types.

They then test eight guards on those attacks. Their score is stark. The models are not safe by default, the team finds. And the guards are not yet fit for real use. A reader who ships tool agents gets a hard check list. It shows which guards help a bit, and where all of them still fail.
arxiv-2601-09392:
Albrecht Böttcher and Ilya M. Spitkovsky revisit a formula for the spectral radius of the Bell-CHSH operator. Their 2026 arXiv paper extends a result of Yuki Fujii and Toyohiro Tsurumaru. The operator comes from the CHSH test, a standard probe of quantum entanglement and nonlocality.

Fujii and Tsurumaru proved their formula on finite-dimensional spaces and sketched a method for infinite dimensions. Böttcher and Spitkovsky give a proof of the original formula that works in all dimensions at once. A unified proof removes the need for dimension-by-dimension approximation tricks. It also firms up a quantity used to bound quantum correlations.
arxiv-2601-09492:
Kaiming Cui and seven co-authors chart how common small close-in planets are around Sun-like stars. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses data from the TESS space telescope. It counts planets with orbits of half a day to sixteen days and sizes from two to twenty Earth radii, around FGK main-sequence stars.

Occurrence rates show how often nature builds each kind of planet. Close-in planets test ideas about how planets form and drift inward. The authors carry out a detailed analysis of the rates across size and orbit length. A clean census like this guides the next round of formation models.
arxiv-2601-09592:
Vincenzo Amato, Carlo Nitsch, Cristina Trombetti, and Federico Villone study how a shape trades off three classic measures. Their 2026 arXiv paper links a region's lowest vibration tone, its stiffness under twisting, and the length of its edge. The three are known as the first Dirichlet eigenvalue, the torsional rigidity, and the perimeter.

The authors optimize the product of eigenvalue and torsional rigidity among sets of fixed perimeter. They treat both general open sets of finite perimeter and convex domains. Results like these guide design work where stiffness and pitch must be balanced at once. The product turns out to be a sharp way to frame that balance.
arxiv-2601-09892:
Katherine Williams Booth, Alexander Nolte, and Yvon Verberne describe a group of maps of a surface by means of a graph. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with quasiconformal maps of a closed surface with at least two handles. These maps stretch shapes, but only in a controlled, bounded way that keeps them tame.

The authors show the group is the same as the symmetry group of a graph built from key closed curves on the surface. The graph carries a natural rough ordering, set by constants that grade how good each curve is. Turning a hard analytic group into graph symmetries makes it far easier to study with bare hands. The result links shape, space, and counting in a single clean object.
arxiv-2601-10092:
Jongseok Kim, Seongae Kang, Jonghwan Shin, Yuhan Lee, and Ohyun Jo join mixed health data to call a health risk. Clinics hold charts, lab facts, and wave signs from the body. Each type codes facts in its own way. A join must keep what each type says best.

Past joins tend to use one fixed blend. They merge types with a plain step. That can lose the strong suits of each type. The team made LeMoF, a join that works by levels. It guides how types meet at each level. The aim is a call that uses each type for what it does best.
arxiv-2601-10292:
Georgia Psychogiou and co authors built a sharp beam antenna with one feed. The antenna works at a set band near the mid range for new cell nets. It sends a beam with a round twist. That twist cuts loss from how a hand set is held.

Sharp beams oft need many feeds. This one uses two crossed strips. One strip is driven. One is a load with a set react term. Strong cross pull twixt the strips makes the beam sharp. The team tuned strip sizes to set that pull. The result is high gain from a small, one feed form.
arxiv-2601-10392:
Hassan Eshkiki and co authors fuse many frames of a cell film into one clean still. Glow based microscopy films live cells. The films are oft noisy. Glow can wax and wane in time. A single frame may miss a trait that the next frame shows.

The team project frames from many times into one image. Their frame keeps the true cell facts of the film. Noise drops as frames join. Traits that blink in time stay clear in the still. The work helps labs read live cell films with more trust. It also cuts the need to pick one best frame.
arxiv-2601-10592:
Delong Chen and co-authors present Action100M, a large dataset of human actions in video. Teaching machines to read actions from sight is a basic step toward machines that act in the real world. That needs big, open sets of labeled video across many domains. The team built their set from online how-to videos.

The dataset draws on 1.2 million internet instructional videos. People in such clips cook, build, fix, and play, so the action range is wide. Open labels let models learn acts beyond a fixed short list. The resource gives vision researchers fresh training data for action recognition in daily life scenes.
arxiv-2601-10692:
Alex M. Potts and a large team of co-authors study phase modes in superconductors held in tiny cavities. A superconductor's phase mode carries deep facts about pairing and energy loss. At low frequencies it is normally hidden by the Anderson-Higgs mechanism. Very thin samples, thinner than the London penetration depth, are the exception.

Such films support a gapless phase mode, the Cooper plasmon, whose path can be reshaped by a nearby screening layer. The team probes these modes at finite momentum inside terahertz microcavities. The work opens a way to watch pairing physics that was out of reach. It may inform new devices that use superconducting films at terahertz speeds.
arxiv-2601-10892:
A. Adhikari and co-authors probe magnons and phonons in arrays of nickel-iron nanodots. Magnons are waves of spin; phonons are waves of strain. Controlling how spin waves couple to strain is a rising theme for future spin-wave devices. The team uses all-optical excitation on ordered arrays of Ni80Fe20 nanomagnets.

They explore spin wave modes that interact with acoustic wave modes, plus a few modes that stay aloof. Light both drives and reads the motion, so no contacts are needed. Such arrays could route signals by spin instead of charge, saving energy. The work serves the spintronics community that designs these wave-based devices.
arxiv-2601-11092:
Leonardo Clarke and co-authors use emission lines to probe distant galaxies beyond cosmic noon. The team analyzes key rest-optical emission-line ratios in 763 galaxies, plus composite spectra from JADES DR3. The galaxies span redshifts from 1.4 to 7, deep into the early universe. Line ratios act as diagnostics of the gas that stars light up.

The ratios probe the ionizing spectrum of young stars and any alpha-element enhancement in the gas. Both trace how early galaxies formed stars and enriched their surroundings. JWST made such spectra routine at these distances. The work helps turn JWST's flood of spectra into a history of the first generations of galaxies.
arxiv-2601-11292:
Yiqi Zhou and seven coauthors build a compiler for compute-in-memory chips. Their 2026 preprint deals with SRAM-based designs that blur memory and math. AI workloads are heavy on data, and moving data costs most. That gap is the known memory wall that slows AI hardware.

Digital compute-in-memory with SRAM can scale to real workloads. But its design space is vast, too vast for hand design. A compiler that builds designs on its own is the fix. The team adds one more trick: approximate computing. AI tasks can take small errors with no real harm. Trading a bit of accuracy can save much energy in the chip.
arxiv-2601-11492:
Kaiwen Wang and eight coauthors build an AI strategy system for boxing. Their 2026 preprint names it BoxMind, a closed-loop expert system. Competitive sports need deep tactical analysis to win. Combat sports like boxing lag in AI-driven analytics so far.

Action dynamics in a bout are complex and fast. Tactical patterns lack a structured form for machines to use. BoxMind closes the loop from analysis to strategy choice. It was validated in elite boxing competition, the team reports. The test stage was the 2024 Olympic Games. A system proven at that level carries real weight. It hints at AI coaches for other combat sports as well.
arxiv-2601-11692:
Bennet Outland, Gretchen Noble, Andrew Smith, and Jack Lissauer test tight four-planet systems. Their 2026 preprint studies orbital stability in such systems. Each system holds four Earth-mass planets around one star. The star has one solar mass in the simulations.

Planets start on circular, coplanar orbits at set spacing. The innermost planet sits at 1 AU from the star. Later semimajor axes are spaced by mutual Hill radii. Equal Hill spacing packs the planets closely together. The team runs simulations to see how long order lasts. Closely spaced systems may collide or eject a planet. The results inform how packed real exoplanet systems can be.
arxiv-2601-11892:
Chao Wang gives a strict proof of a continued fraction claim for minus pi over four. The claim came from the Ramanujan Machine, a tool that guesses maths forms by search. A guess needs a proof to count as maths.

He uses linked rules for the Gauss hypergeometric function. Those rules show the claimed form is a cleaned form of a known ratio. The work turns a machine guess into a proved fact. It also shows how such guesses can be checked with care.  The proof gives the guess a firm place in maths.
arxiv-2601-11992:
Kari Kamtila, Joseph Dongho, Prosper Rosaire Mama Assandje, and Thomas Bouetou Bouetou study a class of free divisors that are not quasi-homogeneous. Divisors are sets cut out by a polynomial set to zero. In Saito's sense, free divisors have a tidy set of linked vector fields.

Their class uses a set sum of monomials with the product of coordinates. They look at duals of Saito's basis for these cases. They also give an application of the results. The work adds to the theory of singular spaces in complex geometry.  The basis work adds tools for divisor maths in this class.
arxiv-2601-12092:
Léon Brenig and Marc Vincke argue that one rule may sit under all of quantum mechanics. The rule is that the Heisenberg uncertainty bound stays the same under a group of special nonlinear gauge transforms. From that rule plus classical mechanics, they derive quantum rules for a free particle.

Their route yields most quantum postulates, such as the Born rule. The wave-function collapse rule does not come out of it. A single base rule would be a deep shift in how quantum theory is framed. The work sets out that claim in full.
arxiv-2601-12292: A team of theorists rank quantum correlations in a hybrid qubit-qutrit system with axial symmetry. The system feels axial and planar anisotropies, dipolar spin links, and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya coupling. They use four gauges: negativity, two forms of nonlocality from uncertainty and measurement, and Bell nonlocality via CHSH. They track how anisotropy, fields, and heat shape the survival of each correlation kind. A ranked map shows which links are hardiest. Such maps guide the design of hybrid quantum devices. The work is in quantum information theory.
arxiv-2601-12492:
M. N. Mazziotta and a large ALICE team report test beam results for a new particle detector. The detector is planned for ALICE 3, a wholly new apparatus for later runs of the Large Hadron Collider. Its job is to identify charged particles at high energy. The design is a Ring Imaging Cherenkov detector with an aerogel radiator.

Its light sensing surface uses arrays of silicon photomultipliers in a proximity focusing layout. The device also has timing capabilities, per the title of the work. Test beam runs check how the prototype performs with real particle beams. Good timing plus ring images would give two handles on particle type at once. Results here guide the final design for the collider.
arxiv-2601-12592:
Dominik Kirst and Haoyi Zeng work in constructive reverse mathematics on a classic theorem of logic. The downward Lowenheim Skolem theorem says every infinite model has a countable elementary submodel. Over classical base theories, it is known to match the axiom of dependent choice. Constructive logic, which demands explicit constructions, allows a finer split of such claims.

The pair refine that known equivalence with care. Assuming only countable choice, they split the theorem into finer parts. One part is dependent choice, and another is a new fragment of the excluded middle. Their title names playful tools in the proof: blurred drinker paradoxes and blurred choice axioms. The work shows how constructive analysis can dissect a theorem brick by brick.
arxiv-2601-12692:
Miguel Cardenas applies dimensional analysis to experiments with Z pinch devices. A Z pinch uses a strong current to compress plasma into a thin column. The behavior of such discharges looks complex, with many variables at play. Cardenas shows it can be captured by only three dimensionless parameters.

Those three parameters can be arranged to draw a surface in three dimensional space. That surface compiles all accessible data on the macroscopic behavior of any discharge. Each possible Z pinch discharge maps to a point on the surface. A compact picture of this kind helps experimenters compare devices and plan runs. It also shows which combinations of settings can ever be reached.
arxiv-2601-12992:
Sujit Bhattacharyya works on gradient bounds for systems of weighted heat type equations. The setting is a weighted space with curved shape, known as a Riemannian manifold. The equations also carry an added term called a potential.

Bhattacharyya derives Bernstein type bounds for two such systems. He works through all the main cases in turn. One split is by the form of the potential, which may be linear or may grow fast. A second split is by the space itself, which may stay fixed or change over time. The work partly settles a question raised in an earlier paper by Bhattacharyya and co-authors.
arxiv-2601-13392:
Shlok Shelat, Jay Raval, Souvik Roy, and Manas Gaur test if language models truly reason or just recall on formal tasks. Such models score well on formal tongue tasks. That score may show true symbol sense or just match of known forms.

Their bench asks models to build finite automata, small state machines, from regular tongues. It holds fact asks and build tasks from public sources. It also holds two kinds of new tasks. Some are hand made with many valid builds. By set of known next to new, the bench splits recall from sense. For AI teams, that split is key to trust on logic tasks.
arxiv-2601-13492:
Eleanore B. Todd and co-authors probe the fringe of a rich galaxy cluster at redshift near two. The cluster is XLSSC 122. At that span, its light left when the universe was young. The team uses the Hubble Space Telescope to read it from its core out to three megaparsecs.

That span is ten times the core radius mark, called R500, which is 295 kiloparsecs here. Few reads reach that far out at such span. The fringe is where new galaxies fall in and the cluster grows. For cluster teams, a first read of the fringe sets the base for deep follow up on how the most rich knots grew.
arxiv-2601-13792:
Léo Pioge, Leonardo Novo, and Nicolas Cerf test a yardstick for boson sampling machines in 2026. Boson sampling sends identical light particles through a network to sample outcomes. Multimode bunching, where particles crowd into few modes, was meant to validate such machines. A high bunching rate was taken as a sign the machine works.

The team shows a catch called anomalous bunching. Partly distinguishable particles can bunch more than perfect identical ones. Time delays between particles drive this odd effect. The result warns that bunching alone can mislead validation of quantum devices.
arxiv-2601-13892:
Andrej Schwanke and co-authors test large language models as drivers of multi-objective optimization in 2026. Such tasks juggle many conflicting goals at once. Models are famed for reasoning, yet they are not the default choice here. Conventional strategies rank high on benchmarks for good reasons.

Classic methods handle numerical inputs with care and model the trade-offs well. They balance exploration with exploitation of the Pareto front, the set of best trade-offs. The team studies hierarchical optimization with language models in charge. The work asks where model reasoning helps, and where numbers still rule.
arxiv-2601-14192: Xiaofang Yang and a large team survey how AI agents can be made more efficient in 2026. Recent years have seen growing interest in extending language models into agentic systems. Agents must remember, use tools, and plan to act well. Each of those skills can waste time, tokens, and compute if done poorly.
arxiv-2601-14392:
I-Hsuan Li, Shutaro Ueda, I-Non Chiu, and Keiichi Umetsu study cold fronts in galaxy clusters in this 2026 paper. They use data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory. Their sample holds three nearby clusters: Abell 496, Abell 2029, and Abell 1644. Cold fronts show as sharp edges in the X-ray surface brightness of the intracluster medium, the hot gas between galaxies.

These fronts come from sloshing, gas swinging in the cluster's gravity well after a past disturbance. Most studies average around the cluster. This one resolves the fronts by azimuth, direction around the center. Readers get a detailed view of how sloshing fronts differ from place to place in each cluster.
arxiv-2601-14492:
Malak Mansour and five co-authors build a strawberry-picking robot in this 2026 paper. Robotic strawberry harvesting is hard under partial occlusion. Leaves hide much of each fruit, which creates significant geometric uncertainty. A grasp plan based on one deterministic shape estimate can be unreliable. From a single partial observation, multiple incompatible 3D completions may all be plausible.

A grasp that looks feasible on one completion may fail on another. The team's system, UNCLE-Grasp, is uncertainty-aware. It plans grasps that hold up across the plausible shapes, not just one guess. Readers get a harvesting method designed for the messy view a robot gets in a real field.
arxiv-2601-14592:
Nicholas Gismondi constructs unusual solutions to fluid-type equations in this 2026 math paper. His class is stationary active scalar equations with a non-odd nonlocal operator in the drift term. Active scalars, like temperature in convection, move the very flow that carries them. He builds nontrivial weak solutions to these equations.

The construction uses a convex integration scheme, a flexible method that builds rough solutions piece by piece. Gismondi shows the solutions lie in specific Besov and Lebesgue spaces, for dimensions two and up. The drift here is non-odd, which breaks a symmetry past work relied on. The states are rough. They are not smooth flows, but they do solve the math in a weak sense. Readers get proof that such equations admit wild, integrable steady states.
arxiv-2601-14792:
Dong Sun, Rahul Nittala, and Rebekka Burkholz test Mixture of Experts models under noise in this 2026 paper. Mixture of Experts models route each input to a few specialist sub-networks. Despite their practical success, their robustness is not fully understood. The team's topic is feature noise: corrupted or jittered input features. Such noise is common when sensors or data pipelines are imperfect.

A router that reads noisy features may send inputs to the wrong experts. The study examines how much that harms the whole model. The abstract in the evidence pack cuts off early, so the detailed findings are not stated there. Readers get a robustness audit for a model family now used at very large scale.
arxiv-2601-15192:
Pratyay Mukherjee and Ritwik Mondal propose a faster way to flip magnetic order. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with antiferromagnets, materials whose atomic magnets cancel out in pairs. Steering that order is a central challenge for next-generation spintronic devices.

The authors analyze switching driven by a field-derivative torque. This torque comes from the time-derivative of an applied terahertz pulse. It acts on the staggered order parameter, the gauge of the paired pattern. The goal is ultrafast switching of the antiferromagnetic state for future fast memory and fast logic devices of the future alike.
arxiv-2601-15992:
Shidan Ma and five co-authors speed up database queries over RDF graphs in a 2026 arXiv paper. RDF graphs store data as linked triples. SPARQL is the language used to query them. Current systems lean on cloud data management. They hit bottlenecks when bandwidth is limited or load is high. The authors explore an edge computing solution. They describe it as the first of its kind for this problem.

Cloud-edge collaboration splits the work. Edge nodes near the user handle parts of each query. The cloud holds the bulk data and the rest of the computation. That split can cut traffic and response time. Knowledge graphs keep growing in enterprise and web use. Query methods that respect bandwidth limits will decide how far they scale.
arxiv-2601-16192:
Ziyi Wu and coauthors lift flat pics and clips to full sphere views with no shape step. Their 2026 preprint deals with wide views that wrap the whole scene. Past lifts align the flat view to the sphere form by shape maths. That needs known cam facts, which wild pics oft lack. Lack of facts blocks use on most real pics and clips.

The new tool, named 360Anything, learns the lift with no shape step. It works on pics and clips from the wild as they come. Sphere views feed rich 3D world builds for play and film. A lift with no cam facts opens that path wide. The team tests the lift on mixed wild sets.
arxiv-2601-16292:
Anh-Duy Pham builds a fast agent model frame in Python with a column store. His 2026 preprint, named AMBER, deals with agent based models. Such models study group acts in nature and in social life. Python frames are easy to use but oft run slow at scale. Scale is just what group act studies need most.

AMBER stores agent traits in columns, not in lone rows. Column stores let code run the same step on all agents fast. Speed with ease of use would open big models to more teams. The frame aims to keep the Python feel users like. It seeks scale with no loss of that ease.
arxiv-2601-16592:
Vinicius Borin and coauthors join weather and train data to read delays in Finland. Their 2026 preprint deals with late trains and their causes. Late runs stem from acts, gear and sky facts as one. Past sets oft hold just one of those fact types. Sets sans weather miss a main cause in north lands.

The team joins sky data to run data for Finnish trains. Joint data lets them weigh how much sky adds to delays. True weights guide where rail teams should spend to cut delays. North rail nets face snow and cold that bend all plans. The work gives a joint set for that study.
arxiv-2601-16692:
Avraham Gal questions fresh claims from a Japanese lab about strange nuclei. The J-PARC lab used fine grain film to catch rare events. In those films, a Xi particle was caught by a light nucleus. Teams then named the bound states they thought they saw. Gal's 2026 preprint checks if those names fit past proof.

An past test at the same lab used a beam on carbon. That test gave a bound state with a set grip strength. Gal sets the film claims next to that gauge. He asks if both tales can be true at once. Such checks keep rare-event claims on firm ground. They also guide new hunts for Xi bound states.
arxiv-2601-17092:
Two strange fractions sit at the core of a pure math hunt. Each has arctanh, a log-type curve, in its base. Their Mellin transforms turn them in wave-like codes. A 2026 preprint works out those codes with care. The fractions live on the span from nil to one. Past that span, they are set to nil for the work.

The codes tie to deep guesses on odd zeta marks. Those marks pair with powers of pi in set ratios. A twin set pairs beta marks with pi powers. Such ties could prove those ratios wild or tame. Pure sums here may crack old number tales.
arxiv-2601-17192:
Sukirt Thakur and a team of eight co-authors gauge heart flow from plain angiograms. A heart flaw called CMD hurts the heart's small veins. Prime tests for it are invasive and uneven. Their 2026 preprint builds PUNCH, a net that works from the angiogram alone. It gauges coronary flow reserve, a key mark of that flaw. Physics rules and doubt marks both sit in the build.

The net learns blood flow from first-rule forms of dye spread. No ground truth flow marks are called for. Doubt marks tell docs when to doubt a call. Non-invasive gauges could find CMD far more oft.
arxiv-2601-17492:
Jin Li and seven co-authors work on fair recommendations from language models. LLM-based recommenders model users in rich new ways. They also copy bias from their training data. That bias can skew who sees which goods, jobs, or news. Fixing it by full retraining costs too much for most teams. The authors seek fairness without that cost.

They name two core challenges that block cheap fixes. Their method must work on a trained model as it stands. Fair picks matter for trust and for law. A low-cost fix could spread fair practice widely. The work serves platforms that suggest goods at scale. It treats fairness as a design need, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2601-17592:
Sivaprasad Omanakuttan and four co-authors build spin codes for quantum error correction. Most codes need local control and stabilizer checks. Those are hard in systems ruled by collective interactions. The authors draw on spin-GKP codes for a new path. They use the Holstein-Primakoff view of spins. Their codes target local and collective noise at once.

Collective systems include atomic ensembles and some solid-state hosts. Codes that fit them widen where quantum machines can be built. Handling both noise types in one code is a strong step. The work gives hardware teams new code options. It may cut the control burden that blocks scale-up. Spin hosts gain a tailored shield.
arxiv-2601-18092:
Nan Chen and co-authors design context-aware help for screen reader users working on computers. Their 2026 preprint starts from a plain fact. Equal access to digital tools is critical for school, work, and social life. Yet mainstream screens are built for sight, so blind users face steep learning curves and frequent blocks. Current support is thin: tutorials target sighted users, and human help lacks scale.

The team studies help that senses when a user is stuck and what they were trying to do. Guidance timed to the struggle could raise independence a great deal. Their title frames the goal as a path from struggle to success. The work serves designers of accessible systems everywhere.
arxiv-2601-18692:
Wei Wu and many colleagues build a base model that lets robots see, read, and act in one frame. Such a model takes a shot and a line of text, then sets the moves of a robot arm. A prized base model must work on new tasks and new arms with small cost in data and chip time. Most past models fall short on one of those counts.

Their model, LingBot-VLA, learns from a huge set of real runs: tens of thousands of hours on nine kinds of twin-arm robots. Real runs teach what mock worlds miss, such as slip and wear. A base trained at that scale could be bent to new jobs with far less fresh data. That would bring arm robots close to the ease of use of text tools.
arxiv-2601-18792:
Brian Liu and Oiwi Parker Jones link brain waves to the feel of speech, to open a new path in the study of how we feel. To read feel from brain acts could change how we grasp joy, fear, and grief. Past sets pair brain data with speech and with its writ form. None pair it with the feel of the speech: glad, sad, cross, or calm. That gap blocks work on feel from the brain.

The pair fill the gap with a tool that grades the feel of text. They run that tool on the writ form of tales read to folk while their brain waves are caught by a fine cap. The brain set thus gains feel tags with no new lab work. A tagged set could teach tools to read feel from the brain. It could also test how feel is built in the mind.
arxiv-2601-18892:
Gleb Aminov and three colleagues show that a deep mark of curved space maths drops out of a classic chain of steps. The mark is a flaw in how a set kind of wave world acts when its shape is stretched in a set way. Such worlds should not care about shape in that way, but a faint flaw stays. The flaw comes in two kinds; the team take on the first kind. It lives in worlds with an even count of dims.

They start from a shape that sums up the curl of space in its full form. A chain of steps, long used for twin flaws of the force kind, then gives the shape flaw in a plain way. That puts the two flaw kinds on the same base for the first time. A shared base firms the maths of such worlds.
arxiv-2601-19392:
Martynas Skrabulis and five co-authors measure shoves smaller than a sensor's own quantum jitter. A mechanical sensor's sensitivity ends at its inherent quantum fluctuations, or so the standard story goes. The team uses an optically levitated nanoparticle, a bead of glass held by light, as their sensor.

By squeezing the bead's motion in a reversible way, they resolve impulsive forces below its zero point uncertainty. The trick does not break quantum rules; it reshapes where the noise sits. Such sensors could weigh the faintest kicks in physics, from tiny particles to faint fields.
arxiv-2601-19592:
Salvatore Tringali and Weihao Yan work in algebra on a question about torsion groups. Their setting is a monoid, a set with an operation for combining elements. From any monoid they build a new one whose elements are finite sets containing the identity. The combining rule multiplies sets element by element.

This construction is called the reduced finitary power monoid. The paper connects its torsion behaviour to a conjecture of Bienvenu and Geroldinger. Torsion concerns elements that return to the identity after repeated combination. Such questions sound abstract, but they test how structure passes from a monoid to sets built from it. The results sharpen our grip on power monoids, a tool in factorization theory.
arxiv-2601-19692:
Jukka John and five colleagues improve a correction used in electronic structure theory. Standard density functional methods contain a known flaw: an electron partly interacts with itself. Self-interaction correction removes that error, but doing it in a fully variational way is hard. Locally scaled versions apply the correction unevenly, where it is needed most.

The team presents a fully variational, locally scaled functional that uses complex-valued optimal orbitals. Complex orbitals give the method more freedom than real ones. Reaching a fully variational form is described as an important milestone for this family of methods. Better functionals mean better predictions of atoms, molecules, and solids, in both ground and excited states. The work strengthens a tool used across chemistry and materials science.
arxiv-2601-19792:
Peter Zeng and a large team of colleagues compare how humans and vision-language models build common ground. In referential communication, a speaker describes an object so a partner can pick it out. Partners succeed by modeling what the other knows. AI agents that partner with people need the same skill.

The authors study how large vision-language models ground references, side by side with humans. They find the two ground language differently. That gap limits collaboration, since the model may misread what its partner intends. Pinpointing the difference shows where training and design must improve. The work matters for any assistant that talks about the visible world with a person.
arxiv-2601-19992:
Soham Sarkar, Tanmay Sen, and Sayantan Banerjee hunt defects in factory images with very few examples. Industrial anomaly detection is hard because defective samples are rare and classes are badly imbalanced. Few-shot settings make it harder still: only a handful of labelled defects exist. Their method, BayPrAnoMeta, generalises an existing meta-learning approach in a Bayesian direction.

Proto-MAML, the base method, adapts using fixed class prototypes and distances. BayPrAnoMeta replaces those deterministic prototypes with probabilistic ones. Modelling uncertainty in the prototypes should help when examples are scarce. Factories need inspection systems that learn new defect types quickly. A method that works from a few shots could cut the cost of quality control. Few shots must do the work of many.
arxiv-2601-20192:
Xiaokai Luo and three colleagues study online change point detection for streams of events that arrive in bursts over time and across many channels. The data are modeled as inhomogeneous Poisson processes, where the event rate itself varies. The task is to spot, as data arrives, the moment the pattern shifts.

Such shifts matter in earthquake monitoring, climate watching, and epidemic surveillance. The authors note this setting is still underexplored in statistics and machine learning. Methods that catch changes quickly, with few false alarms, would give agencies earlier warning when a monitored system starts to behave in a new way.
arxiv-2601-20592:
Ali Basirat, Danial Namazifard, and Navid Baradaran Hemmati probe language contact inside the internal layers of a monolingual language model. They ask whether structural traces of contact with other languages survive in the representations a model learns. Their case study is Persian, a language with a rich contact history.

They expose a Persian-trained model to languages with varying degrees and types of contact with Persian, then inspect its intermediate representations. If contact leaves a measurable trace, model internals could become a new source of evidence for historical linguistics, complementing texts and speaker data.
arxiv-2601-20792:
Thomas Brackin argues that where a privacy policy puts facts can hide them in plain sight. His 2026 paper studies how major companies organize their policies. Policies are meant to give users notice of data practices. Brackin finds a pattern he calls jurisdiction-siloed disclosure. Key facts appear in firm, specific form only inside regional sections.

Those sections carry labels like California Residents or EU and UK Users. The general sections, by contrast, use vague or qualified words for the same practices. Most readers never reach the regional parts, so the clear facts stay unseen. His audit covered more than a hundred major companies and flagged hundreds of possible instances. The paper shows how structure alone can blunt the notice a policy claims to give.
arxiv-2601-21092:
Marvin Sextro, Weronika Kłos, and Gabriel Dernbach teach models to predict how cells respond to perturbations in new settings. Their 2026 paper presents MapPFN, which learns causal perturbation maps in context. Planning interventions in biology needs models that adapt to unseen contexts. A model must spot the mechanism at work in each new system. Single-cell datasets, though, span few contexts. Old methods cannot use new evidence at test time.

MapPFN is built to adapt on the spot. It uses fresh evidence as it predicts. That style mirrors how a scientist updates beliefs after one experiment. Better adaptation could guide drug and gene studies with less data. The paper targets treatment-effect modeling in biology.
arxiv-2601-21192:
Wun Yu Chan and seven co-authors ask if smarter reasoning makes for better text embeddings. Their 2026 paper compares embedding models built from unlike backbones. Top embedding models now derive from decoder-only language models. Contrastive learning adapts them for search and matching. Reasoning models raise a natural question. Does enhanced reasoning yield superior semantic pictures? The team tests reasoning-trained models as embedding starts.

An embedding turns text into numbers that capture meaning. If reasoning training deepens grasp, embeddings should improve. If it narrows the model, they might not. The paper measures that transfer at once. Search, retrieval, and recommendation all ride on embedding quality. The answer guides which base models builders should pick next.
arxiv-2601-21392:
Chunpeng Du, Zongyang Li, Yali Zhang, Yikang Lu, and Attila Szolnoki study how cooperation grows when agents learn from a shared score signal. Q-learning is a standard frame for such studies, since it says how agents update the value of each act. Reputation is known to help cooperation grow.

Past models baked reputation into payoffs, states, or partner choice. Those routes blur the effect of the learning signal itself. The authors instead shape the learning signal directly inside a combined Q-learning rule. That clean design shows how much of the cooperation gain comes from the signal alone.
arxiv-2601-21892:
Jian-Feng Cai, Haixia Liu, Zhengyi Su, and Chao Wang revisit a standard trick for steering image generation. Classifier-free guidance lets users push a diffusion or flow model toward a prompt by extrapolating between two predictions. It works well in practice, but it rests on a heuristic linear step that is sensitive to the guidance scale.

The authors give the method a principled reading through optimization. On that basis, their 2026 preprint improves guidance for flow matching. It projects the guided path onto a manifold. That keeps the path on the surface where valid data live. Better guidance means stronger prompt control with fewer artifacts, a daily concern for everyone generating images and video with these models.
arxiv-2601-21992:
Simon Ekhammar, Nikolay Gromov, Bogdan Stefański, and Charles Thull test a conjectured tool for string theory across its full range. The Quantum Spectral Curve should give the spectrum of strings in a particular curved space. That space is a stack of spheres and flat directions. It carries Ramond-Ramond charge.

The team solves the curve numerically from weak coupling to strong coupling. At strong coupling, the spectrum organizes into flat-space string mass levels. The masses follow a universal square-root scaling in the string tension. Finer splittings appear beyond that leading order. Their 2026 preprint confirms that picture. Checks like this build confidence that the spectral curve truly captures string physics where no other method can compute.
arxiv-2601-22292:
Manuela Chacon-Chamorro, Luis Felipe Giraldo, and Nicanor Quijano study how groups of agents can stay strong when things go wrong. Their 2026 preprint centers on shared resilience: the power to foresee, resist, bounce back from, and adapt to shocks. Mixed groups, where each agent has its own aims, face the strain most.

The team focus on how to learn reward rules that build that shared strength. Their setting is learning by trial and error, with many agents at once. Strong rules could help fleets of robots or grids ride out faults. The work names a goal the field has largely skipped.
arxiv-2601-22392:
