athanasius-against-the-heathen-contra-ge:
Young Athanasius of Alexandria opened his career with a broad case against pagan religion, Against the Heathen. Idols, he argues, are dead wood and stone dressed up by human hands. The treatise appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition, often paired with his work on the Incarnation.

He calls the old myths immoral and finds them unable to explain the order of the world. Only the Christian God, he claims, accounts for both creation and human reason. The logic is confident and systematic for so young a writer. Readers meet the future champion of Nicaea already armed with formidable arguments.
athanasius-de-decretis-defence-of-the-ni:
Critics attacked the Council of Nicaea's key word, homoousios, meaning of one substance with the Father. Athanasius defended that choice in De Decretis, his Defence of the Nicene Definition. The treatise appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

The fathers at Nicaea chose the term, he argues, precisely to block Arian evasions about the Son. Every softer phrase had been twisted, so a hard one was needed. Athanasius walks through the council's reasoning like an insider, which he was. No other writer did more to make Nicaea's decision stick across the empire. The treatise still anchors study of what the council meant by its boldest phrase.
athanasius-de-sententia-dionysii-npnf2-1:
Arians had begun quoting Dionysius of Alexandria, a respected earlier bishop, against the faith of Nicaea. Athanasius came to his predecessor's rescue in De Sententia Dionysii. The treatise appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Some of Dionysius's phrases sound careless, Athanasius grants, but his intent was sound. Read in context, the old bishop opposed the very errors his name was used to support. The book performs theological damage control with unusual fairness. It also teaches a lasting lesson in reading the fathers with charity rather than hunting for traps. Careful readers still cite it when old words get used in new fights.
athanasius-defence-before-constantius-ap:
Summoned to answer charges before Emperor Constantius, Athanasius prepared a formal self-defense. His Defence Before Constantius survives in written form in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. The bishop addresses the very ruler whose party kept driving him into exile.

Facts, dates, and documents do the heavy lifting, delivered with unshakable dignity. Athanasius denies plotting against the emperor and answers each slander in turn. A bishop facing down an emperor makes for high drama in any age. The speech also shows how carefully he built his case, like a lawyer who expected the record to outlive them both.
athanasius-defence-of-his-flight-apologi:
Critics called Athanasius a coward for fleeing when soldiers came to arrest him. His Defence of His Flight answers the charge directly. The short treatise appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Flight, he argues, can obey God's timing just as the apostles' escapes did. Scripture honors those who withdrew until their hour came, and condemns only needless rashness. A personal attack becomes a small theology of prudence under persecution. Among his fighting works, this one feels the most human: a great man explaining himself to people eager to judge him. Its calm tone under attack only sharpens the force of its case.
athanasius-festal-letters-npnf2-1892:
Each year the bishop of Alexandria announced the date of Easter to the churches of Egypt. Athanasius turned those notices into full pastoral letters, the Festal Letters gathered here. They appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Calendar notes grow into theology, encouragement, and gentle correction for distant flocks. Some letters were written from exile, others from seasons of triumph, and the tone shifts with the years. Together they form the heartbeat of his long rule. A shepherd writes to his people year after year, and readers can watch a whole episcopate unfold.
athanasius-four-discourses-against-the-a:
Four long discourses form the heavy artillery of the Arian controversy. In them, Athanasius argues from scripture that the Son is fully God, not a creature made by God. The Four Discourses Against the Arians appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Text after text receives close handling as he dismantles the Arian reading of key verses. The argument is demanding, systematic, and patient across hundreds of pages. Together the discourses laid the theological ground under the Nicene faith. Many judges call them the books that won the fourth century for orthodoxy. Patient readers still find them the fullest ancient case for the Son's true divinity.
athanasius-history-of-the-arians-histori:
Partisan to the core, Athanasius's History of the Arians tells the doctrinal war from inside his own camp. Court intrigue, violence against bishops, and shifting creeds fill the narrative. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

He names names and spares nobody, least of all the emperors who backed his enemies. Modern scholars read the history with care, checking its charges against other sources. Even so, no other text conveys the bitterness of the fourth-century fights so vividly. History here is a weapon, and Athanasius wields it without apology or restraint.
athanasius-on-the-councils-of-ariminum-a:
In 359, rival councils at Ariminum and Seleucia nearly gave away everything Nicaea had won. Athanasius analyzed the disaster in On the Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia, known as De Synodis. The work appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

He shows how Arian word games trapped tired bishops into signing soft creeds. At the same time he builds bridges to moderates who could still be won back. History and strategy run together on every page. The book reads as theology practiced as statecraft, by a man who understood both creeds and crowds. It also preserves creeds and letters from councils whose own records are lost.
athanasius-on-the-incarnation-of-the-wor:
Why would God become a human being? Athanasius answers in On the Incarnation of the Word, one of the most admired theological books ever written. The 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition carries the text. He wrote it young, yet its clarity has never faded.

Creation, left to itself, was sliding back toward nothing, he argues, and only its Maker could remake it. God became man, in the famous line, so that people might become godlike. Repentance alone could not repair the damage, so the Word took flesh and died to defeat death. C. S. Lewis praised the little book as a masterpiece, and few readers have disagreed since.
athanasius-personal-letters-npnf2-1892:
Beyond the famous fights over Arianism, Athanasius wrote letters as a friend and pastor. The Personal Letters gather that quieter side of his output. They appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

He comforts the persecuted, advises the puzzled, and grieves beside the bereaved. Monks receive counsel on prayer; colleagues get news, thanks, and the odd rebuke. The controversialist of the great treatises steps aside, and a warm, wise counselor takes his place. Readers who know only the polemics will find the private man unexpectedly gentle. Taken together, the letters round out the fullest picture we have of his daily work.
athanasius-synodal-letter-to-the-bishops:
A council of bishops sent a joint letter across the sea to their colleagues in Africa. The Synodal Letter to the Bishops of Africa urges them to hold fast to Nicaea against Arian pressure. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition, under Athanasius's name.

The letter warns against new creeds and shifting formulas designed to blur the Son's full divinity. Behind it stands the machinery of fourth-century orthodoxy: bishops writing to bishops, slowly building consensus. Short and firm, it asks for loyalty more than argument. Historians value it as a snapshot of how the Nicene cause organized itself.
athanasius-the-historia-acephala-npnf2-1:
A fragmentary chronicle of Athanasius's exiles and returns survives without its beginning, hence its name: the Historia Acephala, the headless history. The bare record appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Dates and postings fill most of its brief lines.

Five banishments under four emperors shaped the strangest career of any ancient bishop. The chronicle lays out that skeleton in plain order, year by year. Historians prize the fragment far beyond its size. It works as a key for dating the whole Arian controversy, anchoring letters and councils that other sources leave floating.
athanasius-the-life-of-antony-npnf2-1892:
A hermit named Antony fled to the Egyptian desert, fought demons, and drew crowds seeking his counsel. Athanasius told his story in The Life of Antony, the biography that launched Western and Eastern monasticism alike. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Part saint's life and part adventure tale, the narrative follows Antony from a rich youth's renunciation to an old man's serene authority. Temptations, visions, and debates with philosophers fill the desert years. Thousands of readers answered the book by seeking God in the wilderness themselves. Augustine's own conversion turned after hearing Antony's story read aloud.
athanasius-to-the-bishops-of-egypt-ad-ep:
An Arian-leaning emperor pressed his policies on Egypt, and Athanasius rallied his fellow bishops by letter. To the Bishops of Egypt, a circular letter, appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Constantius and his court stand behind every line of it.

Athanasius documents violence against churches and exposes the intrigue driving it. He warns his colleagues which teachers to shun and which confessions to demand. The letter shows the great defender working as a strategist, holding a network together under pressure. Church politics rarely comes rawer than this dispatch from the center of the storm.
athanasius-tomus-ad-antiochenos-npnf2-18:
Years of schism in Antioch left rival orthodox parties refusing to share communion. Athanasius brokered peace in a formal statement called the Tomus ad Antiochenos. The short document appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

He stays precise about what truly matters and generous about the words used to say it. Both parties could sign without surrendering their core confession. The great controversialist appears here as a peacemaker, which surprises readers who know only his polemics. The tome still offers a model for ending a church split without giving up the truth. Its mix of firmness and tact remains rare in the heated records of that age.
basil-the-great-on-the-holy-spirit-npnf2:
Basil the Great wrote On the Holy Spirit to settle a fight over a few small words: how the Church should praise the Spirit. His treatise argues that the Holy Spirit is fully God. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition, and theologians call it the foundation stone of the doctrine of the Spirit.

Basil builds his case from scripture and from the Church's own worship, where the Spirit receives equal honor. Denying the Spirit's divinity was fashionable at court, so the book took courage as well as genius. His care with words is masterful; he refuses traps set by opponents watching every phrase. The work completed the doctrine of the Trinity for the Eastern Church. Its arguments still anchor teaching on the Spirit today.
basil-the-great-the-hexaemeron-nine-homi:
Nine sermons on the six days of creation, preached at Caesarea to working people, make up Basil's Hexaemeron. The Homilies on the Six Days of Creation appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Basil took his text from the opening of Genesis and his examples from the world outside the church doors.

Light, waters, plants, birds, and beasts each draw wonder and close attention. Scripture blends with the natural knowledge of his day, which he handles with respect. Artisans in his audience heard their own world praised as God's handiwork. The sermons inspired Ambrose and Augustine to attempt the same subject. Ancient preaching on nature rarely sounds this beautiful or this fresh.
basil-the-great-the-letters-of-basil-the:
More than three hundred letters survive from Basil the Great, and they read like the working archive of a saint who also ran a province-sized church. The Letters of Basil the Great appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Resistance to Arianism fills many of them, but not all.

Basil organizes allies, founds hospitals and poorhouses, counsels friends, and manages unruly monks. One letter begs grain for a starving town; the next settles a point of doctrine. The man credited with inventing the Christian hospital appears here in daily action. Administrators and pastors alike can study how he joined prayer to paperwork. Few ancient collections show leadership under pressure so fully.
biblia-sacra-vulgata-clementina-1592:
Jerome's Latin Bible, revised and issued under Pope Clement the Eighth in 1592, served as the Catholic Church's official scripture for nearly four centuries. The Biblia Sacra juxta Vulgatam Clementinam presents that Clementine Vulgate in Latin. Trent's council had declared the Vulgate the Church's authentic text, and this edition fixed its form.

Mass, schools, and theology across Catholic Europe all ran on these pages. Commentaries, sermons, and university debates quoted this wording for generations. Latin readers meet the Bible exactly as medieval and Counter-Reformation Christians knew it. The edition also anchors the history of the biblical text in the West. Anyone studying old quotations needs this version open beside them.
biographies-of-working-men-pg6492: Science writer Grant Allen profiles men who rose from humble beginnings through talent and hard work — engineers, inventors, and explorers among them. Each short life is meant to show what determination can achieve without wealth or rank. Written in the hopeful Victorian spirit of self-help, the book celebrates the dignity of labor and the power of perseverance.
blavatsky-from-the-caves-and-jungles-of-:
Young H. P. Blavatsky wrote home from her treks in India, and From the Caves and Jungles of Hindostan prints those notes in 1892. She had first writ them in her own tongue for a home crowd. Temples, caves, gurus, and strange tales fill her brisk, wry notes.

In these notes her famed Masters first take shape on the page. Hints of wise men who guide her path run through the treks. Fans call the book the seed of her whole myth. It also shows her gift as a vivid, fun guide. She wrote the notes at first in her home tongue of Russia. Their shift to English gave the West its first long look at her trek.
blavatsky-theosophical-glossary-1892:
Work on the words of a new creed fills The Theosophical Glossary, set out in print in 1892, just past H. P. Blavatsky's death. She had built a tongue for her creed from terms of the East, old myths, and lore of the occult. New fans oft got lost in that dense mix.

Each term gets a short gloss in this A to Z guide. Words from India, Greece, Egypt, and the Jews sit side by side. The guide is the first word book of the creed. It still helps fans crack her vast, dense books. Blavatsky died the year past this book came out in full. Her aides saw the press work through, from her notes and drafts.
bosanquet-history-aesthetic-1892:
A History of Aesthetic, published in 1892, is Bernard Bosanquet's survey of theories of beauty from the Greeks to the nineteenth century. It was among the first full histories of the subject in English, and it taught the field its own past.

Bosanquet moves from Plato and Plotinus through medieval and Renaissance thought to Kant, Hegel, and the moderns. His own idealism colors the story: art's history becomes spirit learning to see itself in form. The scholarship is generous, giving each age its due before judging it. Students used the book for decades, and its narrative still shapes how aesthetics is taught.
cia-0000009592:
France's current situation in October 1949 turns on a government shake-up, a CIA paper reports: Premier Henri Queuille resigned on October 5. The heading adds that the fall came as a direct result of pressures the title cuts off. France's Fourth Republic changed premiers often.

Cabinet crises in Paris were routine, yet each one tested the pro-American center against Gaullists and communists. Analysts explained who might form the next government and what would change. The paper shows political reporting at its most workmanlike: names, factions, and odds. It also captures why allies found the Fourth Republic so hard to rely on.
cia-0000009992:
Svay Rieng province, in Cambodia, is named in a January 1973 sighting of an American prisoner of war. Svay Rieng juts into South Vietnam like a beak, and its border country saw years of cross-border war. The report's heading notes a publication detail in shortened form.

A prisoner inside Cambodia that late in the war belonged to the border sanctuary story. His case could not be settled by the Paris process alone, since Cambodia's own war raged on. Officials filed the sighting for a Cambodian accounting that never fully came. This file keeps the claim, province and month attached.
cia-0000011592:
Communist plans for Laos were the subject of a special estimate, SNIE 68-2-60, issued in November 1960. Laos had slid into civil war that year, with the Pathet Lao backed by North Vietnam and the Soviet Union. American officials feared the small kingdom might fall and open Southeast Asia to wider communist gains.

The estimate weighs what the communists most likely meant to do next in Laos. It judges their talks, their fighting, and their ties to Hanoi and Moscow together. As a special estimate, it carried the community's focused judgment on a crisis that soon drew the United States into a long secret war.
cia-0000012292:
A conversation with Richard Helms about a report on large-scale Soviet military matters was recorded in August 1961. The report's source is blanked out in the title, but the file sits in the Penkovsky stream. Reports of Soviet preparations were the colonel's richest product, and they were argued over at the top before they were believed.

The record preserves the spoken side of the case, the talk behind the memos. Officers weighed scale, proof, and risk in a room rather than on paper. For readers, it is an oral trace of the summit business that paper alone never quite captures.
cia-0000012392:
Meeting number one, London, April 20, 1961, at the Mount Royal Hotel: the Penkovsky debriefings open with this record. Oleg Penkovsky, a Soviet intelligence colonel, had come to London with a trade delegation and a head full of secrets. His British and American handlers met him face to face for the first time, in a hotel the other guests took for ordinary.

The record opens the meeting series that fills much of this file. Session one set the pattern: hours of questions, answers, and growing trust. For readers, it is the first session of the Cold War's greatest debriefing, dated and placed.
cia-0000013892: An American pilot was captured and then handed to a Vietnamese security agent, in a CIA note dated October 6, 1967. The handover step is the heart of this short report. Passing a prisoner to security staff moved him from the battlefield into the prison system. The note traces that first link in a long chain of custody.
cia-0000014192: Probable reactions to certain U.S. courses of action are forecast in a CIA paper dated May 5, 1965. The paper stays general in its title, naming no single act. Its job was to guess how friends and foes would answer American moves. Such forecasts were a standard tool when officials weighed bold steps in the Cold War.
cia-0000014692: David Keppel, espionage, and Julius Rosenberg meet in a CIA file dated October 3, 1950. Keppel's name recurs in the Fuchs and Rosenberg circles of files. The fall of 1950 was the height of the atom spy hunt. A file tying a contact to Rosenberg shows how agents stitched the ring together, name by name.
cia-0000014792: Anti-Semitism and the Rosenberg Case, an essay by Lucy Dawidowicz, fills a CIA file dated October 1, 1971. The file notes what followed the essay's first words, clipped in the title. Dawidowicz asked whether bias against Jews had shaped the trial's fate. Keeping her essay shows the case still argued, on new grounds, in 1971.
cia-0000015492: Congressional letters were forwarded for a fitting reply in an untitled CIA record dated in 1961. Members of Congress often passed on mail from voters who wanted answers on saucers. Staff then owed a reply that was careful, formal, and safe to sign. The routing note shows that duty in motion, with the people's questions moving up the chain.
cia-0000020392: Information on Letelier and a man named Arria fills an untitled CIA record dated in 1976. Orlando Letelier was then the best-known Chilean exile voice in Washington. The title gives Arria no first name, so none is supplied here. Pairing the two names suggests shared circles among exiles, and the agency kept notes on those circles through that tense year.
cia-0000022492: Two prisoners of war were sighted in Gia Luong District, Ha Bac Province, a CIA record dated in 1973 reports. Ha Bac lay northeast of Hanoi, in country crossed by air routes of the war. The sighting came in the year American prisoners were meant to come home. Reports after the peace deal carried special weight, since each name bore on the final accounting.
cia-0000039792:
National Intelligence Estimate number 99, dated September 5, 1953, estimates the world situation through 1955. An estimate of this kind gathers the shared judgment of the whole intelligence community. Its canvas is the entire world at the height of the early Cold War.

Inside, the estimate weighs the balance between the Soviet bloc and the West. It looks ahead two years, judging where conflict was likely and where calm might hold. Readers can test its forecasts against the real 1954 and 1955. They can see how the young intelligence community read its world. That world was still shaped by war, empire, and new weapons.
cia-0000041192:
Broadcasts from North Vietnam carried more of Jane Fonda's alleged impressions, in a CIA record dated July 2, 1972. Like its companion file, this one uses the word alleged for her remarks. The talks in question were said to involve the prisoners she met.

Inside, a second set of reported impressions joins the first in the files. Keeping each broadcast separate let analysts track how the story changed. The file shows Hanoi's radio campaign in its daily form. One broadcast at a time, the visits and talks were turned into a steady stream of messages aimed at American listeners.
cia-0000045192:
A priest denied Duarte's remarks on the kidnapping negotiations, in a CIA record from Cuba dated October 1, 1985. Havana's voice entered the Salvadoran crisis through this denial. A priest speaking for the other account gave it a distinct tone.

Inside, the rebuttal of the president's version is preserved. Two accounts of secret talks cannot both be wholly true. The denial forced readers to choose between a president and a priest. The file holds that contest in miniature, a sign of how the kidnapping's story was fought over in public long after the talks themselves had ended.
cia-0000045492:
Yok cited a pledge by resistance forces to find the MIAs, in a CIA record dated October 1, 1986. Resistance forces in Southeast Asia still worked the old battlefields. Their local reach exceeded anything foreign searchers could manage alone.

Inside, the pledge to search for the missing is recorded as cited. Promises of help were common in the accounting's long diplomacy. Follow-through was rarer than promises in that long diplomacy. Every pledge was filed and dated for that reason, so later claims could be checked against it. The record preserves this 1986 vow from the resistance side, in the years when the search depended more and more on such local partners.
cia-0000048992: The massacre at El Mozote is the subject of a CIA item dated January 3, 1982, filed with the Truth Commission records. At El Mozote, soldiers killed hundreds of civilians, most of them women and children, in the war's worst single atrocity. The government denied it for years, which is why each paper in the file still matters.
cia-0000049092: Colonel Oscar Edgardo Casanova Vejar's involvement in the murder of the American churchwomen is the subject of a CIA item from 1984. Involvement, in the title's careful word, can cover many things, and the item's pages carry which one applied here, in the files' careful language. The item survives in the Truth Commission files.
cia-0000095092: Discrepancies between views of outgoing and incoming administrations in Mexico are the subject of declassified CIA document 0000095092, dated September 3, 1976. The heading promises a comparison across a change of government. Readers find a short declassified item on that gap in views, one of several Mexico records the agency filed in the same few days.
cia-0000096492: The Outlook for Hong Kong is the title of declassified CIA document 0000096492, dated July 5, 1967. The heading promises a forward look at the colony in four words. The brief file is a short declassified outlook item, companion to the agency's situation report on Hong Kong filed two months earlier in the same catalog run.
cia-0000098692: National Intelligence Bulletin article titled Angola: Press Reports of Captured, with the phrase cut short, is declassified CIA document 0000098692, dated October 1, 1975. The heading promises press-based reporting on Angola. Readers get the second of two same-day bulletin records on Angola, the pair showing one day's coverage of a single country in two forms.
cia-0000105892: Decision to Cancel, for Health and Security Reasons, President Sukarno's Sche is the heading, cut off mid-word, on declassified CIA document 0000105892, dated July 5, 1965. The title gives the reasons in full: health and security. What scheduled item was canceled breaks off at Sche in the released heading. The brief record is a cancellation notice from 1965 Jakarta reporting.
cia-0000107492: Communist China's Balance of Payments 1950-65 is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000107492, dated April 1, 1966. The heading sets a long span, fifteen years of China's payments with the outside world. Balance of payments is the ledger the title names. The brief record is a long-range economic study item, filed in the spring of 1966 as released.
cia-0000117892: Cuban International Activities Inimical to US Interests is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000117892, dated October 4, 1972. The heading uses a formal word, inimical, meaning harmful, for Cuban acts abroad. US interests are the harmed side named in the title itself. The brief record is an activities assessment item from the autumn of 1972 in the files.
cia-0000126892: A July 1977 CIA document covers South Africa's uranium enrichment program, with part of the file deleted before release. Pretoria's nuclear effort was among the Cold War's worst kept secrets. The paper preserves what the agency could report about that program at the time. Enrichment work mattered because it was the long road to a possible weapon, and tracking it shaped American pressure on Pretoria through the decade that followed.
cia-0000132292:
Situation Report 601 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series looks ahead to the opening moves of the ground war against Iraq. The record carries a January 1, 1991 date, weeks before the ground campaign actually began, so the report is a forecast rather than an after-action account.

Inside, analysts preview how the land phase of the war might open and what Saddam Hussein might do in reply. The second half of the headline is cut off in the record title. For readers, the interest is in comparing the agency's advance picture of the ground war with the campaign that followed.
cia-0000132592: Cuba possibly returning the Shell refinery to its British-Dutch owners fills item 14 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated August 5, 1960. The headline breaks off at the word ownership. The refinery fight had become the revolution's sharpest economic clash with foreign firms. The short item tracks talk of a restoration that season.
cia-0000135692: A document in Spanish dated 6 November 1960, held in the CIA's declassified 2506 Brigade papers. The brigade was a force of Cuban exiles in training for an amphibious landing against Castro's government. The record for this item names no subject, unit, or author. It belongs to the fall 1960 layer of the brigade's paperwork, preserved in the original language. Anything beyond that must come from the document's own pages.
cia-0000135892: From the CIA files comes a instruction dated 3 May 1954, long since declassified, on an instruction titled Nerve War Against Individuals, its named author deleted from the heading. Behind the paper stands PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA campaign against President Arbenz that closed with the 1954 coup in Guatemala. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000135992: The declassified CIA cable dated 1 February 1954 takes up views on the reasoning of IDEN B about communist actions, the heading breaking off at the end. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Read on its own terms, the record shows the operation at work in its own words, with some names still blacked out.
cia-0000136192: From 1 May 1954 comes a CIA cable, since declassified, on communication between SEMANTIC and a name cut off as seq, reported onward for ONTRICH. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. The paper trail here is small but direct, a single piece of the huge file the operation left behind.
cia-0000136692: The catalog dates this Spanish-language 2506 Brigade document to 3 January 1961 and marks the date as estimated. An earlier summary presented it as a cable that crossed channels and drew a quick reply; the record shows no such thing, and that account is dropped. What stands is a Spanish document of the exile brigade, then in training, released in the CIA's declassified 2506 files with an estimated date.
cia-0000140392: A researcher in hypnotism is recommended in this January 1957 letter. It concerns the military use of hypnotism. The man received his degree this year. cia-03177792: CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1958/04/05, a CIA publication. The April briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
cia-06772392: THE SITUATION IN VIETNAM, a CIA assessment. The Vietnam briefing. This file preserves that declassified paper. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
constantine-the-great-the-oration-of-the:
An address on religion, credited to Constantine himself, speaks to an assembly of Christian hearers. The Oration of the Emperor Constantine to the Assembly of the Saints survives in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Whether every word is the emperor's own remains debated.

The speech argues for one God from philosophy and prophecy alike. Most famously, it claims that the poet Virgil foretold Christ in verse. Pagan learning is pressed into Christian service throughout. Genuine or polished by other hands, the oration shows how the first Christian emperor wished to be heard: as a theologian seated on a throne.
constitution-grenada-1992: Grenada's 1973 Constitution, restored 1992, frames its island state. It survived invasion. The Tower library holds the full text. It weathered a storm. Troops landed. Order returned. Votes resumed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-kuwait-1992: Kuwait's 1962 Constitution, restored 1992, frames its emirate. It grants a lively parliament. The Tower library holds the full text. It survived invasion. Tanks rolled. Emir returned. Assembly debated. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-palau-1992: Palau's 1981 Constitution, amended 1992, frames its island republic. It guards the reefs. The Tower library holds the full text. It freed a Pacific gem. Trust ended. Votes ruled. Corals glowed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-surinam-1992: Suriname's 1987 Constitution, amended 1992, frames its republic. It ended army rule. The Tower library holds the full text. It freed Guiana. Soldiers left. Voters came. Jungle voted. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
cyril-of-jerusalem-catechetical-and-myst:
Eighteen lectures prepared converts for baptism in fourth-century Jerusalem, and five more explained the rites afterward. Cyril of Jerusalem delivered that course, preserved as the Catechetical and Mystagogic Lectures. They appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Nothing fuller survives from ancient Christian initiation.

Cyril walks candidates through the creed, article by article, in plain and warm language. After baptism, the mystagogic talks unveil what the water, oil, and bread and wine truly mean. Readers see exactly what the fourth-century Church taught and how it taught it. The setting adds drama: these words were spoken within sight of the places where Jesus suffered and rose. Teachers still mine the course for its method.
engels-utopian-scientific-aveling-1892:
Socialism: Utopian and Scientific is Engels's short, clear digest of the Marxist view of history and society. Edward Aveling translated this English edition, published in 1892, from chapters Engels first wrote as a polemic in German. At about sixty pages, it became the most read pamphlet of the movement.

Engels contrasts early socialist dreamers, who sketched perfect societies, with the scientific socialism he shared with Marx. That science rests on historical materialism, the claim that production shapes law, politics, and ideas. Generations of new recruits met Marxism first through these pages. Its plain style made hard ideas open to working readers everywhere.
ephraim-the-syrian-selections-from-the-h:
Ephraim the Syrian earned a title no other poet of the early Church can match: the harp of the Holy Spirit. Selections from his hymns and homilies, written in Syriac on the empire's eastern frontier, appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. His medium was song as much as argument.

Faith, repentance, and paradise glow through his verses, which congregations sang rather than merely read. Ephraim taught doctrine by melody, answering heresy with hymns people could carry home. His images of Eden and the tree of life remain startlingly fresh. The greatest poet of the Syriac Church speaks here in English dress. Readers who know only Greek and Latin fathers will find a whole new climate of devotion.
europmc-pmc10034092:
Guo and co-authors review off-target effects in CRISPR and Cas9 gene editing in a 2023 paper. CRISPR tools cut DNA at chosen sites with great speed and ease. Yet the Cas9 enzyme can also cut at similar sites that were never intended, and those stray cuts can cause harm.

The review explains why off-target cuts happen and how labs detect them. It covers improved enzymes, guide design, and delivery tricks that cut the error rate. The paper is a practical guide to making gene editing safer for research and future therapy.
europmc-pmc10234592:
Low back pain across the world is charted by the GBD 2021 Low Back Pain Collaborators in a 2023 study. Back pain is the top cause of years lived with disability worldwide. The team gathered data for 1990 to 2020 and projected the burden forward to 2050, country by country.

Their analysis gives rates of back pain and disability for regions and nations. It also weighs the risk factors behind the pain, such as work strain and excess weight. The projections warn of a growing load as populations age. Health planners can use the figures to prepare.
europmc-pmc10376292:
Satam and co-authors surveyed DNA reading tools in 2023, with a focus on the newest wave. The wave is called next-generation sequencing, or NGS for short. It reads millions of DNA pieces at once, at speed and at low cost. Past gains have cut errors and sped up the work still more.

Satam tracks how the tools serve gene studies of cancer, germs, and microbe groups. Clinics use them to spot rare gene diseases and to guide care tuned to one patient. That tuning rests on maps of gene changes and gene activity in each case. Open problems include sharper accuracy and better software for the flood of data. Costs must also keep falling for wider use.
europmc-pmc10584692:
The GBD Spinal Cord Injuries Collaborators charted spinal cord injury worldwide from 1990 to 2019. Such injury is a major cause of early death and lasting disability. It can stem from falls, road crashes, and other trauma. The study pools data for 204 nations and areas.

In 2019, 20.6 million people lived with spinal cord injury. New cases that year came to 0.9 million new cases. Total counts rose sharply over those years, with prevalence up 81.5 percent since 1990. Rates per head, once age was weighed, barely moved. Men bore higher rates than women in each count. Falls led the causes, at 477,000 cases, then road injuries at 230,000. Neck-level injury was more common than injury below the neck.
europmc-pmc12169392:
Beniczky and a global panel updated seizure classification in 2025. The panel works for the International League Against Epilepsy. Clear seizure classes guide diagnosis and treatment worldwide. The prior framework dated to 2017, and field use exposed gaps.

Thirty-seven experts from all regions revised the system by consensus voting. Public comments brought seven more experts into the task force. Four main classes remain: focal, generalized, unknown, and unclassified. New rules split features that change care from features that merely describe. Beniczky aims for a system clinicians can apply the same way everywhere.
europmc-pmc12254192:
GBD 2021 Stroke Risk Factor Collaborators measured stroke burden and risks in 2024. Stroke strikes when blood flow to the brain fails or a vessel bursts. Fresh global numbers guide care, prevention, and funding choices. The team covered the years 1990 to 2021.

Estimates span 204 countries for new cases, deaths, and disability. In 2021, stroke ranked as the third most common cause of death. Burden was also tied to 23 risk factors in six clusters. Clusters range from air pollution to metabolic risks. GBD 2021 Stroke Risk Factor Collaborators show where prevention can cut harm most. Blocked-vessel strokes made up about two thirds of new cases.
europmc-pmc1386692:
Ratziu and co-authors tested a blood test for liver scarring in fatty liver disease in 2006. Liver biopsy is the standard for grading fatty liver damage. The blood panel, FibroTest, was validated for viral hepatitis and alcohol disease. Whether it works for fatty liver was untested.

One group held 170 suspected patients at a reference center. A second held 97 patients across centers, plus 954 blood donor controls. Biopsy grading used a five-stage scale from none to cirrhosis. Test accuracy was measured with standard diagnostic statistics. Ratziu checks if a needle-free panel can stage fatty liver.
europmc-pmc1472692:
A few wild data points can bend a fitted curve and spoil a result. Motulsky and Brown offered a fix in 2006 for nonlinear regression, the fitting of curved models to data. Standard fitting assumes scatter follows a bell shape, so outliers drag the curve hard.

Their ROUT method first fits with a hardy method that resists outliers. It then flags points that stray too far, using a rule that limits false alarms. In tests on fake data, false flags stayed near one to three percent. Real outliers were caught well. Motulsky suggests the two-step route makes outlier hunting a routine part of curve fitting.
europmc-pmc1769492:
Rice splices its gene messages in many more ways than once thought. Campbell and co-authors analyzed alternative splicing in rice in 2006, using over 1.1 million public sequence tags and 30,000 full-length copies. A parallel analysis in Arabidopsis allowed a monocot-dicot comparison.

Over 30 percent of supported rice loci showed alternative splicing. Most loci still made only two or three variants. The commonest gap between alternative acceptor sites was 3 base pairs in both species, matching mammals. Most variations fell in protein-coding regions and would change the protein meaningfully. Campbell finds splicing widespread but restrained in scale per gene.
europmc-pmc1802092:
Riaño-Pachón and colleagues launched PlnTFDB in 2007, a database that gathers plant transcription factors in one place. Transcription factors are proteins that raise or lower the rate at which target genes are read. They steer growth, development, and stress responses, and breeders use them to reshape plant traits.

Before this work, no single repository offered near-complete factor sets for sequenced plant genomes. PlnTFDB opened with five species: thale cress, poplar, rice, and two small green algae, Chlamydomonas reinhardtii and Ostreococcus tauri. A web interface lets users browse the sets and follow links into species-centered daughter databases. The resource was built to support cross-species comparison and the search for shared regulatory modules. Such comparisons can guide rational design of plants grown for biomass.
europmc-pmc1949492:
Nielsen, Buus, Lund and colleagues built NetMHCpan in 2007, a predictor that estimates peptide binding for any human MHC class I protein of known sequence. Peptide binding to these molecules is the most selective step in cellular immune recognition of pathogens. The human system is hugely variable, with over 1,500 registered variants, far too many to test one by one.

The method trains on a large database of known peptide and HLA interactions, using both the peptide and the HLA sequence as input. It outputs a quantitative affinity for any pairing, including variants never tested in a lab. Bench tests on newly predicted binders, cross-checks, and recovery of known HIV epitopes and natural presented peptides all validated it. Clustering variants by predicted taste may guide which new molecules to characterize first.
europmc-pmc2125392: A medical paper contributing to the biology of peripheral nerves in transplantation. The grafted nerves. This article preserves that neurology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2125492: A medical paper on proteose intoxications and injury of body protein, metabolism of dogs. The poisoned protein. This article preserves that biochemistry. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2126292: A medical paper on acid production graphically registered as an indicator of the vital processes. The graphed acid. This article preserves that physiology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc212692:
Simmer and co-workers ran a genome-wide gene-silencing screen in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans in 2003. RNA interference, shortened to RNAi, switches genes off using double-stranded RNA. A feeding library covered nearly 90 percent of the worm's 19,427 predicted genes. In normal worms it revealed functions for only about 10 percent of genes. The team suspected a mutant strain called rrf-3, being hypersensitive to RNAi, would reveal more.

Feeding the library to rrf-3 mutants produced new loss-of-function effects for 393 genes. That raised the count of genes with a known phenotype by 23 percent. The new effects spread across many phenotype classes. The team also measured variability between experiments and found persistent false negatives. Using screen results, they cloned seven existing mutants with visible traits. The data set strengthens functional genomics in the worm.
europmc-pmc2128292: A medical paper on experimental syphilis in the rabbit, cutaneous syphilis part one. The skin pox again. This article preserves that venereology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2131292: A medical paper on influence of light on the growth of a transplantable neoplasm. The lit tumor again. This article preserves that oncology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2140392: A biology paper on the nature of the growth rate. The speed of growth. This article preserves that biology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2235892:
Cikos, Bukovská and Koppel compared six analysis methods in 2007 for relative quantification of gene messages by real-time PCR. This technique measures fluorescent signals as DNA copies multiply, and the analysis method can strongly sway the result. The team quantified four cytokine transcripts in a rat model of colon inflammation. They tested accuracy on samples with known relative amounts, and reproducibility within and between assay runs.

The relative standard curve method and the comparative Ct method performed best. Three efficiency-based methods also performed well when average amplification efficiency was used. Using each gene's individual efficiency significantly worsened those methods' results. The sigmoid curve-fitting method performed moderately and needs careful data choices. All methods could flag genes whose efficiency truly differed. The authors advise matching method choice to experimental design.
europmc-pmc2270292:
Heazlewood and a large team created mouse models in 2008 linking mucin misfolding to gut inflammation resembling ulcerative colitis. MUC2 mucin, made by intestinal goblet cells, forms the gut's protective mucus barrier. Human ulcerative colitis shows depleted goblet cells and a thin mucus layer. Using random chemical mutagenesis, the team found two distinct mutations in the mouse Muc2 gene that produce colitis-like disease, then characterised the pathology in detail.

All mutant mice developed mild spontaneous intestinal inflammation by six weeks, with chronic diarrhoea. By one year, 25 and 40 percent of the two strains had severe clinical disease. Mutant goblet cells stored less mucin, showed precursor build-up and clear signs of endoplasmic reticulum stress, the cell's protein-folding overload response. Gut permeability doubled. Human ulcerative colitis tissue showed similar precursor accumulation and stress signs, even where uninflamed.
europmc-pmc2329592:
Lombaert and co-authors tested stem cell treatment for dry mouth in 2008. Radiation for head and neck cancer often damages the salivary glands, leaving patients with lasting dry mouth. Stem cells are cells that can grow into several mature cell types, so the team hoped they could rebuild gland tissue.

They grew mouse salivary gland cells in small balls that held stem-like cells marked by proteins named Sca-1, c-Kit, and Musashi-1. Picking out the c-Kit cells enriched the stem cells. In the lab these cells matured into gland cells that made amylase, a saliva enzyme. When placed into irradiated mouse glands, even a small number restored gland shape and saliva flow for the long term. Cells from treated mice could be grown again and help a second mouse.
europmc-pmc2363992:
Bagnardi, Blangiardo, La Vecchia, and Corrao pooled the evidence on alcohol and cancer in 2001. They covered 18 cancer sites, searching studies from 1966 to 2000. In total 235 studies with over 117,000 cancer cases went into the analysis.

Risk rose most strongly for cancers of the mouth, throat, food pipe, and voice box, climbing steadily with dose. Weaker but clear links appeared for cancers of the stomach, colon, liver, breast, and ovary. Even 25 grams of alcohol a day, roughly three small drinks, raised risk for all of these. No consistent link showed for pancreas, lung, prostate, or bladder cancers. Adjusting for smoking changed the voice box, lung, and bladder results most. For most sites there was no safe threshold dose in the data.
europmc-pmc2410292:
Carlson and a large team screened thousands of cancer patients for distress in 2004. Over a four-week sweep, 3,095 patients at a Canadian cancer centre completed a symptom inventory and a checklist of common problems. Full data came back for 2,776 patients, averaging 60 years old.

In all, 37.8% scored in the clinical range for general distress. Men more often showed body-focused symptoms, called somatisation, and women more often depression, while anxiety matched between sexes. Distress ran highest in lung, pancreatic, head and neck, Hodgkin, and brain cancers. Patients from minority groups, with lower income, or on active treatment were also more likely to be distressed. Nearly half of those in the clinical range had never sought support and did not plan to. The authors said services must reach out rather than wait.
europmc-pmc2442192:
Fabian and colleagues measured flu virus in the breath of infected patients in 2008. How flu spreads, by large droplets or by fine floating particles, decides which controls work. The team recruited patients at three Hong Kong clinics within three days of falling ill, confirmed by rapid tests.

Twelve patients with confirmed influenza A or B breathed onto Teflon filters while a counter sized the particles they exhaled. Virus RNA turned up in the breath of four patients, a third of the group: three of five with influenza A, and one of seven with influenza B. Emission rates ran from under 3.2 to 20 virus RNA copies per minute. Over 87% of exhaled particles were under one micrometre wide, fine enough to float. The authors said normal tidal breathing can carry flu virus in such fine particles.
europmc-pmc2481392:
Ospina-Alvarez and Piferrer re-checked claims of temperature-set sex in fish in 2008. In some reptiles, nest temperature decides sex, a system called temperature-dependent sex determination. Textbooks said the same system was very common in fish, with three different response patterns to warmth.

The authors audited all 59 fish species where the claim had been made, checking for sex chromosomes and whether the test temperatures occur in the wild. Many celebrated cases collapsed into ordinary genetic sex determination that heat merely perturbs. In the species with genuine temperature control, the pattern was always the same: warmer water means more males. A rise of just 1 to 2 degrees could shift a balanced brood to three males per female. That makes such species vulnerable to climate warming, they warned, even though true cases are far rarer than believed.
europmc-pmc2552992:
Chen and colleagues examined in 2008 how cigarette smoke drives lung damage in COPD, a progressive disease that destroys lung tissue and narrows airflow. Their focus was autophagy, the process by which cells digest and recycle their own parts, which microscope images showed running high in COPD lungs. The team exposed human lung cells to cigarette smoke extract to find the switch.

Smoke rapidly triggered autophagy by lowering the activity of enzymes called HDACs, freeing two factors, Egr-1 and E2F, to switch on the autophagy gene LC3B. Blocking Egr-1 cut the response, and blocking autophagy protected cells from smoke-induced death. Mice lacking Egr-1 resisted smoke-driven autophagy, cell death, and emphysema, the lung destruction that marks the disease.
europmc-pmc2573892:
Razick, Magklaras, and Donaldson built a unifying index in 2008 for protein interaction data scattered across nine databases. Records of which proteins bind which live in BIND, BioGRID, IntAct, and others, each naming proteins differently, so the same interaction appears many times under mismatched labels. Their system, iRefIndex, generates a key for each record from the protein sequences themselves and a hash algorithm.

Records whose keys match count as the same interaction, however the sources labelled them. Mapping source references to current sequence records also yields a score flagging malformed or outdated entries for the databases to fix. Participant keys let users pull every interaction for a protein regardless of the reference used. The index is published in a standard format for free use.
europmc-pmc2634792:
Little and the expert STrengthening the REporting of Genetic Association Studies working group set out guidelines in 2009 for reporting studies that link genes to disease. Such studies had grown fast, doubling in number between 2001 and 2008, yet many reports left out key details. Missing details made it hard to judge which claimed gene links were real.

The group built their advice as an add-on to the STROBE rules for health studies that observe people rather than test treatments. Their checklist asks authors to state clearly how people were chosen, how genes were measured, and how the numbers were handled. It also covers lab methods, possible bias, and how results were checked. Clearer reports, they argue, let readers weigh the proof and combine results across studies with more trust.
europmc-pmc2656492:
Azizi and colleagues set out in 2009 the second phase of a long health program in Tehran, run with the Tehran Lipid and Glucose Study Group. Iran was shifting fast toward city diets and less active lives, and diseases such as diabetes and heart disease were rising. The study, begun in 1999, planned to run at least twenty years.

In the first phase, the team measured over 15,000 residents older than three. They recorded blood fats, blood sugar, blood pressure, and body size. They also took heart tracings and stored a DNA bank. In phase two, 5,630 people received a lifestyle program while 9,375 served as a comparison group. The program worked through schools, housewives, and high-risk adults, with city officials, police, media, and local leaders helping to deliver it. The goal: test whether community-wide changes in diet, smoking, and activity delay chronic disease.
europmc-pmc2730292:
Jernigan and co-authors, with the National Anthrax Epidemiologic Investigation Team, reported in 2002 the investigation of the 2001 bioterrorism anthrax attacks in the United States. The first inhaled anthrax case since 1976 appeared in a Florida media worker in October 2001. A national search through clinics and labs then looked for more cases and common exposures.

From early October to late November, twenty-two cases were confirmed, eleven inhaled and eleven skin cases, and five inhaled cases died. Twenty patients handled mail or worked where contaminated mail was processed or received. Bacteria from patients, four powder envelopes, and many site samples matched by molecular typing, which showed one source strain moving along mail paths.
europmc-pmc2800192:
Daigneault and colleagues compared ways of turning a lab cell line into stand-ins for macrophages, the tissue guard cells that eat germs and debris. The line, called THP-1, is easy to grow, but simple treatments may leave the cells only half changed. In 2010 they tested two chemical triggers against real macrophages grown from human blood cells, called MDM.

Neither trigger alone matched the real cells. A modified plan, treating with the chemical PMA and then resting the cells five days without it, came much closer. Those cells gained more power units and waste sacs, resisted cell death, ate particles well, and answered bacterial signals much like real macrophages, while staying flexible in their responses.
europmc-pmc2811892:
Bermejo-Martin and a large team profiled the early immune response in 2009 to the new pandemic flu virus, called nvH1N1. They measured twenty-nine signaling proteins and antibody levels in blood taken within five days of first symptoms, comparing twenty hospitalized patients with fifteen mild cases and fifteen healthy donors.

Both patient groups showed strong innate signals, meaning first-response alarms, and no detectable antibodies yet. Only the hospitalized group carried high levels of two helper T-cell signal sets, Th1 and Th17, which are also linked to autoimmune flares. Three signals in particular marked the sickest patients. The authors say whether this surge helps or harms still needs study.
europmc-pmc2829492:
Zhou and colleagues found in 2010 why some breast cancer cells stop answering to the drug Taxol, and how to make them listen again. Taxol works well at first, yet most patients' cancers grow resistant over time. The team compared resistant cells grown from a breast cancer line with their drug-sensitive parents.

Resistant cells carried far more of an enzyme called LDH-A, which steers sugar breakdown toward lactate, a pattern known as the Warburg effect. Silencing the enzyme's gene made resistant cells sensitive to Taxol again. An LDH blocker called oxamate hit resistant cells hardest, and pairing it with Taxol killed them together more strongly than either alone, by pushing them into programmed death.
europmc-pmc2885492:
Harrison and co-authors probed in 2009 how inflammation produces the fatigue and mental fog of being sick, using a vaccine as a safe trigger. Sixteen healthy men received either typhoid vaccine or salt water in a crossover design, then performed a demanding word-color task inside a brain scanner two hours later. Blood tests confirmed the vaccine raised an inflammatory messenger, interleukin-6.

Vaccine recipients reported more fatigue, confusion, and poor concentration by three hours. During the task, inflammation changed activity in brain regions that sense the body's internal state, including areas that track signals from the organs. The pattern fits an interoceptive route, where the brain reads immune signals from the body and reshapes motivation and effort. Sickness behavior looks like a brain state, not mere weakness.
europmc-pmc2945792:
Betel and colleagues introduced a learning method called mirSVR for ranking where small regulatory RNAs called microRNAs bind their target messages, in a 2010 study. Predicting such targets reliably remains an open computing problem.

The method trains on sequence and context features of predicted binding sites and scores each site by how strongly the target drops. In large tests the combined tool matched rival predictors at finding real targets and gauging their fall. Notably, it recovered many confirmed sites that break the usual rules, sites that are neither conserved across species nor matching the standard pattern.
europmc-pmc300692:
Kondo, Kim, Lechpammer, and Kaelin showed in 2003 that blocking a single oxygen-sensing factor stops kidney tumours lacking the VHL tumour suppressor from growing. Loss of VHL causes inherited and sporadic clear-cell kidney cancers by failing to destroy that factor when oxygen is plentiful.

A version of the factor HIF2-alpha that cannot be tagged for destruction overcame the suppressor's restraint on tumour growth, in a way needing its DNA binding. Conversely, quietening HIF2-alpha with short RNA strands was enough to stop VHL-defective kidney cancer cells forming tumours. The result welds tumour suppression by VHL to control of this one factor's gene programme.
europmc-pmc3018492:
Braun and colleagues tracked the plastic chemical bisphenol A in urine across pregnancy in a 2011 study of nearly four hundred women. Prenatal exposure may harm development, yet how steady a person's levels are was unknown.

Three samples per woman, at two pregnancy points and at birth, showed levels wobbling so much that one sample poorly represents the whole pregnancy. Cashiers, who handle thermal receipts, carried the highest levels. Eating canned vegetables daily also tracked with higher levels, while fresh produce and fish did not. A single spot test, the authors warn, badly misjudges exposure.
europmc-pmc3061292:
Litvak and coauthors described in 2011 the brain wave tools inside SPM8, a widely used free software package for brain imaging. The package handles recordings of electric and magnetic brain signals, called EEG and MEG, within the same framework as its better known scanner tools. The paper lays out three main analysis routes the software offers.

One route runs statistical tests on scalp maps, time and frequency images, and three dimensional source images, with safeguards against false positives. A second route rebuilds likely brain sources using probability based methods, for single subjects or groups, and can borrow guidance from scanner images. A third route builds causal models of how brain areas drive each other. The tools connect with a partner toolbox for standard preprocessing. Together they let labs build custom pipelines, from raw signals to publication figures, in one environment.
europmc-pmc3101192:
Baek, Li, and Sassetti found in 2011 why tuberculosis bacteria can shrug off antibiotics that kill them easily in a dish. Treating tuberculosis takes months, a fact long blamed on slow growing, dormant bacteria in the body. The team showed that many different stresses flip one shared switch in the bacterium, redirecting its carbon into fat storage and away from its central energy cycle.

That switch slows growth and blunts antibiotic killing as a direct result. Mutant bacteria unable to flip it kept growing under stress and stayed drug sensitive, even inside an infected host. The pathway thus explains a real slice of drug tolerance during infection, not just in glassware. The authors propose jamming the switch as a way to shorten tuberculosis therapy, one of the field's oldest goals. Their mutants offer a test bed for finding such jammers.
europmc-pmc3123192:
Regina Lamendella and colleagues sequenced DNA from pig faeces to map the swine gut in a 2011 paper in BMC Microbiology. Gut microbes shape pig health and growth, and pig waste can carry germs dangerous to people, yet the community's working genes were largely unknown. Their survey read well over a hundred million DNA letters.

Two broad bacterial groups dominated, with one genus especially common in pigs. Sugar breakdown was the single biggest job found among the genes. Genes for stress survival, cell defences, and resistance to antibiotics were also plentiful, many of them closest to genes from gut bacteria. The authors suggest farm practices, including feed and drug use, shape this community, with lessons for animal care and food safety.
europmc-pmc3123292:
Sarel Fleishman and colleagues introduced a scripting system for protein modelling in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. The underlying Rosetta software can dock molecules, redesign protein sequences, and model shapes, but using it meant editing program code. That barrier kept many non-specialists from trying advanced modelling tasks.

Their system lets users describe a modelling job in a simple text file. Users mix building blocks such as docking, redesign, and loop rebuilding, then run the job without touching the core code. Workflows can be tested and shared quickly. The paper shows examples ranging from steadying a protein to designing binders for DNA and small molecules. The authors aim to open serious molecular design to a wider circle of researchers and students.
europmc-pmc3142492:
Joan Vermeulen and colleagues reviewed signs that predict loss of daily independence in older people in a 2011 paper in BMC Geriatrics. Frailty raises the risk that an older person can no longer manage washing, dressing, and other daily tasks at home. Knowing which single physical signs warn earliest could target help where it counts.

From thousands of papers, twenty-eight long-term studies of high quality survived screening. Slow walking speed and low activity stood out as the strongest warnings of coming disability. Weight loss, weak legs, poor balance, and weak grip also predicted decline. Studies defined their measures too differently to pool into one number, a caveat the authors stress. Still, they recommend watching these signs in community-dwelling older people to trigger timely support.
europmc-pmc3153392:
Thomas Lang and colleagues showed that fatty muscle predicts hip fracture in older adults in a 2010 paper in the Journal of Bone and Mineral Research. As people age, fat creeps into muscle, weakening it and raising fall risk. Whether that fatty change itself forecasts a broken hip was unknown, so the team scanned the thighs of nearly three thousand people in their seventies.

Over about six years, dozens of hip fractures occurred. People whose thigh muscle scans showed more fat faced clearly higher fracture risk, even after accounting for bone density, muscle size, strength, and walking performance. None of those other muscle measures stayed predictive once fatty change was included. The scan trait seems to capture something about muscle quality that matters for fracture risk.
europmc-pmc3176892:
Gregor Thut and colleagues gave the first direct proof that rhythmic magnetic stimulation can entrain natural brain rhythms in a 2011 paper in Current Biology. Brain waves correlate with perception and attention, but whether they cause anything stayed open. The team targeted a rhythm over the brain's attention region, identified by magnetic recording, with stimulation bursts tuned to its own tempo while recording brain waves.

Three marks of true entrainment appeared. The rhythm was induced during stimulation, it grew progressively as the train continued, and the effect hinged on the rhythm's phase just before each burst. Different burst patterns and a dummy head ruled out artefacts. The result shows the stimulation acts by syncing real neural oscillators, explaining its tempo-specific effects on behaviour.
europmc-pmc3187792:
Marco Pitino and colleagues silenced aphid genes by feeding the insects on engineered plants in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Gene silencing by double-stranded RNA is a key research tool in aphids, but earlier delivery meant injecting insects or feeding artificial diets, far from real life. The team instead made plants produce the silencing RNA against two aphid genes, one gut and one saliva related.

Aphids feeding on the plants showed gene activity cut by well over half for both targets, matching the older methods. europmc-pmc3261192:
Cecele Denman and colleagues found a better way to grow natural killer cells for cancer therapy, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. These immune cells attack tumors, but they expand poorly in culture, live briefly, and are scarce in blood, so getting enough cells is the main obstacle to treatment. europmc-pmc3281992:

The team tested that dependency in mouse embryonic stem cells lacking PRC2.

europmc-pmc3310792:
Perera and colleagues showed that dengue virus rewires the fats inside the mosquito cells it infects, in a 2012 study. Dengue sickens tens of millions of people yearly and rebuilds the inner membranes of infected cells into factories for copying itself. Using precise chemical measurement tools on infected mosquito cells, the team cataloged how the fat mix changed.

A distinct set of fats appeared in infected cells, and the change ran far deeper inside the isolated copying factories. Fats that bend membranes or change how easily they merge became more common, along with signaling fats tied to cell structure. Blocking the cell's main fat building enzyme still let cells live but sharply cut virus copying. The findings frame fats as active partners in infection, not just raw material.
europmc-pmc3396592:
Hosseini, Hoeft, and Kesler presented a software toolbox in 2012 for comparing brain networks between groups using graph theory. Graph methods reveal how large brain networks are organized, but few pipelines made group comparison easy. Their toolbox, called GAT, wraps the workflow in a graphical interface.

It builds networks, measures local and global layout, finds hubs and modules, and stress-tests networks against random or targeted damage. Built-in statistics reduce sensitivity to arbitrary cutoff choices. To show it off, the team compared gray-matter networks of leukemia survivors with healthy peers. The survivors' networks showed altered small-world layout, backing the idea of widespread brain injury after treatment.
europmc-pmc3439392:
Wyld, Morton, Hayen, Howard, and Webster pooled published studies in 2012 to compare quality of life across treatments for chronic kidney disease, using utility scores. Such scores compress health into a single number that health economists need when weighing treatments. The treatments ranged from dialysis in its several forms to kidney transplantation.

Transplantation earned the highest utility of all, giving patients the best-rated quality of life. Home-based automated peritoneal dialysis came second, ahead of other dialysis arrangements. The ranking matters because kidney care is expensive and lifelong, and small quality differences multiply across many patients and years. Their pooled figures give planners consistent numbers drawn from the whole literature rather than single studies.
europmc-pmc3477592:
Xiong and colleagues asked what shapes the bacteria living in salty lake mud across the Tibetan Plateau, in Environmental Microbiology in 2012. Bacteria sort themselves by place and chemistry in soils and seas, but lake sediments were little studied. The team read bacterial DNA from sediments of fifteen lakes spread over a vast, high region, and compared communities with lake chemistry and distance.

The sediment communities proved rich and distinct from soil ones. Acidity, measured as pH, best predicted which bacteria lived where, even in these alkaline lakes. Distance mattered too: farther lakes held more unlike communities. Xiong's group argues both chemistry and history govern these hidden communities, a pattern planners of microbial surveys should expect.
