Gunga Din honors an Indian water carrier braver than the men he serves. Kipling's driving rhythms and honest soldier talk broke with polite Victorian verse and stayed popular for generations.
kneipp-my-water-cure-1892:
Sebastian Kneipp, a Bavarian priest, claimed cold water saved his life, and My Water Cure spread his method worldwide. The English edition of 1892 reports thirty years of testing at Wörishofen, where crowds came seeking help. Kneipp's system used water in many forms, plus herbs, food, and daily routine.

Affusions, baths, wraps, and barefoot walks in wet grass all have their place and their rules. Kneipp explains which treatment fits which complaint, and how gently to begin. His cure made hydrotherapy a world movement, and health resorts still use versions of his water treatments today.
krafft-ebing-psychopathia-chaddock-1892:
Richard von Krafft-Ebing published Psychopathia Sexualis in German in 1886. The English text here is Charles G. Chaddock's translation of 1892. Krafft-Ebing was a psychiatrist who catalogued sexual behavior that his age called perversion. Case histories, many in Latin in the early editions, fill the book.

He coined or spread terms such as sadism, masochism, and fetishism. His aim was medical and legal: to place such cases before doctors and courts. Modern readers fault his labels and his era's bias. Yet the book founded the study of sexual pathology. It shaped both psychiatry and the language still used for desire's extremes.
kyd-spanish-tragedy-1592:
Thomas Kyd's Spanish Tragedy, first staged in the late 1580s and printed in 1592, set the pattern for Elizabethan revenge drama. Kyd was a London playwright about whom little else is known. His play was quoted, copied, and parodied for a generation.

Don Andrea's ghost and Revenge watch the action from above. Hieronimo, a Spanish marshal, finds his son Horatio murdered and feigns madness while he plots his answer. The play within the play, the letters in blood, and the final carnage all became stock devices. Shakespeare's Hamlet grew directly from this soil, and Kyd's tragedy still holds the stage.
laing-human-origins-1892:
Samuel Laing, a Scottish writer and former official, published Human Origins in 1892. He applied Darwin's ideas to the earliest history of humankind. The book appeared serially first and reached a wide popular audience.

Laing discusses the antiquity of the human race and the Aryan question. He follows early humans toward the first steps of civilization. His tone is brisk, rational, and Victorian to the core. Some positions now read as dated period pieces. The work remains a readable snapshot of 1890s popular Darwinism. Laing brought the same plain skepticism to religion, history, and human beginnings alike.
leo-the-great-the-letters-of-leo-the-gre:
Pope Leo the First faced down Attila the Hun outside Rome, and governed the Church with the same nerve by letter. The Letters of Leo the Great appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Doctrine, discipline, and diplomacy share his desk in these pages.

His famous Tome to Flavian, read aloud at the Council of Chalcedon, fixed the Church's teaching on Christ's two natures. Bishops across the world wrote to him, and his answers set precedents for centuries. The letters show a pope ruling a universal Church by pen, courier, and sheer clarity. Few collections reveal so well how Rome's authority actually worked. Students of doctrine and church order both need this correspondence.
leo-the-great-the-sermons-of-leo-the-gre:
Ninety-six sermons survive from Leo the Great, the pope who talked Attila out of sacking Rome. The Sermons of Leo the Great cover Christmas, Easter, the saints' days, fasting, and almsgiving. They appear in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Leo preaches with doctrinal precision and pastoral warmth in the same breath. Great feasts become lessons in what the incarnation means for ordinary believers. His Christmas sermons, urging Christians to recognize their dignity, are quoted to this day. Theology turns into food for everyday people without losing its edge. These are the classic sermons of the early Roman Church, from its greatest early pope.
limborch-historia-inquisitionis-latin-16:
Philipp van Limborch published his Historia Inquisitionis at Amsterdam in 1692, in Latin, the language of learned Europe. The text here is that original edition, the one Samuel Chandler later turned into English. Limborch, a Remonstrant professor, wrote the classic Protestant history of the Inquisition from the Toulouse records.

The work traces persecution from the early church to the papal tribunal and the Albigensian wars. Appended stands the Liber Sententiarum, the book of sentences of Toulouse, his documentary proof. Limborch argued from paper, not from polemic, and that made his book hard to answer. It fixed the image of the Inquisition in the European mind for two hundred years.
limborch-liber-sententiarum-tholosanus-1:
The Liber Sententiarum is the sentence book of the Inquisition of Toulouse for the years 1307 to 1323. Philipp van Limborch published the Latin record at Amsterdam in 1692, as the proof volume of his history of the Inquisition. It is a first-order trial source: the tribunal's own register of its judgments against the men and women of Languedoc.

Page after page names the accused, the errors laid on them, and the penances set. These run from yellow crosses and pilgrimages to prison on bread and water, or the flames for the relapsed. Cathars and Waldensians pass through the register beside careless talkers caught by informers. Historians of heresy still quarry this book. Its dry Latin is the sound of the machine working.
lodge-modern-views-electricity-1892:
Oliver Lodge set out his full view of electricity in this book of 1892. He treats electric force as the work of the ether, the unseen stuff in all space. The book was the high mark of Victorian ether physics in a clear, strong form.

Lodge deals with charge, sparks, and the flash of lightning, all as strains in the ether. He tells of his own trials with sparks and Leyden jars, shown with care. For the lay reader of its day, the book made the new science of electricity plain.
macdonald-hope-of-gospel-1892:
George MacDonald, the Scottish writer whose fantasies taught Lewis and Tolkien, preached the sermons gathered in The Hope of the Gospel in 1892. The book holds his most hopeful theology in pulpit form. At its center stands the goodness of God the Father.

MacDonald argues that God's love reaches every soul, and that punishment serves healing rather than revenge. He reads the words of Jesus as proof that no one is finally shut out from mercy. Victorian readers who feared an angry God found in these sermons a gentler, sterner gospel at once. His fairy tales carry the same hope in story form.
mead-simon-magus-1892:
G. R. S. Mead was the chief scholar of the Theosophical Society. His essay on Simon Magus came out in 1892. Simon is named in the Book of Acts as a sorcerer of Samaria. Church tales made him the first great foe of the faith.

Mead sifts the old church tales to find the man past the myth. He asks if Simon taught a deep Gnostic scheme of his own. Old texts in Greek and Latin give the sparse facts he works with. The essay is a sober bid to save a dark name from pure slur.
medicina-practica-or-practical-physick-c: Medicina practica, or Practical Physick, 1692. The practical medicine. This book preserves that work. It waits for future eyes. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
morris-news-from-nowhere-1892:
William Morris answered Bellamy with his own utopia, News from Nowhere, first printed in 1890. The text here is the 1892 Kelmscott Press edition, from Morris's own press. His narrator wakes in a future England remade by revolution. Money, parliament, and grimy industry have vanished from the land.

Guest, the visitor, travels the Thames valley asking how the change came. Craft work, beauty, and free fellowship fill the answers he receives. Morris called the book a utopian romance, and its charm carries the doctrine. The socialist England he pictures grows from his love of medieval craft. It remains a beloved counterweight to harder utopias. Kelmscott printing makes the copy itself handsome.
murdoch-point-barrow-expedition-1892:
John Murdoch served with the United States party that spent two years at Point Barrow, Alaska, in the early 1880s, and his report came out in 1892. Point Barrow is the far north tip of Alaska. The party went to study weather, land, and the people there.

Murdoch wrote the part on the Inupiat, the Inuit group of that coast. He set down their tools, dress, homes, and crafts, and their rites and shamans. It is one of the first close records of life at the edge of the known map.
newes-from-scotland-1592:
Newes from Scotland, printed in 1592, reports the North Berwick witch trials of 1590 and 1591. Dozens of people stood accused of raising storms against King James the Sixth at sea. Doctor Fian, a schoolmaster, stands at the center of the tale.

The pamphlet gives his examination, his torture, and his death in grim detail. It claims the accused met the Devil and plotted the king's death on the waves. The case shaped the king's own later book on witchcraft, Daemonologie. Historians treat the pamphlet as the founding text of the Scottish witch hunt, and its charges still shock.
openalex-w1952843992: Eight years of converter conferences — boiled down. This 1972 NASA report indexes and digests cesium-diode results from the 1963-to-1971 conferences. The compilation gathered materials, outputs, and lifetimes into one handy desk reference for working engineers.
openalex-w2028567092: Feeding 9 billion needs fish back on the menu. Béné and colleagues' 2015 paper argues fish — feeding 4.5 billion people much of their animal protein — must anchor future food security. The paper made the nutritional and food-security case for fisheries.
openalex-w2035187492: Bagasse is ethanol waiting to happen — if lignin lets go. A 2011 study profiled sugarcane bagasse after lignin removal for better enzymatic digestibility. The work mapped chemical and structural changes that free the sugars for fermentation.
openalex-w2074331492: Back-pain forms need local versions to work. A 2001 study brought the Roland-Morris questionnaire to Brazil. The work gave Brazilian doctors a tested back-pain measure — three translators, one consensus version, fully validated.
openalex-w2075851892: Pregnant women in PNG skip antenatal care — why? Andrew and colleagues' 2014 qualitative study explored factors affecting attendance at and timing of formal antenatal care in Madang, Papua New Guinea. The interviews revealed the barriers keeping mothers away.
openalex-w2123354892: Stopping HIV drugs raised heart risk — inflammation explained why. A 2012 SMART look studied inflammation, clotting, and heart disease in people with HIV. Pausing therapy raised heart risk over staying on drugs — the trial's warning, heeded at last.
openalex-w2133643992: Simple tests save newborn lives. A 2012 Health in Action paper covers point-of-care tests to strengthen health systems and save newborn lives. The catalog record is thin, but the paper covers bedside diagnostics for newborn survival.
openalex-w2155551592: Catching mosquitoes that feed and rest outdoors is one of the hardest parts of malaria research, and a 2013 study in Malaria Journal tests a fix: barrier screens, simple mesh panels set out to intercept mosquitoes as they travel. The screens give researchers a better way to collect resting, blood-filled mosquitoes, so they can identify whose blood they fed on and learn how transmission happens outside homes.
openalex-w2414478892: How often do protons smash when they collide? This 2016 Physical Review Letters paper measures the inelastic proton-proton cross section at 13 TeV with the ATLAS detector, using just 60 microbarns-inverse of data. Selecting collisions with rings of scintillator detectors, the team pins down a fundamental number that underlies every other measurement at the LHC's top energy.
openalex-w2601300492: Does dirty air trigger asthma attacks? Individual studies disagree, tangled in moderating factors. This 2017 PLoS ONE systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis pools the evidence on outdoor air pollution and asthma exacerbations in children and adults. The synthesis clarifies when and how pollution pushes asthma over the edge.
openalex-w2775643792: Leishmaniasis treatments are failing — and drug resistance is a fundamental reason. This 2017 PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases paper argues that reevaluating treatment guidelines for Old and New World leishmaniasis is urgently needed. The review maps the 21st-century challenge: parasites outpacing the drugs meant to kill them.
openalex-w2915443992: Bacterial cellulose — grown by microbes, not trees — is strong, pure, and biodegradable. This 2019 Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems paper explores it as a raw material for food and food packaging. Cost has confined it mostly to biomedical uses; the review maps how it could break into the kitchen.
openalex-w2951495492: The global program against lymphatic filariasis treats hundreds of millions yearly — and a single-dose triple-drug regimen could accelerate elimination. This 2019 PLoS Medicine multicenter, cluster-randomized study tests the safety of double- versus triple-drug mass administration. The results determine whether the faster regimen is safe to roll out.
openalex-w2979994192: PTSD risk is heritable, but robust genetic variants had never been found. This 2019 Nature Communications international meta-analysis — over 30,000 cases and 170,000 controls — identifies sex- and ancestry-specific genetic risk loci. The findings finally give the biology of trauma a genomic foothold.
openalex-w4416399692: Backyard chickens can carry drug-resistant germs to their keepers. This study tested backyard broiler chickens and their human contacts for multidrug-resistant Klebsiella. The authors typed the strains and resistance genes. A One Health study of resistance hopping from coop to kitchen.
openalex-w7138893692: How long does the coronavirus live on hospital room surfaces? This study swabbed the rooms of COVID patients in airy single rooms, pairing gene tests with live-virus culture. The team sized up the true infection risk. A germ-control study of surfaces versus air.
openalex-w7204128392: Social media turned campaigning into a free-for-all, and this article asks how democracy survives it. The authors study digital political ads and electoral integrity through constitutional and comparative law: fake news, paid boosts, and the line between speech and sabotage. A legal study of elections in the age of the feed.
openalex-w7204226692: In the Amazon, the river sets the prices. This case study looks at a small building-materials retailer in Tefe, Amazonas, and how the Solimoes River's seasonal rise and fall shapes its purchasing, costs, and profits. The authors show hydrology driving economics. A vivid example of business at the mercy of the waters.
openalex-w7204237392: Bullying poisons school life for victims and bystanders alike. This article offers a practical guide: how to spot bullying and how to build a culture of peace and tolerance in its place. The authors cover the emotional, social, and academic damage, then turn to solutions. A compassionate handbook for schools ready to act.
openalex-w7204251392: Tocantins created a formal penal police career, and this study asks whether the upgrade worked. The authors investigate how institutionalizing and valuing the career affected the quality of sentence enforcement in the state. The research links professional dignity to public outcomes. A public-security study of what happens when a job gets the respect it was missing.
openalex-w7204442892: Farm soils in the tropics trap phosphorus, a key plant food, where crops cannot reach it. This farm-science study tested how different phosphate fertilizers free up phosphorus over time in soils of varied texture. The authors measured which sources kept the nutrient open to roots longest. Hands-on soil science for growers battling tropical ground.
openalex-w7204989892: Underground water feeds towns across Brazil's dry northeast, but rock aquifers can be polluted. This study maps how vulnerable a crystalline aquifer system is to contamination in Varzea Alegre, Ceara. The authors trace the geology and the human pressures on the water below. A technical hydrogeology study with direct stakes for everyone who drinks from a well in the region.
openalex-w7206207892: Caring for a sick relative at home is hard, and families often feel unprepared. This study set out to learn what home caregivers struggle with most, then built an educational tool to help them. Based on qualitative research from 2019, the authors designed teaching material aimed at daily home care. Practical and humane, it treats family caregivers as learners who deserve real support.
osler-principles-practice-medicine-1892:
William Osler published The Principles and Practice of Medicine in 1892, and it remade medical teaching. The first edition ran past a thousand pages, with an index. Osler wrote from wide ward experience and a gift for clear order. His book made bedside teaching the heart of a doctor's training.

Disease by disease, he gives causes, signs, course, and treatment in plain sequence. Students learned to watch patients closely and record what they saw. The textbook defined modern clinical medicine for a generation of doctors. Later editions kept growing under his hand. The first edition shows his method at its freshest. Its clarity still impresses.
oudemans-great-sea-serpent-1892:
Antoon Oudemans, a Dutch zoologist, gave the sea serpent a scientific hearing in 1892. The Great Sea-Serpent weighs some 162 sighting reports in one long, strict treatise. Oudemans ran a zoo and knew animal form as few men of his day did.

He sorts the reports, throws out the frauds and the drunk tales, and keeps a hard core he cannot shake. His verdict: a great unknown sea mammal, kin to the seals, swims behind the best accounts. The book founded the study of the serpent as a branch of zoology. Every later writer on the theme must answer Oudemans first.
pearson-grammar-science-1892:
Karl Pearson was a mathematician who helped found the modern use of statistics in science. His 1892 book The Grammar of Science lays out what science can and cannot claim to know. A young Albert Einstein read it with friends and took its lessons to heart.

Pearson argues that science describes how things happen in order, rather than why they must happen. Laws of nature, in his view, are short summaries of observed patterns, not hidden forces. His stress on measure, doubt, and clear terms shaped how a whole generation thought about method. The book closes by asking what counts as a cause, and answers with patterns, not powers.
peladan-amphitheatre-des-sciences-mortes:
Joséphin Péladan published L'Amphithéâtre des Sciences Mortes in 1892 in Paris. Péladan, who styled himself a Rosicrucian mage, wrote on art, faith, and occult lore as one linked cause. The dead sciences of his title were the old arts of magic, astrology, and alchemy.

Péladan argued that those lost arts held truths about the soul that modern science and a dull church had forgotten. He mixed essays on occult teaching with calls for a revival of beauty and Catholic mysticism. The book is part manifesto, part lecture hall for his ideal order. It captures the theatrical, high style of the French occult revival of the 1890s.
penotus-palimbios-or-the-alchymists-ench: Penotus palimbios, or The Alchymists Enchiridion, 1692. The alchemist's handbook. This book preserves that work. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
petrie-ten-years-digging-1892:
W. M. Flinders Petrie sums up ten years that changed the dig in Ten Years' Digging in Egypt, out in 1892. Petrie came to Egypt in 1880 as a youth with a keen eye. By 1892 he had shown that pots, scraps, and layers of soil can date a site with more truth than grand finds of gold.

He tells of camps, crews, false scraps, and hard won finds in brisk prose. His ways of dig and list set the rules all digs since then use. The book is a log and a creed in one. It marks the birth of the true dig.
phrenology-proved-illustrated-and-applie: Phrenology Proved, Illustrated, and Applied, 1892. A later edition. This book preserves that work. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
plos-pbio-0020092:
Hiroki Kuroda, Oliver Wessely, E. M. De Robertis, and their team studied how embryos form their nerve tissue in PLOS Biology in 2004. They used the frog Xenopus, a classic model for early development. Neural induction is the step where outer cells are told to become brain and spinal cord.

Signals named chordin and noggin block certain cues, while another signal, β-catenin, pushes from a different layer. The study shows both the outer layer and a deeper layer send needed signals. That two-source picture revises simple textbook accounts. It helps explain how embryos set up the nervous system so reliably, and why faults in these signals cause severe birth defects.
plos-pone-0000092:
Sebastian Breuert, Thorsten Allers, Gabi Spohn, and their team studied DNA copying in salt-loving microbes in PLOS ONE in 2006. Halophilic archaea live in brines that would kill most life. Many carry several copies of their genome in each cell, a state called polyploidy, and the team showed that copy number is regulated, not random.

Cells adjust their genome count with growth stage and conditions. Extra copies can serve as backup DNA for repair in a harsh home. Regulated polyploidy also changes how inheritance works in these microbes. The finding widens the known range of genome strategies and may explain how these archaea stay so hardy in salt flats and brines worldwide.
plos-pone-0000192:
Arjan B. te Pas, Enrico Lopriore, Marissa J. Engbers, and colleagues published this neonatal study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It concerns very preterm infants with respiratory distress syndrome, babies born too early whose lungs cannot yet work on their own. The paper is a case-control study of early breathing support and bronchopulmonary dysplasia, the chronic lung damage that can follow.

How a fragile newborn is ventilated in the first hours can shape lung health for years. The authors compare early respiratory management between infants who did and did not develop the chronic condition. The findings inform one of the most delicate balancing acts in intensive care.
plos-pone-0000292:
Roger Hullin, Jan Matthes, Sibylle von Vietinghoff, and colleagues published this heart cell study in PLOS ONE in 2007. L-type calcium channels control the heartbeat's electrical trigger in the ventricle. The authors report that increasing the auxiliary beta-2 subunit of these channels leads to single-channel activity characteristic of heart failure.

Heart failure involves electrical remodeling of heart cells, not just weaker muscle. Showing that one subunit's rise reproduces failure-like channel behavior names a culprit in that remodeling. The work may point to channel components as drug targets for a condition with few good treatments.
plos-pone-0000392:
Roman Nawroth and colleagues studied enzymes outside cells that influence pancreatic cancer, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The enzymes, extracellular sulfatases, edit sulfate groups on cell-surface molecules. In doing so they tune the Wnt signaling pathway, a growth-control system often hijacked by tumors.

The authors report that these sulfatases raise the growth and tumor-forming ability of human pancreatic cancer cells. Pancreatic cancer is among the hardest cancers to treat, so any lever on its growth matters. Enzymes sitting outside the cell are also easier for drugs to reach than ones inside, which makes the pathway a possible target for new treatments.
plos-pone-0000492:
Marianne A.B. van der Sande and colleagues studied cytomegalovirus infections passed from mother to baby before birth, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Congenital cytomegalovirus infection can cause hearing loss and developmental harm, yet it is little studied in Africa. The team followed a birth cohort in a peri-urban West African setting, measuring risk factors and clinical outcomes.

Which mothers pass the virus on, and which babies are harmed, are the questions that shape screening policy. Most existing data came from rich countries, where the virus behaves differently amid different living conditions. This cohort adds evidence from a high-exposure setting, where the large majority of adults already carry the virus.
plos-pone-0000592:
Giampiero Favato and colleagues built a budgeting model for Italian health care, described in PLOS ONE in 2007. ASSET, short for Age/Sex Standardised Estimates of Treatment, estimates how much prescribing a population should need given its age and sex mix. The research model aims to improve the governance of prescribing funds in Italy.

Drug budgets handed out by headcount alone overfund young regions and starve older ones. Standardizing by age and sex makes allocations fairer and exposes overspending that demography cannot explain. Health systems everywhere face the same problem, so a transparent model from Italy has readers far beyond it.
plos-pone-0000692:
Rachel M. Craddock, Helen E. Lockstone, David A. Rider and co-authors proposed studying schizophrenia through T cells, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Decades of research into the causes and biology of schizophrenia have left understanding incomplete. That gap has real consequences for both diagnosis and treatment. The authors investigate whether differences between patients and controls appear in immune cells.

Altered T-cell function is their starting observation, and they offer these cells as a cellular model of the disease. Blood cells are far easier to sample than brain tissue. A working cell model would let researchers probe molecular disease mechanisms, and test drugs, without touching the brain itself.
plos-pone-0000792:
Kimberley A. Phillips, Chet C. Sherwood and Alayna L. Lilak measured the brain's great bridge in capuchin monkeys for PLOS ONE in 2007. The corpus callosum connects the two cerebral hemispheres. Sex differences in its overall area and regional subdivisions have been reported in humans. Some researchers suggested that pattern might be a unique human adaptation, since no other species had shown it.

Capuchins break that claim. Their title reports that corpus callosum morphology in these monkeys is influenced by both sex and handedness. Handedness is a strong capuchin trait, making them a sharp test case. A monkey parallel weakens purely human stories about brain wiring and gender.
plos-pone-0000892:
Kathryn Fontaine, John Cooley and Chris Simon looked for fathers' mitochondria leaking into hybrid cicadas, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Mitochondria, the cell's power plants, are normally passed down only by the mother. Exceptions keep turning up, most often in crosses between different lines or species.

Periodical cicadas of the genus Magicicada offer a sharp test case, since distinct broods can cross. The team checked hybrids for paternal leakage, cases where the father's mitochondria also appear. Such leakage matters because many studies use mitochondrial DNA as a clean record of maternal lines. If fathers sometimes contribute too, that record needs more care.
plos-pone-0000992:
Elisabeth Fayard, Jason Gill, Magdalena Paolino and colleagues studied thymus growth in mice missing a key signaling protein, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The thymus is where most T cells are raised. A signaling chain called PI3K helps guide that development, and faults in its parts can stall young T cells early.

The team deleted PKB alpha, also called Akt1, a central link in that chain. They then watched how thymic development changed without it. Knowing which single link matters, and which are backed up by others, maps the control system for T cell production. That map underlies work on immune deficiency and recovery.
plos-pone-0001092:
Paola Branduardi, Tiziana Fossati, Michael Sauer and colleagues engineered yeast to make vitamin C and gained stress resistance, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Industrial yeast work in huge reactors under many stresses that cut growth and output. Reactive oxygen species, damaging oxygen byproducts, are a chief stress factor, attacking cells directly.

Yeast does not naturally make vitamin C, a classic antioxidant. The team report that biosynthesis of vitamin C by yeast leads to increased stress resistance. A self supplied protectant beats dosing a reactor from outside. The result is biotechnology with a simple logic: give the worker cell the shield it lacks.
plos-pone-0001192:
A second dengue infection is often more dangerous than the first. Tao Dong and colleagues followed patients through secondary dengue virus infection in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Dengue is one of the most important diseases spread by arthropod vectors, and over half the world's population now lives in areas at risk.

The authors report high secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines, immune alarm signals, alongside the loss of high-avidity cross-reactive killer T cells as the infection progressed. Most dengue infections cause no symptoms, but a subset turns severe. Tracking which immune responses rise and fall may help explain why, and which patients need closest care.
plos-pone-0001292:
Watching another person in pain activates brain circuits similar to feeling pain oneself. Claus Lamm and colleagues asked what modulates that empathic response, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Empathy is not all-or-none; it is strongly shaped by interpersonal and situational factors.

Using functional magnetic resonance imaging, the authors assessed how sensory and affective responses during empathy for pain are modulated. Their title poses the study's question: what are you feeling? The work separates the brain's mirroring of another's sensation from its emotional coloring, and shows what tips the balance between them.
plos-pone-0001392:
An Pan and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on low mood, body fat signals, and swelling in older Chinese adults. Work in west countries had tied low mood to both fat and body swelling. The team asked whether the same links held in China. Their data came from 3,289 middle aged and older adults.

The authors compared mood scores with blood markers of swelling and with fat made signals. They weighed the links while taking age and other traits into account. The results extend the mood and body link beyond west groups. They also raise the point that care for low mood may need to watch heart and weight risks too.
plos-pone-0001492:
Hilary Gerber, Yana Pikman, and Robert Fisher published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a kinase that switches on other kinases in yeast. These kinases drive cell division and gene use in all complex cells. Most species need the switch, and fission yeast was thought to be an odd case with two. The team tested one of them, called Csk1.

They show Csk1 is needed for normal rates of DNA swap repair and for standing up to DNA harm. That broadens its job past cell division alone. Yeast repair paths mirror our own, so the work informs human DNA care studies. It also settles a point of debate on yeast kinases.
plos-pone-0001592:
Valentina Folgiero and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on why a breast cancer drug stops working. Tamoxifen is the most used hormone drug for breast cancer. Its gains in added care are well logged in large trials. Yet many tumors learn to resist it. The team traced one route to that resistance.

They show a surface complex switches on a kin receptor that helps tumors dodge the drug. That receptor's rise marks a shift in the tumor's growth drives. Blocking the route could restore the old drug's power. The work gives drug teams a paired target to test in resistant cases.
plos-pone-0001692:
Björn P. Johansson, Oonagh Shannon, and Lars Björck reviewed a bacterial enzyme with drug potential in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The enzyme is IdeS, made by Streptococcus pyogenes, a common cause of strep throat. IdeS cuts IgG antibodies with unusual precision, snipping one bond and disabling the antibody.

Harmful IgG antibodies drive several autoimmune diseases and can cause acute transplant rejection. An enzyme that removes them cleanly could become a treatment. The full text covers how IdeS works, its specificity, and the medical settings where it might help. Turning a bacterium's weapon against the immune system into a tool for calming that same system is the paper's central, elegant idea.
plos-pone-0001792:
Anna Le Tortorec, Roger Le Grand, Hélène Denis, and their co-authors tracked virus in semen-producing organs in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Indirect evidence suggests the male genital tract may be a source of persistent HIV shedding in semen during antiretroviral therapy. Sampling those organs in HIV-positive people without symptoms is hard, so the phenomenon was poorly understood.

Using SIV, the monkey counterpart of HIV, the team examined semen-producing organs during acute and chronic stages of disease. The full text gives the tissue results and where the virus persisted. A hidden reservoir in the genital tract matters for transmission risk and for any strategy aiming to cure HIV infection outright.
plos-pone-0001892:
Sergi Lozano, Alex Arenas, and Angel Sanchez used real social networks to test how cooperation spreads, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. They ran the Prisoner's Dilemma on two networks drawn from true ties between people. In that game, each player can help the group or cheat for gain. The two networks gave very unlike rates of cooperation.

That gap could not be explained by the broad stats of each network, such as size or link count. The team argues the cause lies in mid-level shape: clumps and hubs inside the network. The lesson for social science is that who sits where in a web of ties can matter more than the web's totals.
plos-pone-0001992:
Roger Jovani and co-authors used flock sizes in a colonial bird to link single acts to group patterns, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Group sizes in nature often follow a power law, in which small groups are common and large ones rare. Shifts away from that pattern may reveal how the acts of single animals build the pattern of the whole.

The team studied a population of lesser kestrels that nest and hunt in groups. They report that truncated power laws, a bent form of the pattern, tie low-level behavior to how the birds group. Field proof of this link is scarce, so a wild case counts for a lot.
plos-pone-0002092:
Li-Min Yang and co-authors built vast libraries of random peptides on ribosomes, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Ribosome display is a cell-free method that links each new protein chain to the ribosome that made it, plus its gene message. Such libraries are becoming a tool to select useful molecules in the test tube, from binding tags to blockers.

The team constructed random peptide libraries of high complexity and analyzed what they held. Complexity matters: the more distinct peptides, the better the odds one fits a chosen target. Their analysis shows how to build libraries rich enough for real selection work.
plos-pone-0002192:
Peter Niewiarowski, Stephanie Lopez, Liehui Ge, and co-authors tested whether heat and moisture change the grip of gecko feet, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A gecko's sticky toes were expected to grip just as well across the temperatures geckos meet in daily life. Earlier tests, though, had given mixed answers on whether that expectation holds.

The team measured adhesion in Tokay geckos and Day geckos under varied temperature and humidity. They found that grip did change with conditions, contrary to the simple expectation. Knowing when gecko grip weakens matters for biology and for engineers copying the gecko's dry adhesive design.
plos-pone-0002292:
Björn Titz, Seesandra Rajagopala, Johannes Goll, and co-authors mapped the protein interaction network of the syphilis bacterium, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Treponema pallidum is a spiral bacterium that has long resisted lab culture, so many of its proteins remain uncharacterized. Interaction networks can place such proteins into a functional context by showing what they bind.

The team built the binary protein interactome of the spirochete, testing protein pairs for direct binding. The map gives unknown proteins neighbors with known jobs, a strong clue to their own roles. For a pathogen this hard to grow, a wiring diagram is a practical substitute for many experiments.
plos-pone-0002392:
Led by Soreq, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Lilach Soreq, Adi Gilboa-Geffen, Sonia Berrih-Aknin, and others. Its subject is identifying Alternative Hyper-Splicing Signatures in MG-Thymoma by Exon Arrays. The vast majority of human genes (>70%) are alternatively spliced.

Although alternative pre-mRNA processing is modified in multiple tumors, alternative hyper-splicing signatures specific to particular tumor types are still lacking. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002492:
Research by Madsen and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Bo Eskerod Madsen, Eliana Marisa Ramos, Mathieu Boulard, and others. Its subject is germline Mutation in RNASEL Predicts Increased Risk of Head and Neck, Uterine Cervix and Breast Cancer. Ribonuclease L (RNASEL), encoding the 2′-5′-oligoadenylate (2-5A)-dependent RNase L, is a key enzyme in the interferon induced antiviral and anti-proliferate pathway.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002592:
Schrempf and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Alexandra Schrempf, Jürgen Heinze, and others. Its subject is mating with Stressed Males Increases the Fitness of Ant Queens. Sexual conflict theory holds that males can raise their own fitness by passing on substances during mating.

Those substances may boost a partner's short-term fertility at a cost to her later life and re-mating. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002692:
Work by Seth M. Barribeau and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008, dealing with major histocompatibility complex based resistance to a common bacterial pathogen of amphibians. The catalog record names Seth M. Barribeau first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Given their well-developed systems of innate and adaptive immunity, global population declines of amphibians are particularly perplexing. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002792:
Research from G. Charles Ostermeier and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers conserving, distributing and managing genetically modified mouse lines by sperm cryopreservation. Authorship is credited in the record to G. Charles Ostermeier and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Sperm from C57BL/6 mice are difficult to cryopreserve and recover. The authors add a further point. Yet, the majority of genetically modified (GM) lines are maintained on this genetic background. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002892:
Haoran Su, Min He, Hongmei Li and colleagues tested a diabetes compound called Boc5 in mice in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Boc5 was one of the first non-peptide drugs to switch on the receptor for GLP-1, a gut hormone that helps control blood sugar. A drug taken by mouth with that action held clear appeal.

In diabetic mice, Boc5 gave lasting control of blood sugar and weight loss, as the title reports. The study builds on the team's earlier find of the compound itself. It offers early proof that a small, non-peptide molecule can do work once thought to need larger peptide drugs.
plos-pone-0002992:
Miguel Rodríguez-Gironés and Ana Llandres modeled the joint evolution of long tongues and deep flower tubes in 2008. The usual story says deep tubes evolve when a plant gains by having a tube longer than its pollinator's tongue. Pollinators, in turn, evolve longer tongues to reach more nectar.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the authors argue resource competition triggers the co-evolution of both traits together. That reframes a classic arms race as driven by rivalry for food. The model can be tested against real flower and pollinator pairs where tube and tongue lengths vary. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003092:
Patrick Hennig, Ralf Möller and Martin Egelhaaf modeled object detection in the fly visual system in 2008. Detecting objects matters when moving through a natural environment; flies land on salient objects and avoid collisions with them. A set of neurons called figure detection cells is likely involved in that task.

Their computational analysis argues distributed dendritic processing facilitates object detection. In other words, splitting computation across the branching inputs of neurons helps pick figures from ground. Published in PLOS ONE, the principle may guide small robot vision, where flies excel on tiny hardware. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003192: Madelyn R. Schmidt and colleagues published a PLOS ONE study in 2008 on placing human B cells into mice that lack their own immune defences. The title states its claim: human BLyS helps B cells taken from human blood to engraft, or take hold, in these mice. No abstract beyond the title was supplied, so no effect sizes are stated here.
plos-pone-0003292:
Mariangela Cavarelli, Ingrid Karlsson, Marisa Zanchetta and colleagues study HIV coreceptor use in children in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. HIV-1 R5 viruses are characterized by large phenotypic variation, reflected by the mode of coreceptor use. The ability of R5 HIV-1 to infect target cells expressing chimeric receptors between CCR5 and CXCR4, called R5 broad viruses, was shown to correlate with disease stage in adults.

The title reports that HIV-1 with multiple CCR5/CXCR4 chimeric receptor use is predictive of immunological failure in infected children. Readers get a viral trait proposed as a warning sign. Early warning of immune failure could prompt closer monitoring or treatment change.
plos-pone-0003392:
Feng Zhang, Yuping Wang, and Hong-Wen Deng compared methods for cleaning up gene studies in 2008. Their topic was population stratification, a hidden mix of ancestries in a study group. That mix can create false links between a gene and a disease. The authors tested several known fixes on simulated data.

Each method was judged on how well it removed the false links. Some fixes held up better than others under strong mixing. The paper gives gene hunters a guide to which fix to trust. Clean methods matter because false gene links waste years of follow-up work.
plos-pone-0003492:
Sidney R. Lehky and co-authors recorded brain cells in monkeys for this 2008 vision study. The inferotemporal area helps recognize objects and scenes. A key question is which frame of reference those cells use. Options include viewer-centered, object-centered, and scene-based coordinates.

Eye position turned out to modulate the cells' responses. Where the eyes point thus shapes the object signal itself. The brain's picture of objects is tied partly to the viewer. That finding informs models of how vision guides reaching and grasping. Object vision feeds nearly all daily tasks, from reading to driving a car.
plos-pone-0003592:
Gwen Liu, Hyeyoung Min, and Sibiao Yue compared two related microRNAs in this 2008 paper. MicroRNA family members often share identical seed regions. Their mature sequences can be near-twins, about twenty-one letters long. Whether such members share the same activity was unclear.

Two microRNAs, mir-181a-1 and mir-181c, act distinctly in early T cell development. The difference traced to letters in their precursor loops. The loop thus tunes what each regulator does. Small details before maturity can separate one family member from another. T cells are the arm of immunity that vaccines most need to train well.
plos-pone-0003692:
Johanna Hung and Michael A. Colicos published this neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Brain activity helps wire the nervous system during growth, learning, and repair after injury. The authors asked how activity in one place can steer growing nerve fibers somewhere else.

They report that waves of calcium moving through astrocytes, the brain's star-shaped support cells, do the steering. Those waves guided neuronal growth cones toward remote regions of activity. The result gives support cells an active directing role in wiring the developing central nervous system. The finding gives growing axons a signal they can follow at a distance.
plos-pone-0003792:
Aaron R. Seitz and Takeo Watanabe published this perception study in PLOS ONE in 2008. People can learn from stimuli they were not asked to attend to, a phenomenon called task-irrelevant learning. Whether that learning is truly irrelevant to the task at hand was unclear. The authors set out to test it.

They probed whether hidden associations form that actually help task performance. If so, the ignored material is not irrelevant at all; the brain quietly uses it. The study questions whether any learning is fully separate from what the mind is trying to do.
plos-pone-0003892:
Naotsugu Tsuchiya, Hiroto Kawasaki, Hiroyuki Oya, and co-authors recorded face processing in the human brain in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article uses direct recordings from inside the skull. Faces are read by a spread-out network of brain areas. What each area adds to face reading was still unclear.

The team sorted face signals by time, frequency, and brain location. One leading view holds that identity is coded in the lower temporal cortex. Direct recordings give rare detail that scalp methods cannot match. The work helps map how the brain pulls identity and other cues from a face.
plos-pone-0003992:
Xiaoyan Zhang, Jianqing Xu, Hong Peng, and co-authors tracked dual HIV and hepatitis C infection in China in 2008. How hepatitis C changes HIV progress has stayed controversial. The study group was former plasma donors infected with HIV. None had started antiretroviral therapy when studied.

Their PLOS ONE article covers 168 such donors and their disease course. Coinfection with hepatitis C virus tracked with slower HIV progression. That direction surprised many who expected faster decline. The result urges care in assuming coinfection always worsens HIV. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004092:
Atsushi Ohazama, Eric B. Johnson, Masato S. Ota, and co-authors studied a receptor that blends signals in development in 2008. How much signaling gets integrated outside cells was underappreciated. Lrp4 belongs to a family of large receptor proteins. It binds secreted blockers of growth signals.

Their PLOS ONE article shows Lrp4 tunes Bmp and canonical Wnt signals together. The integration happens during tooth development in their study. One receptor coordinating two pathways helps pattern growing organs. The work lifts extracellular integration into normal developmental thinking. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004192:
Konstantinos Mavromatis and colleagues published this genome study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Halothermothrix orenii is a bacterium that lives without oxygen and loves both heat and salt. It was isolated from sediment in a Tunisian salt lake and belongs to the order Halanaerobiales in the phylum Firmicutes.

The team read its complete genome and report a single circular chromosome of about 2.58 million DNA letters. The sequence shows how a microbe is equipped to thrive in hot, salty, oxygen-free mud. Such genomes also serve biotechnology, since their enzymes keep working under harsh conditions.
plos-pone-0004292:
Neil Sidell and colleagues published this study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Phenylketonuria, or PKU, is a metabolic disorder caused by a faulty enzyme that should break down phenylalanine. It leads to high phenylalanine and to abnormal breakdown products, among them phenylacetate, known as PA. In recent years PA had attracted interest for possible anti-cancer effects, raising a safety question.

Using a PKU mouse model, the team examined carcinogenic effects linked to the disorder's chemistry. They watched the mice for signs of tumours over time. A metabolite that patients carry for life deserves scrutiny, whether it turns out protective or harmful.
plos-pone-0004392:
A small set of brain cells controls puberty and fertility. Those cells release GnRH, a hormone that starts the reproductive chain. Roberto Salvi, Yvan Arsenijevic, Marco Giacomini, and co-authors asked where such cells can come from. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper used the fetal hypothalamus, the brain region where GnRH cells work. Stem-like cells from it were grown as floating balls called neurospheres.

Neurospheres can turn into neurons and support cells under the right conditions. The authors report these fetal cells could also gain a GnRH character. That means the tissue holds the potential to make hormone-releasing cells. The finding bears on how the reproductive control system forms. It may also guide future cell-based research.
plos-pone-0004492:
One faulty copy of a mitochondria gene shortens life in fruit flies by raising chemical stress, report Sha Tang, Phung Khanh Le, Stephanie Tse, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The gene, Opa1, makes a protein that works in the inner membrane of mitochondria, the cell's power plants. Faulty copies cause dominant optic atrophy, an inherited loss of vision in people.

The protein helps mitochondria fuse, shapes their inner folds, and controls cell death. The team bred flies with one mutated copy, matching the human condition. Those flies produced more reactive oxygen species, harsh chemicals that damage cells, and lived shorter lives. The fly model ties a human blindness gene to energy and stress inside cells.
plos-pone-0004592:
The way cancer cells burn sugar may protect them from stress-driven death, a yeast study by Christoph Ruckenstuhl, Sabrina Buttner, Didac Carmona-Gutierrez, and co-authors explores in PLOS ONE in 2009. Otto Warburg observed that cancer cells often run intense glycolysis, sugar burning, even when oxygen is present. At the same time their mitochondrial respiration falls.

Research had focused on a possible link between this Warburg effect and tumor growth. The team used yeast as a model for cancer metabolism. They show the Warburg effect suppresses apoptosis, programmed cell death, when oxidative stress strikes. That protective angle may help explain why tumors adopt this metabolism. It also suggests that blocking the sugar-burning mode could re-expose cancer cells to stress.
plos-pone-0004692:
Albert Lecube and colleagues found that diabetes alone raises the risk of low oxygen at night in obese patients, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Type 2 diabetes and obesity are now top threats to health in the West. Obesity is also the main driver of sleep apnea, where breathing stalls in sleep.

Sleep apnea can in turn harm blood sugar control. The team compared obese patients with and without diabetes to split the two risks. They found diabetes adds risk on its own for deep drops in night oxygen. The result argues for sleep checks in obese patients with diabetes.
plos-pone-0004792:
David Aviezer and colleagues evaluated a plant derived human enzyme for Gaucher disease in preclinical and Phase I work, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Gaucher disease is a progressive storage disorder caused by lack of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase. The lack leads to dysfunction in multiple organ systems as fatty material builds up in cells over years without treatment.

Intravenous enzyme replacement is the accepted standard of care. The team tested an enzyme grown in plant cells for safety and activity. A plant source could lower cost and supply risk. Early human data are reported. These findings offer a firm starting point for the next round of testing.
plos-pone-0004892:
Bradley Alsop led a team that watched actin move as a ring forms and fades in grasshopper sperm cells for PLOS ONE in 2009. When an animal cell splits in two, a ring of actin and myosin forms and squeezes the cell in half. The ring is built fresh for each split and then taken apart when the split is done.

The team tracked where the actin goes as the ring is built and rebuilt. Actin from old sites is reused in the new ring, which saves time and stock. These large cells make the moves easy to film and test. The work helps explain how cells split fast and clean, a step key to growth and sperm making.
plos-pone-0004992:
Tumors do not grow alone. They recruit support cells called fibroblasts. Erika Spaeth and colleagues traced where those fibroblasts come from. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They followed mesenchymal stem cells near tumors. The stem cells transition into tumor-associated fibroblasts.

The converted fibroblasts help build the tumor's fibrovascular network. That network supports further tumor progression. The study shows cancers drafting the body's repair cells into service. Blocking the transition could starve tumors of support. The finding identifies a fresh point of attack. It targets the tumor's neighborhood rather than the tumor itself.
plos-pone-0005092:
Drug-company money has bent medical research before. Funded doctors have hyped pills and widened disease definitions. John McPartland examined that problem in one corner of medicine. His PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The corner is obesity research on the endocannabinoid system. That system helps regulate appetite and weight.

The paper reviews the evidence while exposing sponsorship bias. It separates real findings from marketing-friendly claims. Academic physicians with industry funding helped enlarge the drug market, earlier research showed. This review asks which obesity claims survive scrutiny. It is a case study in following the money behind medicine. Readers learn to ask who paid before they believe.
plos-pone-0005192:
Folk cures, herbal remedies, and home treatments sell in a huge global market worth tens of billions of dollars. Many of these treatments have never been shown to work, and some may do harm. Tanaka and colleagues asked in PLOS ONE in 2009 why such treatments persist and spread.

Using models of how culture spreads, the authors show how prestige, ritual, and hope can keep weak remedies alive. A cure does not need to work to be passed on, if people copy trusted healers or heal by chance while using it. The work explains the staying power of medical myths.
plos-pone-0005292:
BDNF is a growth factor that supports neurons in the striatum, a brain region hit hard in Huntington's disease. Less BDNF reaching the striatum is implicated in that disease. Gokce and colleagues mapped the striatum's quick gene response to BDNF in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Within a short time, BDNF changed the activity of many genes. Those changes depended on two signal routes, MEK and ERK, inside the cells. Knowing the pathway shows how a brief growth signal is converted into lasting gene programs that keep striatal neurons alive. Drugs for this brain disease have failed again. Again, so a clear map of the paths a known growth factor uses is a firm base for the next round of tests.
plos-pone-0005392:
A vaccine built on laminarin, a sugar from seaweed, raises antibodies against beta-glucan, a sugar in fungal cell walls. Those antibodies protect mice against major fungal pathogens, from Candida to Cryptococcus. Torosantucci and colleagues explained that protection in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Protection was associated with a restricted binding specificity toward beta-1,3 glucan. The antibodies also inhibited fungal growth and adherence to host cells. Narrow, precise binding, rather than broad stickiness, marks the protective response, a useful lesson for fungal vaccine design. Fungal drugs are few and harsh, and germs grow wise to them fast. So a vaccine that trains the body to block fungi at the wall is a plan of a new and prized kind.
plos-pone-0005492:
Xiao-Jun Wang and Donna Zhang studied how cells control a master defence switch in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The protein Nrf2 turns on a set of genes that protect cells from poisons and stress. Keeping that switch at the right level is vital, since too much or too little can harm the cell.

The team found that another protein, called ENC1, holds Nrf2 down by slowing its production. That brake works at the stage where the gene's message is read into protein. A new layer of control like this helps explain how cells tune their defences.
plos-pone-0005592:
Uppoor Bhat, Marianna Halasi, and Andrei Gartel studied antibiotics that target a cancer protein in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. FoxM1 is a protein that switches on growth genes and is made in excess by most human tumours. That makes it an appealing drug target.

Using a cell test, the team had found that a group of antibiotics called thiazoles block FoxM1. Here they showed that these drugs push human cancer cells into death. Old antibiotics with a new target could be reshaped into cancer drugs, saving years of safety testing. Because FoxM1 is scarce in normal adult tissue, drugs against it might spare healthy cells more than most cancer drugs do.
plos-pone-0005692:
Catherine Miller and colleagues studied in 2009 how two common parasites pull the immune system in opposite directions. Toxoplasma, a single-celled parasite, drives a strong Th1 response, the type that attacks germs inside cells. The liver fluke Fasciola drives a Th2 response, tuned more to worms and allergy.

Many people and animals carry both kinds of infection at once. The team asked what happens when the two signals collide in one host. The clash can blunt one response or distort both. Knowing the outcome matters for vaccine design and for treating mixed infections, which are the rule in much of the world.
plos-pone-0005792:
Lynn Sims, Dennis Garvey, and Jack Ballantyne refined the family tree of Y-chromosome haplogroup G in 2009. This paternal lineage group, marked by the M201 change, is uncommon in the general United States population. Only eight sub-markers were known, and several were rare or unhelpful.

The team characterized new SNP markers that split the group into cleaner branches. A finer tree sharpens ancestry testing and population history for men carrying this lineage. Forensic labs also gain better markers for tracing paternal lines. The work is careful groundwork: each new branch must be proven on real samples.
plos-pone-0005892:
Takaaki Tsunematsu and co-authors reported in 2009 a surprise: a supposed tumor suppressor acts as an oncogene in head and neck cancer. RUNX3 normally helps a growth-control pathway suppress tumors, and its loss aids several cancers. Yet in head and neck tumors its levels ran high.

The team found RUNX3 actually promotes growth in this cancer type. Context flips the protein's role, a caution against one-size labels in cancer genes. Treatment ideas based on restoring RUNX3 could backfire here. The study argues for testing each gene's role cancer by cancer.
plos-pone-0005992:
Gene chips produce floods of data, and the core signal can drown in the flood. Eric Yang, Richard Almon, Debra DuBois and colleagues built a way to pull that signal out in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper presents a method for finding global transcriptional dynamics, meaning the broad pattern of gene activity that runs through a whole experiment.

Spotting the shared pattern matters because each chip run also carries quirks of its own. A method that parts the core response from the noise turns raw numbers into knowledge labs can use. The work serves any field that reads gene activity at scale, from drug testing to basic cell biology.
plos-pone-0006092:
Methamphetamine floods the brain with dopamine, and the flood itself does damage. Subramaniam Jayanthi, Michael McCoy, Genevieve Beauvais and colleagues traced that damage in the rat striatum in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper tracks endoplasmic reticulum stress, a strain in the cell's protein-folding workshop, after methamphetamine exposure.

Blocking the dopamine D1 receptor blunted the stress response, marking the events as D1 receptor-dependent. A named receptor behind the harm gives treatment research a target to test. The work adds a cell-level account of methamphetamine's toll, useful for a drug whose brain damage has long been clear in users but murky in mechanism.
plos-pone-0006192:
Preeclampsia is a dangerous rise in blood pressure during pregnancy with no simple cause. Alain Stepanian and colleagues ran the ECLAXIR study, reported in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper, to test a genetic lead. The illness shares risk factors with heart artery disease, hinting at shared roots in blood vessel harm.

The team checked two variants in the gene CX3CR1, which helps white blood cells move and stick to vessel walls. They looked for links between those variants, vessel injury, and preeclampsia. Studies like this sort real genetic risks from false leads. Even careful negative or mixed results narrow the search for the illness's true drivers.
plos-pone-0006292:
Ovarian cancer is often found late, which makes it the deadliest gynaecological cancer in the United States. Eati Basal and colleagues tested a blood marker candidate in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The folate receptor alpha protein is a logical early detection target because tumors display it.

Functional folate receptor alpha proved elevated in the blood of ovarian cancer patients, per the title. A blood signal that rises early could cut the disease's mortality. The result supports further work toward a screening test. Early detection remains the strongest lever against this cancer.
plos-pone-0006392:
Mediterranean climates occur on five continents and shelter five global biodiversity hotspots. Kirk Klausmeyer and Rebecca Shaw projected climate shifts across those regions in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They combined downscaled results from many atmosphere-ocean models under three emissions scenarios.

The study determined projected spatial shifts in Mediterranean climate zones. Species will need to move as their climate moves. Protected areas fixed on maps may no longer cover the right habitat. The authors assess adaptation potential to guide conservation planning. Maps of this kind help park staff plan for a warmer, drier time ahead.
plos-pone-0006492:
Bernadette Dutia, Stuart Reid, Derek Drummond, and colleagues built a way to watch virus infection in living animals for PLOS ONE in 2009. Finding individual virus-infected cells during long-term infection is critical. It advances understanding of how diseases persist and progress. The team created a novel Cre recombinase imaging system for that purpose.

Their system tracks lymphotropic virus infection, infection of immune-system tissue, in vivo. Cells that the virus enters switch on a visible marker. Researchers can then follow infected cells over time in the living body. Such tracking can reveal hidden reservoirs that keep infections going.
plos-pone-0006592:
Jorge Osorio, Keith Iams, Carol Meteyer, and colleagues compared monkeypox viruses in mice using imaging in PLOS ONE in 2009. Monkeypox viruses cause human monkeypox, a zoonotic smallpox-like disease endemic to Africa. They are of worldwide public health and biodefense concern. Using viruses engineered for in vivo imaging, the team compared pathogenesis in mice.

Imaging lets researchers watch infection spread in the living animal over time. Comparing strains reveals which are more virulent and where they go. Such data guide vaccine and treatment testing. Working with a select agent requires care, and imaging reduces the number of animals needed.
plos-pone-0006692:
Sara Leschner and colleagues watched Salmonella bacteria invade tumors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Certain bacteria that can live without oxygen gather inside solid tumors. Given through the blood, they prefer tumor tissue over healthy tissue. How they find and enter tumors so efficiently was still unclear. The answer matters for using bacteria as cancer therapy.

The team studied Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium entering tumors. Invasion came with strong bleeding inside the tumor. A signaling molecule called TNF-alpha promoted that hemorrhage. The bleeding may help bacteria reach and spread through tumor tissue. Understanding the process could make bacteria-based cancer treatments safer and more effective.
plos-pone-0006792:
Jiang Tan and colleagues mapped a histone mark across the genome of human stem cells turning into bone in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mesenchymal stem cells can renew themselves and form several tissues. Epigenetic marks help decide which fate they take. The mark studied sits on lysine nine of histone H3. The team analyzed it genome-wide during osteogenic differentiation.

Promoter microarrays covering the human genome supplied the data. Changes in the mark accompanied the shift toward bone cells. Mapping those changes reveals genes being silenced or released. The map guides efforts to steer stem cells reliably. Controlled bone formation matters for repairing fractures and bone loss.
plos-pone-0006892:
Richard A. Klinghoffer and colleagues screened for genes that tune a major signaling pathway in PLOS ONE in 2009. The pathway centers on beta-catenin, kept low by a destruction complex. A kinase in that complex, GSK3, marks beta-catenin for disposal. The screen used lentiviruses to deliver genetic changes. It searched for modulators of beta-catenin and GSK3 signaling.

The screen identified dihydrofolate reductase, DHFR, as a modulator. DHFR is famous as a target of antifolate drugs. Finding it in this pathway was unexpected. The link suggests old drugs may influence Wnt signaling. It also adds a metabolic enzyme to a developmental pathway's control list.
plos-pone-0006992:
Brian Bednarski, Albert Baldwin, and Hong Jin Kim revisited a cancer signaling protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. NF-κB is a transcription factor that can switch on protective genes in tumor cells. That protective role has been blamed for tumors resisting chemotherapy. Yet some studies claimed the same factor helps the drug doxorubicin kill cells instead.

The team tested targeted inhibition of the canonical NF-κB pathway. Blocking it made doxorubicin's killing effect stronger, not weaker. Their result challenges the reported death-promoting role. It supports pairing NF-κB blockers with standard drugs to break chemoresistance.
plos-pone-0007092:
Miguel Alcaide, Ciro Rico, Santiago Ruiz, and colleagues traced blood meals in insects in PLOS ONE in 2009. About a quarter of recent pandemics began with vector-borne pathogens. Knowing which animals those vectors feed on is central to control. Modern molecular tools have greatly improved that detective work.

The team built a universal DNA barcoding method for blood meals. It identifies vertebrate hosts from the blood inside arthropods. One method for many hosts and vectors simplifies field studies. The resulting feeding networks show where a pathogen travels, and where to break its route.
plos-pone-0007192:
Loyal A. Goff, Jonathan Davila, Mavis R. Swerdel, and colleagues searched for new microRNAs in human stem cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA pieces that help control gene activity. They are needed both to keep stem cells unspecialized and to guide later development.

More microRNAs had been predicted by computers than had ever been found in cells. The authors pull down the protein Ago2 to capture microRNAs actually in use. They apply the method in embryonic stem cells and neural precursors, confirming predicted microRNAs that are truly expressed.
plos-pone-0007292:
Carlos Gershenson and Luis A. Pineda explained why buses bunch together in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Public transport vehicles often arrive in clusters instead of evenly spaced. The authors call this the equal headway instability, where equal spacing between vehicles breaks down and vehicles aggregate into inefficient convoys.

The phenomenon is pervasive in public transport systems. It had rarely been studied apart from specific scenarios. The authors analyze the instability on its own terms. Their explanation shows why schedules fail even without traffic jams. Transit planners can use the insight to design services that resist bunching.
plos-pone-0007392:
Maroya D. Spalding and Sean T. Prigge studied an enzyme that strips a key chemical tag from proteins in 2009. In the 1950s, researchers found enzyme activity in bacterial extracts that inactivated pyruvate dehydrogenase complexes. The enzyme cut the lipoamide bond, removing a cofactor those complexes need to burn sugars for cellular energy production.

The enzyme is lipoamidase. The authors examine its amidase domain in living cells. They report the domain specifically inactivates lipoylated proteins in vivo. Their PLOS ONE work may turn lipoamidase into a tool for studying malaria parasites, which depend on lipoylated enzymes.
plos-pone-0007492:
Antigoni Elefsinioti, Marit Ackermann, and Andreas Beyer published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on gene maps used across biology. Researchers read new data against maps of which genes and proteins work together. Those maps are built by merging many data banks. The catch is overlap: the same link is often stored more than once. Counting it again and again warps the map's sense of what is well linked.

The authors tackle that overlap head-on. They offer ways to correct for doubled proof when data banks are merged. Cleaner maps give a more honest view of how genes work as a team. Honest maps matter, since researchers use them to guess what unknown proteins do. They also use them to read the results of new tests. Removing double counts is plain work, but it guards every claim built on the map.
plos-pone-0007592:
Alejandra Rangel and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on brain signaling in mice carrying a mutant prion protein. Prion diseases cause spongy degeneration of the brain, dementia, and disturbed brain rhythms. The hallmark is a misshapen form of the normal prion protein. The team examined the hippocampus, a memory center, in the mutant mice. They measured the receptors for the brain's main brake and accelerator signals, GABA and glutamate.

Receptor expression was altered in the prion-mutant hippocampus. Synaptic facilitation and long-term potentiation, two measures of how connections strengthen, changed with it. Those shifts help explain the memory and rhythm problems of prion disease. A memory circuit cannot work when its brakes and accelerators are mis-set. The study charts that mis-setting in detail, giving prion science concrete targets for intervention.
plos-pone-0007692:
Amedeo D'Angiulli and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks how early childhood shapes later school skills. Teachers rate children entering kindergarten with a tool called the Early Development Instrument. Low scores flag children who may be at risk.

The team linked those early ratings to basic skills tests taken in fourth grade, across a whole population. They asked how well early vulnerability predicts later reading and math skills. Findings like these help school systems judge whether early screening is worth its cost, and where extra support should go.
plos-pone-0007792:
Catherine Au and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines how the worm C. elegans handles manganese, an essential but risky metal. Too much manganese can cause a Parkinson-like illness. In mammals, a transporter called DMT1 is a major route for manganese uptake.

The worm carries three cousins of that transporter, named SMF-1, SMF-2 and SMF-3. The team characterized all three proteins. Each responds to manganese levels in its own way, and each is regulated differently. The division of labor helps explain how animals balance a needed nutrient against its toxicity.
plos-pone-0007892:
Eduardo Nascimento and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It shows that gene patterns early in dengue fever can predict its outcome. Dengue ranges from a mild fever to a life-threatening illness. Doctors cannot easily tell at first who will worsen.

The team profiled gene expression in blood cells during the early acute febrile stage. They built the signatures from genome-wide microarray data. The signatures were then validated with a second method, quantitative PCR. A blood test that forecasts severity could guide hospital care. In outbreaks, it could direct scarce resources to the highest-risk patients.
plos-pone-0007992:
Ferhat Ay, Fei Xu, and Tamer Kahveci tackled a hard computing problem in cell biology for PLOS ONE in 2009. Gene networks can be modeled as switches that are on or off. Their settled states, called steady states, show how the network will behave in the long run.

Finding every settled state grows hard fast as networks grow. The team's methods scale that search to much larger networks than older tools could handle. Big, true-to-life networks can now be mapped in full, which helps modelers test ideas about disease and drug effects before lab work begins.
plos-pone-0008092:
David Rand and Thomas Pfeiffer compared the three doors into one famous journal in PLOS ONE in 2009. The journal PNAS lets authors enter by direct submission, through an editor, or through a member's sponsorship. Critics had long suspected the doors were not equal.

Citation counts, the field's rough score of impact, differed by door in a steady pattern. Papers from some tracks drew more notice than others, year after year. The audit does not prove favoritism, but it gives reformers hard numbers about a system often judged by rumor. The comparison covers the journal's own records across its tracks.
plos-pone-0008192:
Lise Geisler Andersen and colleagues combined data from thirteen Nordic cohorts in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their meta-analysis asked whether birth weight relates to later physical activity. Events before birth may shape the risk of chronic disease in adult life. They may also shape habits such as how much people move and exercise.

The authors pooled results on leisure time activity in adolescence and adulthood. Pooling many cohorts gives a firmer answer than any single study. Whatever the link, it bears on how early life echoes into adult health. The work speaks to research on the roots of long-term disease risk.
plos-pone-0008292:
Andrea Perne and colleagues studied heart drugs with cancer effects in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Cardiac glycosides are widely used to treat heart failure. They block the sodium-potassium pump in cells. They are also highly toxic to cells, and studies suggested anti-tumor activity. Trials in cancer patients were already under way.

The team demonstrated how these drugs kill human cells. They induce cell death by inhibiting general protein synthesis. Without new proteins, cells cannot sustain themselves. A clear mechanism strengthens the case for testing these drugs in cancer. It also warns where toxicity may arise.
plos-pone-0008392:
Suewei Lin, Yaling Huang, and Tzumin Lee studied fly brain development in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Nuclear receptors are transcription factors controlled by small ligand molecules. They govern many critical processes, including brain development. The Drosophila genome holds eighteen nuclear receptor genes. The team explored their roles by focusing on one called unfulfilled.

Unfulfilled regulates axonal guidance and cell identity in mushroom body neurons. The mushroom body is the fly brain's learning center. Guidance errors would miswire those neurons. The finding shows a single receptor shaping both wiring and identity. It advances understanding of how brains are built.
plos-pone-0008492:
Kiyotaka Tokuraku and co-authors image protein clumping in real time in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Clumping of proteins plays a major role in brain disorders such as Alzheimer disease. The peptide amyloid-beta is a key clumping protein in that disease. Yet no one had directly imaged its clumping as it happened. Steps include small clusters forming and then growing into fibers. The team use novel quantum-dot probes for the task.

Quantum dots are tiny glowing particles that can tag peptides. With them, the authors watch and measure aggregates as they form. Real-time views reveal rates and stages once hidden. The method may serve drug tests that aim to block clumping.
plos-pone-0008592:
Julie Miller and co-authors study song practice in young birds in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Trial-by-trial variability during motor learning is encoded by the basal ganglia. That variability matters in both humans and songbirds. It helps reinforce optimal motor patterns, including speech and birdsong. The parallels between birdsong and speech learning are many. The team ask if song practice itself promotes vocal variability. They focus on a key stage of sensorimotor learning in juveniles.

They find practice promotes acute vocal variability at that stage. After practice sessions, young birds sing more variable songs. That variability may fuel learning by exploring motor options. The result links a brain learning circuit to the benefits of practice.
plos-pone-0008692:
Sylvain Cardinaud, Shelley Starck, Piyanka Chandra, and colleagues explored a shortcut in immune watchfulness. Their article came out in PLOS ONE in 2010. Killer T cells patrol the body by reading scraps shown on cell surfaces. An infected cell must show viral scraps fast, before new viruses escape. Short, cut-down protein pieces seem to feed that speedy display.

The team examined how these trimmed pieces are made and used. Such pieces can help healthy watchfulness by speeding the alarm. Viruses, though, may bend the same shortcut to hide. Understanding the trick could shape vaccines that train T cells more effectively.
plos-pone-0008792:
Jack Sipe, T. Michael Scott, Sarah Murray, and colleagues searched blood for signs of an overactive cannabis-like system. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Severe obesity raises the risk of diabetes, heart disease, and stroke. The endocannabinoid system helps govern appetite and fat storage. It runs hot in obesity, feeding the problem. Reliable blood markers of that overdrive were lacking.
