The team measured candidate biomarkers in people with severe obesity. Certain markers tracked with the system's activation state. Such markers could sort patients for treatments that block the system. They may also track whether weight loss calms the system down.
plos-pone-0008892:
Sean Watts, Melissa Uhl, Stephen Maurano, and colleagues ranked the threats facing a rare coastal plant. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The plant is a hemiparasite, tapping other plants while making some food itself. Cordylanthus rigidus subspecies littoralis survives in few places. Recovery plans must choose which threats to fight first. Simply helping everything at once wastes scarce funds. Small, focused studies can rank the dangers instead.

Their threat-ranking approach weighed each factor's impact on the plant. Interactions between threats were considered, not just single effects. Ranked lists let managers fund the highest-value actions. Rare species everywhere could borrow this triage method.
plos-pone-0008992:
Yoseph Kram, Stephanie Mantey, and Joseph Corbo charted how light sensors arrange themselves in bird eyes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Birds have among the richest colour vision of any backboned animal. Their retinas hold five kinds of cone cells for sensing light. Four support colour vision with four channels; a double cone handles motion.

Each cone type spreads across the retina in its own even pattern. The five mosaics form independently, each spacing itself without orders from the others. Self-organisation by each type builds the whole orderly layout. How the tiles form may explain how fine bird colour vision is wired.
plos-pone-0009092:
Claire Repellin and co-authors gave mice a small viral RNA and watched their lymph tissue swell, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Epstein-Barr virus infects most humans and is tied to several cancers. Nearly all tumours linked to it make a small non-coding RNA called EBER1. Non-coding RNAs regulate genes without building proteins.

Mice engineered to express EBER1 developed lymphoid hyperplasia. Some went on to develop lymphoma, a cancer of lymphocytes. The viral RNA alone pushed lymph tissue toward cancer in this model. That strengthens the case that EBER1 helps EBV cause tumours in people.
plos-pone-0009192:
I. Martin Sheldon and co-authors published this veterinary study in PLOS ONE in 2010. After calving, about four in ten cattle develop infection of the womb lining. The illness, a form of pelvic inflammatory disease, hurts fertility and milk output. Common gut bacteria, Escherichia coli, are often found at the scene.

The team tested whether ordinary E. coli or only certain strains can cause this disease. They report that specific strains are indeed pathogenic for the womb lining. Those strains triggered pelvic inflammatory disease in both cattle and mice. Knowing the culprits are particular strains, not the whole species, sharpens how vets can prevent and treat the infection.
plos-pone-0009292:
Jennifer Schrack, Eleanor Simonsick, and Luigi Ferrucci published this measurement study in PLOS ONE in 2010. A portable device called the Cosmed K4b2 lets researchers measure breathing outside the lab. That opens the door to costing everyday activities in clinics and homes. First, though, the device must prove accurate against trusted standards.

The team compared the portable system during steady-state walking. Walking at a constant pace gives a stable energy demand to measure. Their comparison shows how well the device tracks that demand. Reliable portable measurement matters for studies of aging and health, where lab treadmills miss how people really move through daily life.
plos-pone-0009392:
Conrad Shyu, Celeste Brown, and F. Marty Ytreberg published this fish study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rainbow trout carry more than one form of the estrogen receptor, a protein that senses the hormone estrogen. Their gene tree hints that the whole fish genome was once copied, leaving spare forms behind. Each spare may since have been tuned to grip hormones in its own way.

The team used computer models to test how well each form holds estradiol, the chief estrogen. Tighter and looser grips show where evolution pushed hard and where it let go. The work links a vast event in fish history to small shifts in how trout sense hormones.
plos-pone-0009492:
Anita Jung and colleagues tested a membrane shaping protein in living fruit flies in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein, endophilin, helps nerve endings take back used signal packets. Part of it, the BAR domain, senses and bends cell membranes. Past structure work hinted at which spots in that domain matter most. The team changed those spots one by one in flies.

Flies with changed domains showed which spots are vital for the protein's job at synapses. Doing the test in a living animal ties structure to real function. The map of the domain helps explain how cells pinch off tiny membrane bubbles. That process underlies every nerve signal.
plos-pone-0009592:
Cassandra Martin and William Wagner weighed a mating risk in field crickets in PLOS ONE in 2010. Female crickets prefer males with certain attractive songs. A male's song, though, also draws parasitic flies that lay eggs on listeners. Those flies can kill the cricket they infect. The team asked whether females near a favored song face greater danger.

Females close to preferred songs did face higher parasitism. Seeking the best mate thus carries a direct cost. The study captures a trade off at the heart of mate choice. It shows how a signal built for love can also summon death.
plos-pone-0009692:
Doctors judge heart disease risk from blood pressure, cholesterol, and family history. Myungjin Kim and colleagues tested a molecular option in PLOS ONE in 2010. They asked whether DNA methylation could flag higher risk. Methylation is a chemical mark that can silence genes.

Methylation patterns differ between people and can shift with age and habits. The study weighed whether those patterns track with known risk for cardiovascular disease. A blood-based mark that flags risk early could guide prevention before symptoms appear. The authors present the approach as a candidate tool that needs wider testing.
plos-pone-0009892:
Reading a word involves sorting it fast: is it a real word or not? Clara Martin, Guillaume Thierry, and Jean-François Démonet measured the brain's response during that sorting. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

ERP stands for event-related potentials, brief brain waves time-locked to a stimulus. The task was visual lexical categorization under sustained attention. Sustained attention means holding focus over a long series of trials. Attention effects can change even very early brain responses. The measurements show how steady attention shapes word recognition moment by moment.
plos-pone-0009992:
Melanoma cells spread by cutting paths through tissue, and enzymes that activate other proteins help them. Claude Lalou and colleagues blocked those enzymes in human melanoma cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The enzymes are proprotein convertases, which switch on proteins by trimming them. Inhibiting them repressed the invasiveness of primary melanoma cells. Primary cells come straight from a patient's tumor. The cells carried altered p53, CDKN2A, and N-Ras genes, common melanoma faults. Slowing invasion matters because spread, not the first tumor, usually kills. Blocking spread is a goal shared by many cancer drugs.
plos-pone-0010092:
The authors were Linshan Shang, Radha Ananthakrishnan, Qing Li, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used adult mouse heart cells to model injury. When blood flow returns after a blockage, tissue can be harmed anew. Compounds called AGEs, tied to diabetes and inflammation, worsen that kind of heart injury.

The team traced how RAGE, the receptor for those compounds, shapes the damage. Two signaling routes, JNK and GSK-3 beta, carried much of the effect. Blocking those routes in heart cells could be a path toward limiting injury after heart attacks.
plos-pone-0010192:
The authors were Beatriz Suárez-Álvarez, Ramón Rodriguez, Vincenzo Calvanese, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study asked why stem cells provoke so little immune attack. Human embryonic stem cells hold promise for regenerating tissue. They show low immune visibility to the body's defense cells. They carry low levels of MHC class-I markers and none of class-II. Those markers are what immune cells use to judge foreignness.

The team studied stem cells made in the lab as well, called induced pluripotent cells. They found epigenetic mechanisms, chemical marks on DNA, regulate those immune markers. Understanding that control matters for safe transplant use of lab-grown cells.
plos-pone-0010292:
The authors were Michael Gao, Ursula Bellugi, Li Dai, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used Williams syndrome to hunt genes behind intelligence. Genetics is the strongest known influence on human intelligence, yet specific genes remain largely unknown. Williams syndrome, a genetic condition with a distinctive cognitive profile, offers a focused way to search for those contributions.

The team related measured gene expression to intelligence scores in this group. They linked intelligence to STX1A, a gene for part of the presynaptic SNARE complex. That complex helps neurons release their chemical messages, tying a release protein to thinking ability.
plos-pone-0010392:
Angela Bithell and colleagues linked a signaling protein to bipolar disorder in PLOS ONE in 2010. In the growing brain, certain young nerve cells switch on a protein called MR-GEF. It helps those cells respond to a signal system named Rap1. The cells in question make GABA, the brain's main calming chemical. Two guide proteins, Dlx1 and Dlx2, control their birth.

The team found MR-GEF levels differed in people with bipolar disorder. A protein from early development showing up in an adult mood illness is a useful clue. It suggests the roots of bipolar disorder may reach back to how the brain was built. That idea has gained ground for several mental illnesses. This study adds a named molecule to the case.
plos-pone-0010492:
Julia Steitz and colleagues reported a candidate vaccine against the 2009 pandemic flu in PLOS ONE in 2010. The new H1N1 virus had spread worldwide, raising fears about vaccine supply. Their vaccine used a harmless adenovirus as a carrier for flu genes. It was built and tested in mice during the pandemic itself. Speed was of the essence, and adenovirus platforms can be made quickly.

In mice, the vaccine produced protective immunity against the pandemic strain. A carrier-based design might be stockpiled or adapted faster than egg-grown vaccines. Mouse protection does not guarantee human success, but it clears a first hurdle. The study shows pandemic vaccine science moving in near real time. It also adds evidence for adenovirus as a flu platform.
plos-pone-0010592:
Ai Xia and colleagues mapped chromosome change in malaria mosquitoes for PLOS ONE in 2010. In Anopheles gambiae, chunks of chromosome often flip end to end. These inversions are not spread evenly across the genome.

The team charted where flips cluster and how the genome is organized around them. Clusters sat in regions that also shape how the mosquito adapts to local conditions. Inversions can lock helpful gene sets together, letting populations specialize. Understanding that layout matters for malaria control, since control tools often work differently on different mosquito populations across Africa.
plos-pone-0010692:
Satya Varanasi and colleagues compared gene activity in spongy bone from different body sites, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bone diseases often strike one site and spare another. The hip, jaw, and skull are built under different loads and from different cell lines, so their inner workings may differ too.

Gene profiles from trabecular bone differed clearly by site. Signaling routes tied to growth and hormones also varied with location. Those site signatures may explain why some drugs help one bone and not another. The work argues that bone studies should name their site and avoid treating the whole skeleton as one tissue.
plos-pone-0010792:
Rob Moonen and colleagues tested a gene variant and blood chemistry in preterm babies, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The amino acid arginine matters greatly for newborn growth and blood flow. A variant called T1405N in the CPS1 gene had been tied to arginine levels in full-term babies. Preterm babies, whose chemistry is more fragile, had not been checked.

In preterm infants, carrying the variant made no clear difference to arginine levels. The study is a clean negative, and negatives steer care away from blind alleys. Feeding and treatment plans for preterm infants need not be split by this gene test.
plos-pone-0010892:
Jianfeng Zhu, Yong-Tao Zhang, Mark Alber and co-authors published this modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2010. How a growing limb decides where bones form, and how many, remains one of development's open puzzles. Recent work suggests early cartilage tissue can organize itself through a local circuit that activates itself while suppressing its surroundings.

The team simulated that core cartilage-forming circuit inside growing limb shapes, under a gradient of a growth signal flowing from the limb tip. Their model reproduced major features of how limb skeletons form and how they changed through evolution, across different geometries. Zhu and colleagues argue that a simple self-organizing network, rather than a detailed blueprint, may lay out the bones. That idea helps explain both normal limbs and fossil transitions such as fins becoming digits.
plos-pone-0010992:
Vici Varghese, Elijah Wang, Farbod Babrzadeh and co-authors published this HIV methods study in PLOS ONE in 2010. A resistance mutation called K65R weakens several front-line HIV drugs, and reports suggested it is commoner in subtype C virus than subtype B. The authors suspected a measurement trap: the test itself might create the mutation it claims to find.

Deep sequencing of patient samples first seemed to confirm more K65R in subtype C. But careful clonal sequencing failed to verify the mutation in key samples, so they ran the deep method on laboratory clones with known sequences. The pattern of the template itself influenced false readings. Varghese and colleagues show that a celebrated subtype difference may be partly an artifact of PCR, a caution for every study that hunts rare variants with powerful sequencers.
plos-pone-0011092:
Smith and Shanley presented a math model in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject was a family of proteins called FOXO, which help control cell stress and lifespan. Many signals linked to aging change these proteins by adding small chemical marks, and the marks interact in complex ways.

The model predicts how FOXO proteins respond when several marks are applied at once. That kind of model lets scientists test ideas in a computer before costly lab work. It may reveal points where aging signals could be adjusted. The work is a tool for research on healthy aging and age linked disease.
plos-pone-0011192:
Lotoski, Simons, Chooniedass and colleagues tested a peanut allergy marker in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some children outgrow peanut allergy, but proving tolerance safely is hard. The team asked whether blood levels of a calming immune signal, IL-10, mark children who have gained true tolerance.

A useful marker would spare children risky food challenges and strict avoidance alike. The study checks whether this candidate signal deserves that role. Allergy care needs tests that separate lasting allergy from resolved allergy clearly. Even a partial answer helps families and doctors judge when a careful food test is worth trying.
plos-pone-0011292:
Nougairede, Lagier, Ninove and colleagues surveyed Marseille during the 2009 swine flu wave for PLOS ONE in 2010. Many residents hesitated to accept the new H1N1 vaccine. The team examined whether the sources people trusted for information tracked with their willingness to be vaccinated.

A likely link between information sources and vaccine acceptance emerged from their data. Where people get news shapes how they judge a new vaccine's risks. Public health teams can use that knowledge to place clear messages in trusted channels. The lesson applies to any fast moving outbreak where rumors compete with official advice.
plos-pone-0011392:
Malavika Subramanyam and colleagues tracked child undernutrition in India from 1992 to 2005 in a 2010 study. India grew richer over those years, yet many children still did not get enough food to grow well. The key question was whether growth was shared: did poor children gain as much ground as rich children, or did the gap widen?

Using national survey data split by household wealth, the team mapped how the burden of undernutrition shifted across social groups over time. Their trend analysis shows who benefited from progress and who was left behind. That record matters for policy, since national averages can hide deepening unfairness. Programs aimed only at average rates may miss the poorest children, whose needs the paper argues should guide where food and health efforts go first.
plos-pone-0011492:
David Razidlo and co-authors showed in 2010 that removing one gene regulator from young bone cells trades bone for fat. Histone deacetylase 3, or HDAC3, helps control which genes skeletal stem cells use as they choose between becoming bone, cartilage, or fat. The team depleted it only in osteo and chondro progenitor cells, the ancestors of bone and cartilage, in mice.

Bone density fell while fat inside the marrow rose, a seesaw shift in what the progenitors produced. One enzyme tipping that balance shows how closely bone loss and marrow fat are linked in aging and osteoporosis. The result cuts both ways as a warning: drugs that block this enzyme family, used in cancer care, might carry a skeletal cost. It also marks a lever that future bone treatments may need to protect rather than pull.
plos-pone-0011592:
Lauriane Cantin and colleagues asked how much rats truly value cocaine, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rats are the most common lab animal in addiction research. Measuring the drug's real value, and how that value changes with repeated use, has long been a central goal for the field.

Drawing on choice experiments, the authors argue that cocaine sits quite low on the rats' scale of rewards. Most rats favour other rewards when given a fair choice, even after drug exposure. That finding supports the idea that many animals show resilience to addiction, and it challenges the view of cocaine as an irresistible reward.
plos-pone-0011692:
Jimee Hwang and co-authors analysed Ethiopia's 2007 Malaria Indicator Survey, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Two years earlier, Ethiopia's health ministry had launched a major push, distributing millions of treated bed nets, widening access to effective malaria drugs and training thousands of village health workers. A national survey then measured what people knew and did.

The authors linked malaria knowledge to protective behaviour in households. Their results show where greater knowledge went together with net use and care-seeking, and where it did not. Health planners can use that map to aim education where it will actually change daily habits.
plos-pone-0011792:
Flavien Devun and co-authors traced how chemical cousins of ubiquinone kill selected cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Prolonged opening of a channel in mitochondria, the permeability transition pore, leads to cell death. Various ubiquinone analogs were known to regulate that pore, but what their regulation meant for cell fate had not been studied.

The team examined the analogs' effects and found a pore-dependent pathway to selective cell death. In other words, the compounds trip the mitochondrion's self-destruct hatch in chosen cells. A controllable death route like this interests cancer researchers seeking targeted killing.
plos-pone-0011892:
Petros Drineas, Jamey Lewis, and Peristera Paschou asked in 2010 how few DNA markers it takes to place where in Europe a person's roots lie. Large studies had shown that huge sets of markers can pin down a person's stock within Europe with great care. The open point was how small a set could be and still work well.

The team used short sets of markers picked for the way they vary from place to place, then worked out map points for the roots of each person tested. A short set makes such tests cheap and fast, and it shows how much place-based signal DNA holds. The same ideas help health studies, where mixed roots can skew links between genes and disease if they are not taken into account.
plos-pone-0011992:
Emily Stieren and co-workers tested in 2010 a popular theory about how inherited Alzheimer's mutations harm brain cells. Calcium balance inside cells is disturbed in Alzheimer's disease, and those disturbances were thought likely to help kill neurons. Familial Alzheimer's mutations, which cause early disease and run in families, were suspected of disturbing that balance directly.

Studying cells carrying familial mutations in the amyloid precursor protein gene, the team found calcium homeostasis was not directly perturbed. A negative finding this clean redirects the field: calcium problems in Alzheimer's may be a downstream effect rather than the mutations' first blow. Knowing where a chain of harm starts matters for choosing drug targets.
plos-pone-0012092:
Richard Williams, Ananthi Anandanadesan, and Drew Purves presented a new way to model food webs in PLOS ONE in 2010. Older models gave each species a place on a single scale, plus a feeding range around that place, but no one had pinned down what that scale really meant in nature. Their version adds chance, so a species can be more or less likely to eat others near its place on the scale.

With the new model, the scale lines up closely with body size. Big species tend to sit high and eat smaller ones below them. That link gives the abstract scale a real-world meaning and helps explain why size so strongly shapes who eats whom in wild food webs.
plos-pone-0012192:
Zackary Cleveland, Gary Cofer, Gregory Metz, and co-authors imaged gas entering the blood in human lungs in PLOS ONE in 2010. Breathing's real work happens in the tiny air sacs, where gases cross into the blood, yet standard tests report only a whole-lung average. That average can hide sick regions among healthy ones until disease is advanced.

Using a special form of xenon gas tuned for magnetic imaging, they mapped uptake region by region inside living lungs. A map can show where transfer fails, not just that it fails somewhere. Such detail could sharpen diagnosis of lung disease and let doctors judge treatments by watching the failing regions themselves improve.
plos-pone-0012392:
Tarek Benameur, Simon Tual-Chalot, Ramaroson Andriantsitohaina and colleagues studied how tiny membrane fragments help grow new blood vessels, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Progenitor cells from bone marrow build fresh vessels after injury, and fragments shed by other cells, called microparticles, can instruct them. The team asked whether a fat-sensing protein named PPAR alpha is required for that instruction to work.

Without working PPAR alpha, the progenitor cells failed to mature in response to microparticles, and vessel growth suffered. The protein thus sits at a required step in the repair pathway. The finding matters for heart and limb diseases where growing new vessels could restore blood flow to starved tissue.
plos-pone-0012492:
James Byrne, Radu Beltechi, Julia Yarnold and colleagues reported early results of a new brain aneurysm treatment, in a 2010 PLOS ONE multicentre study. Flow diversion places a dense mesh stent in the artery so blood is steered past the aneurysm, which then clots and seals. The method promised to treat large aneurysms that coils and surgery handle poorly.

Across several centers, the prospective study recorded how the first patients fared with the devices. Early experience defines both the promise and the complications of a new device class. Those lessons shape patient selection and technique as flow diversion moves from novelty to standard care.
plos-pone-0012592:
Alessandro Bitto, Chad Lerner, Claudio Torres and colleagues exposed cells to a growth factor for long periods, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. IGF-I is a trophic factor that keeps many cell types alive and growing, yet reduced IGF-I signaling extends lifespan in several organisms — a paradox. The team asked what chronic, rather than brief, exposure does to a cell's housekeeping and survival.

Long-term IGF-I exposure decreased autophagy, the cell's recycling system, and lowered cell viability. A growth signal that slowly disables cleanup could explain part of the lifespan paradox. The result adds mechanistic support to the idea that dialing down growth signaling protects long-term cellular health.
plos-pone-0012692:
Lukov and Goodell mapped how a cancer-linked protein is marked for destruction. LYL1 is a gene switch found at high levels in T-cell leukaemia patients. Their 2010 study asked what tells the cell's shredder, the proteasome, to destroy this protein.

A rich stretch near the protein's start, called a PEST site, gave the order, and it worked without needing a phosphate tag first. Knowing the disposal route may let drug makers lower LYL1 in leukaemia cells. It also adds a case to the rules of protein control. Similar disposal signals appear on many short-lived gene switches.
plos-pone-0312792:
Davis Kibirige and colleagues pooled twenty studies, covering over eleven thousand adults with diabetes in Uganda, on how common five long term diabetes complications are and what drives them. Diabetes is rising fast in Uganda, and complications from eye, kidney, nerve, foot, and vessel damage drive disability. Searches spanned five major databases in May 2024.

Pooled results showed a high burden of chronic complications, though the summary here stresses the overall verdict over single rates. Factors tied to each complication were gathered by narrative synthesis across studies. Regular screening and tighter early control of blood sugar and pressure, the authors urge, should become routine in Ugandan diabetes clinics.
plos-pone-0327692:
Sex workers in Nairobi faced close contact with many clients as COVID-19 arrived, raising fears of rapid spread. Su D Yang and colleagues followed a cohort of about one thousand women enrolled just before the pandemic, testing blood samples roughly a year later, in this PLOS One study.

About twenty-eight percent carried antibodies showing past infection by the follow-up visit, and the share rose steadily through the period. About a quarter of the women were living with HIV. Questionnaires on behavior and symptoms let the team test which traits traveled with infection. The authors describe steady, widespread transmission rather than an explosive outbreak in this high-contact group.
plos-pone-0332792:
Sakinah Awangharun and Norlidah Alias test a teaching module for intensive care nurses in Malaysia. Their 2026 study concerns weaning patients from mechanical ventilation after heart surgery. The task demands deep knowledge plus careful reasoning. Nurses read patient data, judge readiness, and justify each ventilator adjustment. No dedicated teaching module for this skill existed in Malaysian nursing education. The authors built one and put it on trial.

Twenty-four nurses in a cardiothoracic ICU took part. The design compared performance before and after the module, without randomisation. Nurses were also grouped against the institute's seventy percent competency threshold. That pass mark governs clinical privileges at the national heart institute involved. A structured module matters because ventilator weaning is high-stakes and learnable. Showing measurable gains would give educators a template for other advanced procedures where nurses carry real decision weight.
plos-pone-0333292:
Geronimo Bejarano and colleagues studied what happened when United States states let patients see a physical therapist directly, without a doctor referral first. Easier access to non drug pain care might cut opioid use. Pill shipment and opioid death data from 2006 to 2014 were compared between states that adopted direct access and states that did not, with several robustness checks.

After adoption, pill volume per person fell by a clear margin, about fifteen percent relative to trend. Opioid deaths did not fall by a clear margin. States that adopted had started with higher pill use and deaths. Removing a referral barrier, the authors conclude, can trim opioid supply, even if death rates need broader action to move.
plos-pone-0337792:
Jérôme Allardet-Servent and seven colleagues search blood for early warnings of severe COVID-19 lung failure. Their 2026 prospective study enrolled fifty-four patients with confirmed COVID pneumonia in France. Five proteins tied to lung lining and vessel injury were measured on set days. Patients were grouped by the strongest breathing support they later needed. Twenty-three eventually required mechanical ventilation.

Three markers were already higher at admission in patients headed for ventilation. One, called sRAGE, stood out with levels more than double the others' group. It also survived statistical adjustment as an independent predictor. A blood draw in the first two days could therefore flag patients likely to deteriorate. Earlier warning means earlier intensive care planning, rather than emergency escalation. The cohort was small and from one centre, so the markers now need testing in larger, mixed hospital populations.
plos-pone-0343792:
Sara M de Jong-Ultee and colleagues studied teamwork inside hospital units built around single conditions, like prostate cancer or geriatric trauma, at one Dutch hospital. Such units promise better value care only if professions truly work together. A coordination survey scored how well teams communicate and respect each other, followed by interviews in four units to explain the scores.

Scores varied hugely between professions inside the same unit, and ran higher among staff who share the same stretch of a care path. Interviews named four drivers: smooth communication, active engagement, mutual recognition, and workable workflow. Old hospital layouts and split record systems still block the daily contact these units need.
plos-pone-0343892:
Louise Burnie and co-authors interviewed twenty competitive women cyclists in 2026 about how the menstrual cycle affects training and racing. Evidence and open talk on the topic remain limited in elite sport, despite symptoms being common.

Riders described wide ranging symptoms that varied in timing and strength. Nearly half had experienced irregular cycles, which some linked to low body weight or eating too little for their training load. Most had mentioned their cycle to a coach, usually only briefly on a training log. Riders welcomed elite athletes speaking publicly, and asked for coaches who can hold fuller conversations.
plos-pone-0345192:
Missing at least a tenth of school days counts as chronic absence, and Caroline Reid-Westoby and colleagues measured it in Canadian kindergarten classes before and after COVID-19. Their 2026 PLOS One study covered more than half a million children across two cohorts.

Absence rates climbed after the pandemic began, continuing a wider attendance shift seen through grade twelve. The team also linked absence to developmental vulnerability measured in the same children, checking language, social, and physical readiness. Kindergarten absence matters because early gaps predict later reading trouble and lower achievement. The authors argue attendance support should start in the very first school year, not after patterns harden.
plos-pone-0345792:
Bernardo Corrêa d'Almeida and Carla Cunha lay out a trial protocol testing whether emotion-focused therapy can help older adults forgive people who have hurt them. Unresolved emotional injuries weigh heavily in later life, yet this therapy has rarely been tailored to people over sixty-five. Seventy volunteers will be assigned either to start twelve weekly therapy sessions at once or to wait twelve weeks before receiving the same help.

Judgement comes in two stages. First the trial asks whether such a study can even run well in this age group, watching recruitment, attendance, dropout, and how credible and satisfying participants find the therapy. Health measures taken during and after therapy, and at two follow-ups, will hint at benefit. Only if this small run succeeds will a full trial follow. No results are reported here.
plos-pone-0345892:
Francois Verster and colleagues calculated how much life diabetes costs New Zealanders, using linked national records for four and a half million people from 2015 to 2019. Few recent local figures existed, and Māori and Pacific peoples carry a heavy share of the disease. The 2026 study built life tables for people with type one diabetes, type two diabetes, and no diabetes, broken down by ethnicity.

Diabetes shortened lives at every age, with the largest losses in the young. Pacific men diagnosed in youth lost around twenty-four years of remaining life with type one diabetes, and Māori men about seventeen, against thirteen overall. Death rates from most causes ran higher with diabetes.
plos-pone-0346792:
Qiaoling Pan and colleagues mined the United States drug safety reporting database for medicines linked to breathing and chest symptoms after lung surgery. Patients often suffer breathlessness, cough, palpitations, and chest pain after these operations, and drugs may play a hidden role. The team used statistical signal methods on the most reported medicines for each symptom.

They flagged four drugs with strong signals and ten with medium signals after lung surgery. Three of the strong-signal drugs treat pulmonary hypertension, high blood pressure in the lung arteries. Closer analysis suggested the link may come from what these drugs do in the body. Such database signals cannot prove a drug caused harm, but they tell doctors where to look first.
plos-pone-0346892:
Funda Uysal tested whether turning lessons into games helps trainee teachers grasp abstract curriculum ideas: objectives, content, learning experiences, and evaluation. One hundred twenty-two student teachers at a Turkish state university were split by a rigorous four-group design that controls for the effect of pretesting itself. Half learned through game-based activities, half through traditional teaching.

The game groups formed far richer mental pictures of the curriculum elements, with especially large gains for content understanding. Journals from those students brimmed with motivation, curiosity, and clearer concepts. Uysal argues gamification deserves a lasting place in teacher education, both for understanding and for the enthusiasm that sustains a teaching career.
plos-pone-0347192:
Jurij Hladnik and colleagues measure how much work giant slalom skiers do with their own muscles in this 2026 PLOS ONE sports science paper. Gravity does most of the speeding in alpine skiing, but skiers also push and absorb with their legs. Five skilled skiers raced a set course wearing satellite positioning and motion-capture systems.

Reconstructing the motion showed skiers absorb far more work than they produce: negative work, braking and controlling, was roughly three times the positive work. Work done along the direction of travel stayed positive, paid for by the absorbing actions. The profiles tell coaches that elite slalom is mostly a strength game of controlled braking, not pushing.
plos-pone-0347292:
Volha Charnysh and co-authors ran two large survey experiments with more than seven thousand five hundred Americans to see who they think deserves help after a climate disaster. Respondents saw an artist's picture of a fictional flood and rated aid for victims whose race and country were changed from one version to the next.

Victims in Brazil or South Africa drew clearly less support than victims in the United States, and the gap was widest among Republicans. Race mattered less and in opposing directions: white Republicans gave less to Black victims at home, while white Democrats gave more. The authors link these patterns to how distant or deserving victims feel to the giver.
plos-pone-0347492:
Judit Gonzalvo, Jorge Escudero, and Xavier Belles study a timing gene in the growing embryo of the German cockroach. The gene normally keeps young insects from maturing too early, but its job inside the egg was unclear. Their 2026 study measures the gene's message across embryo life and silences it in mothers to see how their offspring develop.

Message levels started extremely high on day one, pointing to supply from the mother, then fell fast. Silencing the gene cut hatching and warped early body formation, with limbs lagging and later stages stalling. In fruit flies the same gene peaks much later in the egg. Shifts in its timing may have helped insect body plans split apart in evolution.
plos-pone-0347792:
Raf Ana Rabbi Shawon and colleagues let camera traps watch a Bangladeshi national park for a year, in this 2026 PLOS ONE conservation study. Nineteen camera stations in Satchari National Park recorded more than eight thousand video clips between May 2024 and April 2025, many of them people rather than wildlife.

The cameras documented hunting and poaching, including people carrying firearms and bows, plus wood collection, tourism, and livestock grazing inside the protected area. Human activity also shifted when wild animals were active. The authors argue protection on paper is failing in practice, and that camera evidence gives park managers a concrete record for enforcement patrols.
plos-pone-0347892:
Katrina Grasby and colleagues used a large Australian twin study to untangle how sleep relates to school performance and attention in children and teenagers. More than five thousand twins, aged roughly nine to fifteen, contributed measures of sleep quality, duration, bedtime regularity, sleepiness, and snoring, alongside reading, mathematics, and ratings of inattention and hyperactivity. Twins let the researchers separate family-level patterns from child-level ones.

Sleep explained only about one percent of the differences in reading and mathematics, but up to seven percent of the differences in inattention and hyperactivity. Where sleep did predict school results, inattention carried most of the effect. The study tempers claims that sleep drives grades directly, while supporting the sleep-attention link that teachers observe.
plos-pone-0347992:
Denise Moerel and colleagues recorded brain waves while people viewed objects shown at eight different rotations, in this 2026 PLOS ONE neuroscience paper. Recognizing a turned object is effortless for humans, and the team wanted to know when the brain builds a representation that no longer cares about the angle.

Computer classifiers reading the brain signals could identify objects within a tenth of a second, even across rotations. Information tied to one fixed angle peaked first, while angle-tolerant information crested later, around a fifth of a second after the image appeared. Showing images very fast weakened both kinds of signal without wiping them out. The sequence suggests the brain first registers a view, then settles on what the object is.
plos-pone-0348192:
Hamidou Ilboudo and colleagues spent a year trapping mosquitoes indoors in five villages at different distances from Burkina Faso's Soum dam, checking whether the reservoir reshapes malaria risk. More than eleven thousand Anopheles mosquitoes were identified by species and tested for the malaria parasite and for what they had been feeding on.

One species dominated, and mosquito density was highest right at the dam, falling with distance. Yet infection rates told the opposite story, peaking in the farther villages of Seguedin and Soala. About a third of the mosquitoes had fed on humans. The authors warn that dam-side control alone would miss the real transmission pattern and call for village-specific strategies.
plos-pone-0348292:
Megan A Catterton and co-authors test a way to read more from flow cytometry, a lab method that shines laser light on cells as they stream past a detector. Each passing cell makes a brief pulse of light, and the team asked whether the shape of that pulse can reveal the cell's size, speed, and dye content. It does this instead of just rough summary numbers.

Using plastic beads of known size and brightness, they confirmed that each property bends the pulse in its own way. Applied to dyed cells, the method showed that cells about to divide look wider in a way that matches their doubled contents. Better pulse reading could sharpen cell sorting and reduce errors caused by uneven flow.
plos-pone-0348392:
Pedro Leitão, Margarida Castro, and Aida Campos identified the distinct fisheries, called métiers, inside Portugal's coastal fleet in 2026 work. Managers need gear level detail to measure pressure on the sea, but a fleet of about five hundred boats using many gears hides that detail.

Logbooks and sales notes from a decade were analysed at haul level. Twenty-eight métiers emerged across six gear families. Octopus traps led, followed by hake nets and scabbardfish longlines. Each métier tied strongly to season, area, depth, and seabed type. Traps and nets worked mostly the northwest, longlines the central west, a geography managers can now target.
plos-pone-0348592:
K. R. Reshma and co-workers combine body-shape study with DNA reading to sort out a family of ticks in India's Western Ghats. These ticks carry germs that sicken people and animals, yet their family tree is unsettled. Their 2026 study collects more than two hundred ticks of ten species across three zones and sequences a standard gene marker, adding dozens of new records.

Shape and DNA agreed on most species names, including five species sequenced for the first time. The family tree did not support most traditional subgroups, suggesting the classification needs rework. Two counting methods found similar numbers of hidden species groups. Some named species showed deep internal splits, hinting at unnamed species hiding inside them.
plos-pone-0348792:
Petronella Pettersson and co-authors reviewed records of one hundred sixty laryngeal cancer patients who had their voice box removed at a Stockholm hospital between 2000 and 2021, in work published in 2026. A feared complication is a fistula, an abnormal opening between throat and skin.

About one in six patients developed the complication. Many factors looked risky alone, including low blood counts, prior radiation, and heart disease. In the final joint model only two stood firm: wider throat surgery and infection after the operation. Infection's very strong link argues for relentless prevention and early treatment in the days after surgery.
plos-pone-0349092:
Eszter Szőke and colleagues pooled the evidence on a blue dye bedside test used to check whether critically ill patients with a tracheostomy are inhaling food or liquid into their lungs. Nurses place dyed food in the mouth and watch for blue appearing in the windpipe suction. From more than two thousand screened papers, six studies qualified, all judging the dye test against camera examination of swallowing.

The dye test almost never cried wolf: when it came back positive, aspiration was essentially certain, and its overall specificity sat above ninety-five percent. Its weakness is the opposite error, missing cases, so the authors insist a negative result in a high-risk patient still demands the camera test. They position the dye as a cheap first alarm bell at the bedside, not a verdict.
plos-pone-0349192:
Nujud A Sinan and Mona S Almujaydil tested whether cafestol, a compound from coffee, can protect kidneys in diabetic rats. Diabetes damages kidneys through inflammation, oxidation, and scarring, and current care slows rather than stops the decline. Rats made diabetic with a standard drug received cafestol by mouth for eight weeks at two doses. Other groups tested the compound alone and alongside a blocker of the pathway under study.

Cafestol eased nearly every sign of kidney injury in a dose-dependent way: less protein leaking into urine, calmer inflammation, restored antioxidant defences, and reduced tissue damage. The protection vanished when the blocker was added, pinpointing the mechanism as the switching-on of a master antioxidant controller in kidney cells. Healthy rats given cafestol showed no kidney harm. The authors present cafestol as a candidate protector worth further study.
plos-pone-0349292:
Chompunuch Klinmalai and co-authors in Thailand compared two lab tests that count virus fighting T cells in 2026. The virus, cytomegalovirus, sleeps in most adults but can wake and harm people with weak immune systems, so doctors track the cells that hold it down.

Blood from thirty healthy volunteers was tested both ways after contact with virus material. One method spots cells making a defence signal in tiny wells; the other stains the cells and counts them by machine. The team also checked antibody levels. Knowing whether the two tests agree helps labs choose and interpret monitoring for patients at risk.
plos-pone-0349392:
Duo An and colleagues tracked diseases caused by asbestos in China across more than three decades, using global burden estimates running from nineteen ninety to twenty twenty-three. They counted new cases, deaths, and years of healthy life lost for the lung-scarring disease asbestosis and for cancers tied to asbestos, including mesothelioma and cancers of the lung, throat, and ovary.

Total case numbers kept climbing over the period, even though rates adjusted for age peaked around the early two thousands for asbestosis and near twenty ten for the cancers. Men and people over sixty-five carried the heaviest load. A modelled rise in deaths appeared during the early pandemic years. The authors call for tighter workplace rules and stronger labour protection laws in China.
plos-pone-0349592:
Angang Cao and colleagues tackled a precision problem inside waste-to-energy plants, where a long hydraulic arm must scrub clogged grates that feed the furnaces. Clogging can cut burning efficiency nearly in half and force shutdowns, but the arm sags under its own weight, spoiling accuracy. Instead of correcting errors after sensors spot them, their method predicts the sag from a stiffness model and compensates in advance.

Simulations of the arm's motion showed the feedforward strategy cut positioning errors by more than ninety percent in every direction, landing far inside the tolerance cleaning requires. Avoiding sensor delays makes the arm steadier as well as straighter. The model-based approach should transfer to other long, flexible machines that must work precisely, from construction cranes to mining rigs.
plos-pone-0349692: He and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on severe acute pancreatitis using gene data from blood. Their combined analysis found programs tied to NETosis, a way white blood cells die while casting webs. They also describe a pattern of weakened adaptive immunity that varies between patient groups. Sorting patients by such patterns could guide care in a disease that shifts fast.
plos-pone-0349792:
Anouk van Oss and colleagues describe a trial testing whether offering palliative care early helps cancer patients treated with radiation for bone metastases. Specialist palliative care improves quality of life, yet it is often offered late or not at all. The trial is nested inside a larger Dutch cohort study of bone metastasis treatment.

Two hundred forty-six patients will be split at random. Half are offered a consultation with the hospital palliative care team, which they may accept or decline. The other half continues usual care without being told about the offer. The main question is whether patients feel more satisfied with their care. The protocol reports the design only; results will follow when the trial completes.
plos-pone-0350192:
Irina Chis Ster, Philip J Cooper, and colleagues measured inflammation and heart-related disease in adults living in farming villages on the coast of Ecuador. These communities are in transition, with rising rates of diabetes and high blood pressure but few studies of blood markers there. Their 2026 survey covered more than nine hundred adults in ten villages, with blood tests, body measures, and health histories.

Half the adults had high levels of C-reactive protein, a general marker of inflammation, and high levels tracked strongly with hypertension, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome. Much of the link ran through body fat. A second marker tied to allergy-type responses showed no such pattern. The authors suggest the first marker could help flag high-risk adults in low-resource settings.
plos-pone-0350292:
Georgina Mathlin and colleagues explored a support service for men in open prisons in England who likely live with personality disorder. Open prisons sit between closed jails and release, a tense halfway space. The service aims to cut returns to closed wings and cut reoffending after release. Interviews covered ten staff and nine men who used or had used the service.

Men described the move to open life as a shock, and the service took time to trust. Once trust formed, they felt known and valued, with help shaped to their own story and path. Staff who built steady, warm bonds enabled that shift. Good resettlement, the study suggests, grows from personal trust as much as from rules.
plos-pone-0350392:
Victor CW Tam and co-authors surveyed trained bystanders in Hong Kong in 2026 about stepping in during a cardiac arrest. A teaching model urges focus on intention to act, yet fears and barriers, sharpened by the pandemic, can hold people back.

Nearly seven hundred trained adults answered an online survey. The team tested how felt barriers fed into attitudes, social pressure, and sense of control, and from there into intention to start resuscitation and use a defibrillator. Worry about infection changed some of those links. Training that tackles real fears directly, the results suggest, may turn more trained bystanders into willing rescuers.
plos-pone-0350692:
Bin Wang and co-authors filmed a small mountain stream fish attempting to pass low weirs, to learn what helps or blocks its upstream journey. Fishway design rules mostly come from large migratory fish, leaving small species like this barred loach relative unstudied. Their 2026 flume experiments varied the fish and the water conditions, recording success rates and the exact strategies used, from pure leaps to leap-and-swim combinations.

Larger fish leaped more and farther, while smaller fish leaned on the mixed strategy. A weir drop of about a hand's span beyond twenty-five centimeters allowed only partial passage under the tested setup. Deeper landing pools and longer resting pools suited the observed leaping. The authors stress these are early observations from one lab setup, needing field confirmation before they harden into design rules.
plos-pone-0350892:
Diabetic foot ulcers are dangerous and often treatable early. Yet many patients delay seeking care. Huiwen Xu and colleagues designed a teaching program to change that. The program builds on a multi-theory model of behavior. A trial will test it at hospitals in two Chinese cities. The protocol appeared in PLOS One in 2026.

Patients at risk will be split randomly into two groups. One group gets routine teaching plus a handbook. The other gets the new four-week program. Follow-up lasts three months. Questionnaires and clinical checks track foot care habits. Decision-making is tracked too. No results are reported yet. The aim is teaching that changes daily behavior.
plos-pone-0351092:
Sudden vertigo sends many people to emergency rooms, and balance exercises can speed recovery, yet clinics underuse them. Solmaz Surano and colleagues ran a trial across nine Swedish hospitals comparing internet-guided balance training with the usual written instructions, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Adults with the sudden vertigo syndrome joined within a week of symptoms starting. Half received six weeks of online exercises, personalized and stepped up as they improved; half got standard paper guidance. Assessors who graded outcomes did not know group assignments. The trial tests whether digital delivery, proven for long-standing dizziness, also works in the acute phase.
plos-pone-0351692:
Mythri Ambatipudi and seven colleagues profile signalling fats called eicosanoids in this 2026 study. These lipids help drive airway remodelling, scarring, and inflammation. Some are tied to asthma and lung fibrosis. The team measured over two hundred fifty of them in more than three thousand adults. Lung health was assessed by breathing tests and CT scans. Findings were checked in a second long-running American cohort.

Fifty-one metabolites tracked with lung function in the first cohort. Twenty-four of those held up in the validation group. Twenty-seven were tied to obstructive physiology, where air struggles to leave the lungs. Linoleic acid derivatives stood out among them. Early structural changes on scans also had metabolic companions. The catalogue gives researchers early-warning candidates and possible drug targets, well before lung disease becomes obvious in the clinic.
plos-pone-0351792:
Per Morten Fredriksen, Nandu Goswami, and Asgeir Mamen followed nearly twenty-three hundred Norwegian schoolchildren for five years. They tested a simple index against how much the children moved and how fit they were. The index divides waist size by height. It flags the belly fat most tied to later health risk. Motion trackers measured activity, and running tests measured fitness, year after year.

Each step up in the index came with less daily active time. It also came with weaker running results and lower aerobic fitness. The pattern held across the whole follow-up. The index is no diagnosis, but it costs almost nothing. A tape and a wall can sort a class in minutes. Schools can use that cheap sort to find children who are drifting into inactivity.
plos-pone-0351992:
Liuye Huang and seven colleagues follow American veterans to test whether COVID-19 infection raises diabetes risk. Their 2026 study uses a prospective cohort run through the Veterans Health Administration. Over twelve hundred veterans without diabetes enrolled between 2020 and 2022. Infected and uninfected participants were tracked for a median of about four years. Records supplied clinic visits, laboratory days, and new diabetes diagnoses. Statistical models adjusted for age, weight, smoking, and prior conditions.

An awkward pattern complicates the question. Veterans who tested positive used less care afterwards. They had fewer clinic days and fewer laboratory tests each year, including fewer glucose checks. Less testing can hide new diabetes rather than prevent it. Any fair comparison must therefore wrestle with detection itself. The study's contribution is exactly that care-seeking lens. It shows why raw diagnosis counts after infection can mislead, and how to correct for missing appointments in the data.
plos-pone-0352192:
Adina Davidson and colleagues ran a two-hour workshop on stubborn problems in health professions admissions. Fifteen people took part. They included faculty, staff, readers of applications, and student ambassadors. Together they framed problems, brainstormed, and built rough drafts of new ideas. The problems were current ones. Applicants now use generative AI. Interviews have moved online. Standard entry tests are being dropped.

The ideas fell into three families. One rebuilt the interview. One brought AI into the process on honest terms. One widened the criteria beyond test scores. No winner was crowned. The point was the method. Any program facing the same pressures can copy the exercise and grow its own answers.
plos-pone-0352992:
Finlayson and colleagues gathered first-hand accounts of pregnancy care with sickle cell disease in a 2026 review. The inherited blood condition shapes both the baby's genetic risk and the mother's health through pregnancy. The team combined studies of women with the disease or its milder trait and of the staff who care for them.

Women described fear and uncertainty, weak understanding among staff, and uneven support from services. In some places they faced stigma, unfair treatment, and poor care. Family and organized support helped where it existed. The authors call urgently for public awareness work and better training for maternity staff who meet this condition rarely.
plos-pone-0353192:
Zhenhua Miao, Ziyan Li, and Yongjie Wang presented in 2026 a planning framework for placing energy storage in modern power distribution networks. Batteries and other storage help local grids absorb solar and wind power, but deciding where storage goes and how big it should be is a hard optimization problem. Their framework works at two levels at once, and it is designed to stay sound under uncertainty about future demand and generation.

The method fixes the network's layout, uses a standard model of power flow, and adds a formal check that voltages stay within safe limits. It is expressed as an optimization problem that computers can solve reliably. Better storage planning lowers the cost of adding clean power to neighborhood grids.
plos-pone-0353292:
Yin, Han, and Chen surveyed social media users on how chatting shapes buying loyalty in a 2026 study. Nearly six hundred users answered questions about talking with other shoppers and with sellers. The team tested whether feeling that a brand is partly one's own links that talk to deeper engagement.

Talk with both fellow shoppers and sellers tied to stronger buying, recommending, influence, and knowledge sharing. Feeling ownership carried part of the effect for influence and knowledge. Skilled opinion leaders strengthened the link between seller talk and ownership. Brands thus gain when community talk feels personal, not only when ads push products.
plos-pone-0353392:
Alanazi and colleagues proposed a cooperative warning system to protect walkers and riders in traffic in a 2026 study. Car sensors miss people hidden by parked vehicles or bad weather. Their system links cars, roadside units, and phones or tags carried by walkers, sharing position and speed directly.

Software fuses the shared data and predicts crash points, then warns both drivers and walkers in time to move. In simulated city crossings, crash chances fell sharply, awareness rose, and alerts arrived faster than with car-only or radio-only setups. Real streets add noise and missing devices, so field trials are the honest next step.
plos-pone-0353692:
Lei Qiu and three colleagues speed up the search for self-healing construction materials in this 2026 paper. Their target is a cement composite laced with tiny capsules that release healing agents when cracks reach them. Simulating how fluids move and cracks spread through such disordered material is accurate but painfully slow. The team instead represents scans of the material as graphs. Grains, pores, and capsules become nodes, their physical connections edges. Graph neural networks then train as fast stand-ins for the heavy simulations.

The graph models predicted permeability more than a hundred thousand times faster than the standard simulation while staying highly accurate. Guided by this active learning loop, the system found a surprising best design: elongated capsules tilted at an angle to the likely crack direction, within a few dozen expensive checks. The authors present the framework as a general shortcut for designing complex materials.
plos-pone-0353992:
Ge Zhang led a team of six authors sorting out social responsibility frameworks for small firms, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Small and medium enterprises face a flood of corporate social responsibility frameworks they cannot afford to follow whole. The team rationalized the many dimensions of CSR toward what actually supports sustainable business performance.

Zhang's streamlined picture shows small firms which responsibility efforts genuinely pay off. Their analysis compared reasoning before and after testing, tightening the model against data. For an owner with no CSR department, a short list of high-value actions beats a thick framework. The study also helps policymakers design support that small firms can use, instead of rules written for corporations with whole compliance teams.
plos-pone-0354092:
Van Hoey and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a trial called IMPROVE, about refilling implanted drug pumps. Such pumps send pain or anti-spasm medicine straight into the fluid around the spinal cord, which helps people whose other treatments fail. Pumps must be refilled on a regular schedule, and each trip to hospital can be a burden.

Eighty-two patients will each have four refills: two at home and two at the clinic, in a random order. Since each person tries both settings, the trial can compare comfort fairly within the same patient. The team will also track quality of life, pain, stress, worry, caregiver strain, safety, and cost. Follow-up spans about a year of refills. If home refills prove more comfortable and fair in cost, the authors argue, home service could become the standard way to maintain these pumps.
plos-pone-0354292:
Jun Wang and Bei Yu analysed more than ninety thousand observational study abstracts to learn who reaches for causal language. Observational data cannot prove cause and effect, so strong causal wording should track evidence strength alone. Their 2026 study used language analysis and regression to test whether author traits predict causal phrasing instead.

Causal language appeared more often in work by less experienced authors. Smaller teams used it more, as did papers with male last authors. Authors from cultures scoring high on uncertainty avoidance, a preference for certainty over ambiguity, also leaned causal. Wang and Yu argue certainty in print is partly social, and editors may need to police causal claims beyond the data's strength.
plos-pone-0354592:
Zhenyu Zhang and three colleagues published this 2026 training study with sixty-four teenage male sprinters in China. For eight weeks, half followed classic sprint training while half did high-intensity interval cross training, which mixes sprinting, jumping drills, and functional strength work. Both plans carried similar overall effort loads.

The cross-training group improved more in the hundred meters, early race splits, ground contact time, and jumping power. Other measures, like the squat jump, showed no clear edge. Zhang suggests cross training as a useful add-on for young sprinters, while noting the narrow sample means bigger studies should confirm the benefit.
plos-pone-0354692:
Reeson and colleagues, in a 2026 study, review outcomes for two hundred one children and teens who completed a year-long treatment program after sexual abuse. The program, run at a dedicated ranch facility, mixes several forms of therapy and support in episodes of care. Survivors face raised risks of trauma symptoms, depression, and self-harm, and no standard best treatment exists.

Most participants were girls, split between younger children and adolescents. From entry to graduation, every measured outcome moved in the right direction: trauma symptoms, depression, anxiety, self-esteem, family functioning, quality of life, and substance use. The largest gains were in teenagers' trauma symptoms, depression, and anxiety, all with big effect sizes. The authors note a limit: only those who finished the year were counted, out of a larger starting group. Even so, they offer the results as rare long-program evidence in a field short on it.
plos-pone-0354892:
Ali Ahmed Salem and co-authors predict how badly pollution coats high-voltage glass insulators, a grime layer that can trigger flashovers and outages. Utilities measure coating severity with a salt-density score, but testing is slow and manual. Four learning models were trained on several hundred records spanning fifteen weather and operating features, tuned two ways, and then interrogated with an explanation method that ranks which features drive each prediction.

A smooth probabilistic model won on accuracy under every tuning style. Keeping only the top ten ranked features beat using five or all fifteen, sharpening accuracy while trimming complexity. Salem and colleagues present the trimmed, explainable models as tools grid crews can actually audit before trusting them with maintenance decisions.
plos-pone-0355192:
Hui Thew and colleagues test in 2026 whether short online videos can help adults in Malaysia who have poorly controlled type two diabetes. Patients at a public clinic were split at random between video lessons plus reminders and usual care. Videos came in several local languages and covered food, activity, medicines, and preventing harm.

After three and six months, the video group knew more about diabetes and felt more able to manage it. Blood sugar, blood pressure, blood fats, and body measures also improved more than with usual care alone. The authors present web based teaching as a low cost extra that clinics could offer widely.
plos-pone-0355292:
Yijie Chen and six colleagues present a faster way to align two LiDAR scans of the same place, in this 2026 paper. Registration matters for robots and self-driving systems, but classic methods match features between scans and then filter mistakes with a slow sampling algorithm; matching fails when scans only partly overlap. Their network skips both steps. It lets each scan summarize itself into a shared set of soft points, weighted summaries of the whole cloud, and computes the alignment directly from the pairings.

Because an attention mechanism emphasizes the parts the two scans share, the soft pairings stay reliable even when shapes are incomplete. Tests on four real-world datasets, from indoor rooms to road scenes and laser surveys, showed the method matching the accuracy of established approaches while running much faster. The authors offer it for robots that must locate themselves quickly in messy environments.
plos-pone-0355392:
Alexis Slentz and colleagues test in 2026 a lab material widely used to pull phenolic compounds out of natural water samples. They ran a well studied river fulvic acid through columns packed with the material and tracked what stayed and what left. Advanced mass measurement let them see changes at the level of single molecular types.

More material in the column removed most phenolics, but it also removed much of the wider carbon pool. What remained shifted toward less aromatic, lighter forms.
