By then the bans on timber and diamond exports had already ended. Liberia had joined the Kimberley Process, the scheme that certifies rough diamonds as conflict-free.

The text renews the arms ban and the travel ban for twelve more months. States must report every arms delivery made under the allowed exceptions. The Council notes with concern how little progress had been made on freezing a former president's assets. The expert panel stays on until 20 June 2008 to track the sanctions and the diamond controls.
un-sc-res-1892:
The Council took formal action on Haiti in Resolution 1892, adopted on 13 October 2009. New senators had just been elected with United Nations help. Security had improved a little but stayed fragile. Food, fuel, and money crises abroad kept pressing on daily life. Prisoners waited years for trial in crowded jails.

The Council extends the stabilization mission, called MINUSTAH, until 15 October 2010. It will field up to 6,940 troops and 2,211 police. Its force shape shifts to match needs on the ground until Haitian police can take more weight. The mission backs the 2010 elections and keeps training and vetting police. Courts, prisons, and border control all need the same steady help.
un-sc-res-192:
Three months after it was created, the Cyprus peacekeeping force received its first renewal. A report from the Secretary-General held that keeping the force for three more months would be useful and advisable. Resolution 192 was adopted unanimously on 20 June 1964.

The Council expressed deep appreciation to the Secretary-General for his work in carrying out the Cyprus resolutions. Thanks also went to the states that had contributed troops, police, supplies, and money to the force. Resolutions 186 and 187 were reaffirmed. All member states were called on to comply with them. The force's stationing was extended for three more months, ending on 26 September 1964. It was the first of many such renewals for the mission.
un-sc-res-392: Under number 392, the catalog lists a Security Council resolution dated to 1976 in the official UN record. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-492: One of the Council's formal texts, Resolution 492 is carried in this catalog under 1981. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-92:
Fighting broke out in and around the demilitarized zone between Israel and Syria in the spring of 1951, and Resolution 92 was the Security Council's response. Adopted on 8 May 1951 by ten votes to none, with the Soviet Union abstaining, it deals with the Israel-Syrian General Armistice Agreement of 20 July 1949.

The Council calls on everyone in the area to stop fighting at once. It reminds both sides of their duties under Article 2 of the UN Charter, under earlier Resolution 54, and under the armistice deal itself. The cease-fire order had come from the acting head of the UN truce team in Palestine on 4 May, and the resolution backs that order with the full weight of the Council.
un-sc-res-992: An official UN record text, Resolution 992 is catalogued in this library with a 1991 date. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 1292, adopted on 29 February 2000, extends the mandate of MINURSO, the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, until 31 May 2000. The Council restates its support for the Settlement Plan and a free, fair and impartial referendum. It notes concern that a smooth, agreed implementation may not be possible. It backs the Secretary-General's plan to have his Personal Envoy consult the parties about the obstacles. The Envoy is to explore ways to an early, durable and agreed settlement.

East Timor was counting down to freedom when Resolution 1392 passed on 31 January 2002. The vote in the Council was not split. A UN team, UNTAET, ran the land for the time being. It helped local leaders build a new state from scratch. The big day was set for 20 May 2002.

The Council kept UNTAET in place up to that date, and no past it. It praised the hard work done by UN staff and by the Timorese. It also looked past the big day. A smaller UN team would stay on to help the new state stand on its own feet.

Sierra Leone's giant UN mission was told to start packing in 2003. On 18 July, the Council adopted Resolution 1492 without dissent. UNAMSIL had grown into one of the largest peace forces on Earth. It had ended the country's civil war by then. The Secretary-General's June report set out the exit paths. War in nearby Liberia still threatened the region.

The text backs his middle path, a modified status quo drawdown. The force would pull out by December 2004. Plans for a small leftover presence are welcomed as well. Key benchmarks for each phase will be watched with care. The Secretary-General must report at each phase's end. The exit thus hinged on Sierra Leone's own police and army standing ready.

Eastern Congo's militia war frames Resolution 1592, adopted on 30 March 2005. Armed groups in North and South Kivu and Ituri kept fighting, with abuses against civilians. A militia attack on MONUC on 25 February 2005 had been condemned, and militia leaders were arrested. The transitional government was preparing elections under the 2002 Global and All-Inclusive Agreement, but state authority in the east stayed weak.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the UN Mission, MONUC, until 1 October 2005. It confirms MONUC may use all necessary means, including cordon-and-search tactics, to stop attacks on civilians and break up illegal armed groups. It presses the transitional government to integrate the army and police, pay and supply them, and disarm fighters with MONUC's help. It demands that Uganda, Rwanda, and Congo stop their territory being used to break the arms embargo. Zero tolerance on abuse by UN personnel is reaffirmed.

Resolution 1692, adopted on 30 June 2006, reshapes the UN presence in Burundi as the country exits a long transition. Burundians had completed a peaceful transfer to an elected government, and talks with the last rebel movement, the Palipehutu-FNL, were moving toward a ceasefire. The mandate of the UN operation there, ONUB, was expiring the next day.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended ONUB until 31 December 2006. It also prolonged permission to shift troops temporarily from Burundi to the Congo mission, up to one infantry battalion, a military hospital, and fifty observers. Finally, it welcomed plans for a smaller integrated UN office to replace the peacekeepers once their work ended.

Liberia's remaining sanctions are renewed by Resolution 1792, adopted on 19 December 2007. The timber measures had already been lifted, and the diamond measures were terminated after Liberia joined the Kimberley Process and built internal controls. A forestry reform law was in force. The expert panel still found too little progress toward the conditions for ending the arms and travel measures.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms embargo and travel ban for 12 months. It keeps exemptions for vetted Liberian security forces. Notice must go to the Sanctions Committee when exempt arms are delivered. The asset freeze under Resolution 1532 (2004) stays in force, with concern at the lack of progress on it. The Panel of Experts is extended until 20 June 2008, to report by 1 June 2008. Any measure can be reviewed at the government's request once it reports the conditions met.

Haiti's stabilization mission is extended at strength in Resolution 1892, adopted on 13 October 2009. Senate elections and constitutional reform had advanced governance, but security stayed fragile, hurricane damage and the food, fuel, and financial crises strained the country. Most prisoners sat in pretrial detention. A former United States president had been appointed UN Special Envoy for Haiti.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends MINUSTAH's mandate until 15 October 2010. It fixes its strength at up to 6,940 troops and 2,211 police, endorsing the Secretary-General's advice to hold force levels while adjusting the configuration. MINUSTAH must support the political process and the 2010 elections, help reform the Haitian National Police under its reform plan, and patrol border areas against trafficking. It must back justice and prison reform and run community violence reduction and quick-impact projects. The Council also backs the Special Envoy's work on jobs, services, and investment.

Three months after creating the Cyprus force, the Council voted to keep it longer. On 20 June 1964, it adopted Resolution 192 without dissent. The Secretary-General judged that three more months would be useful and wise. The Council thanked the states that sent troops, police, supplies, and cash.

The text restates the founding decisions of March 1964. It calls on all member states to comply with them. It then extends the force's stay to 26 September 1964. Brief repeats like this became the pattern for Cyprus. No side wanted the peacekeepers gone while the island's feud stayed unsolved.

Catalogues often misfile this one under Bahrain. The text names a Himalayan kingdom instead. Bhutan had long kept itself apart from world bodies. In 1971 it chose to step forward. Resolution 292 was passed with no votes against on 10 February 1971. The Council met for the 1566th time that day.

The members backed Bhutan's bid in full. They told the General Assembly to admit the kingdom. The Assembly did so that fall. Bhutan came in as a landlocked state between India and China. Its kings ruled with care, opening the country at a slow pace. This short text marks the moment that closed kingdom took a seat among nations.

Schoolchildren in Soweto marched against racial discrimination on 16 June 1976, and South African police shot at them. Killings and wounding of Africans followed across South Africa. African states brought the facts to the Council. Resolution 392 was adopted by consensus three days later, on 19 June 1976.

The Council strongly condemned the South African government. It had turned to massive violence against the African people, including schoolchildren and students. The Council expressed deep sympathy for the victims. It restated that apartheid is a crime against the conscience and dignity of mankind. Apartheid was also called a serious disturbance to world peace. The struggle of the South African people to end it was recognized as legitimate. South Africa was told to end the violence and take urgent steps to abolish apartheid.

A Caribbean island state sought its United Nations seat in the autumn of 1981, soon after independence from Britain. Resolution 492, adopted unanimously on 10 November 1981, deals with the application of Antigua and Barbuda. The Council examined the application. It then recommended to the General Assembly that Antigua and Barbuda be admitted to membership in the United Nations. That single recommendation is the whole text of the resolution.

Fighting broke out in and around the demilitarized zone between Israel and Syria in May 1951. The zone had been created by their armistice agreement of July 1949. A cease-fire order from the acting chief of staff of the Truce Supervision Organization, issued on 4 May, had not stopped the fighting. Resolution 92 was adopted on 8 May 1951.

The Council noted the outbreak with concern. It called on the parties, and on the people in the areas concerned, to stop fighting at once. Both sides were reminded of their duties under the Charter. Article 2, paragraph 4, which bans the threat or use of force, was named. Their duties under the armistice agreement and under the Council's earlier resolutions on Palestine were also recalled. The short text is a cease-fire call, issued while guns were still firing in the zone.

Sanctions on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, made up of Serbia and Montenegro, blocked its ships on the Danube in 1995. The Iron Gates locks on the river needed repairs. While the locks on the right bank were being fixed, river traffic faced a problem. Resolution 992, adopted unanimously on 11 May 1995, opens a narrow gap in the sanctions for that repair work.

The Council allowed Yugoslav-flagged or Yugoslav-controlled vessels to use the Iron Gates I locks on the left bank. The permission lasted only while the right bank locks were under repair. Romania, helped by European sanctions monitors, had to watch the traffic strictly. Cargoes would be inspected, and any vessel caught breaking the sanctions would be turned away. The exemption would end at once if the sanctions committee reported a proven violation. The Danube Commission was to report when the repairs were done.
vincent-of-lerins-the-commonitory-of-vin:
How can believers tell true doctrine from new error? Vincent of Lerins answered with a famous rule: hold what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all. His Commonitory sets out that test for orthodoxy. It appears in the 1892 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Tradition, for Vincent, works like a compass when novel teachings claim the Church's name. He allows real growth in understanding, so long as the faith itself stays the same in kind. Every later age has quoted his rule, Catholic and Protestant alike. Short and sharp, the book remains the best one-volume guide to the idea of doctrinal continuity. Its calm logic still settles, and stirs, arguments.
vinogradoff-villainage-in-england-1892:
Vinogradoff published Villainage in England in 1892, the book that made his name. He was a young Russian scholar who came to England and mastered its manorial records as few Englishmen had. His subject was the villeins, the unfree peasants bound to the manor, whose true legal state was then disputed.

Working from the manor rolls themselves, he showed that villein tenure had firmer customary protection than the lawyers' theory admitted. The rolls revealed peasants buying, selling, and inheriting land under the lord's court for generations. The book was a doctoral bombshell: it rewrote the history of the unfree peasantry from primary evidence. Medieval studies in England were remade by its method. Serfdom's England stands documented at last, in the records of the manors where the villeins themselves appear.
wells-southern-horrors-1892: Southern Horrors, Lynch Law in All Its Phases, Ida B. Wells's 1892 exposé. The lynching horror. This book preserves that classic. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it.
what-is-phrenology-with-addresses-delive: What is Phrenology, 1892, the institute addresses. The files keep it safe. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it.
white-steps-to-christ-1892:
Ellen G. White wrote Steps to Christ in 1892, a small devotional book that outgrew every other Adventist title. White, the prophet of Seventh-day Adventism, guides the reader step by step: God's love, the sinner's need, repentance, faith, prayer, and growing into a life like Christ's. The chapters are short and warm.

Millions of copies in many tongues made it the most widely read book of her movement. New believers still receive it as a first handbook of the spiritual life. Its plain path from guilt to peace explains its reach far beyond Adventist homes.
wollstonecraft-vindication-1792:
Mary Wollstonecraft published A Vindication of the Rights of Woman in 1792 in London. Wollstonecraft wrote in the heat of the French Revolution's debates on rights. She argued that women are not naturally weaker in mind than men, only denied a real education.

She demanded schools where girls learned beside boys and women could earn their own living. Weakness and silliness in women, she said, came from training that made them ornaments, not partners. The book answered Rousseau and other writers who praised that training. It is widely read as the founding text of feminism, and its call for equal schooling still drives debate.
workshop-on-electronic-texts-proceedings: The 1992 Workshop on Electronic Texts gathered digital pioneers in Washington. E-texts were new. The Tower library holds the proceedings. It dreamed digital. Scholars met. Texts flowed. Future seeded. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
wright-man-and-glacial-period-1892:
G. Frederick Wright, an American rock scholar and priest, wrote this big plain book on man and the ice age in 1892. He had roamed the ice beds of America and dug in the gravel claims of the west. The book tells the whole tale for the lay reader of his day.

Wright sets the ice sheets and their melt in place, then fits stone age man in the frame. He backs claims for a great age of man in America that most peers soon set aside. The book marks the high tide of the deep age case in the United States.
yeats-countess-kathleen-1892:
The Countess Cathleen, Yeats's verse drama of 1892, was a founding play of the Irish dramatic revival. In a famine-stricken Ireland drawn from folk tale, demons walk the country buying souls for gold, and the starving sell.

Countess Cathleen, a great lady of the old order, sells her own soul to ransom her people's back, and heaven must judge the bargain. The play stirred controversy: clergy attacked its theology while nationalists claimed it as a parable of Ireland. Yeats revised it for years. In print here in its revised text, it shows the revival beginning in poetry and legend.
zola-downfall-1892:
Chatto and Windus issued The Downfall in a new revised edition in 1893. The title page names Ernest A. Vizetelly, war correspondent in 1870 and 1871, as translator. Part one runs from the Rhine to the Meuse, with maps supplied.

The Franco-Prussian War of 1870 destroys an empire across these pages. Common soldiers live the march to Sedan, the emperor's capture, and the fall of Napoleon the Third. History arrives as mud, hunger, and fear for men on the ground. Vast in scope, the 1892 novel forms the shattering peak of the Rougon-Macquart set. Many readers rank it with the greatest war novels ever written.
